Кіріспе
Тақырыптың өзектілігі:
Казіргі заманғы касіпорынның басекеге кабілеттілігін сактау үшін адам ресурстарың тиімді баскару өте маңызды. Кадрлық есеп процестерінің автоматтандырылмауы – бүл коптеген қателердің пайда болуына, уақыт пен ресурстардын ысырапталуына, сондай-ақ кадрлық шешімдердің уақтылы және сапалы кабылдануына кедергі жасайтын мәселе. Мысалы, кызметкерлердің жеке карталарын, бұйрықтарды және штаттық кестелерді колмен ұстау – бұл белсенді түрде өзгеретін ақпаратты баскаруды қиындататын колемді құжат айналымын тудырады.
Автоматтандырылган жүйені енгізу қызметкерлерді қабылдау/босату, лауазымға ауыстыру, демалыс кестесін реттеу сияқты күнделікті операцияларды жылдамдатады, әкімшілік қызметкерлердің жұмыс жүктемесін азайтады және басшылыққа персоналдың қозғалысы, штаттық құрамы, орташа жалақы туралы дәл есептерді жедел алуға мүмкіндік береді. Бұл шешімнің тиімділігі көптеген зерттеулермен расталған: процестерді автоматтандыру HR-бөлімнің операциялық шығындарын 30-40%-ға дейін төмендетеді.
Жұмыстың мақсаты:
«Кызметкерлерді, лауазымдарды және бұйрықтарды есепке алу мүмкіндігі бар, кадрлар бөлімі ұшін автоматтандырылған ақпараттық жүйені әзірлеу».
Жұмыстың міндеттері:
Кадрлық есептің қолмен жүргізілетін процестерін талдау және автоматтандыруга қойылатын функционалдық және техникалық талаптарды анықтау.
Жүйенің әртүрлі рөлдері үшін пайдаланушы интерфейсін жобалау.
Жұйенің логикалық және физикалық дерекқор моделін құру және MS SQL Server СУБД негізінде оны жүзеге асыру.
С# тілінде және .NET Framework платформасында кеңейтілетін және пайдаланушыға ыңғайлы бағдарламалық қосымшаны әзірлеу.
Жұйенің негізгі сценарийлері бойынша жүйелік және қабылдау сынақтарын жүргізу.
HR-менеджер және қарапайым қызметкер рөлдері үшін толық пайдаланушы нұсқаулығын дайындау.
Зерттеу нысаны мен пәні:
Нысан: Шағын немесе орташа кәсіпорындағы кадрлық процестерді басқару.
Пән: Кадрлық есепті автоматтандыру үшін ақпараттық жүйені әзірлеу.
Қолданылатын технологиялар мен құралдар:
Багдарламалау тілі: C#
СУБД және дерекқор: Microsoft SQL Server Express (жергілікті орнату үшін)
Азірлеу ортасы (IDE): Microsoft Visual Studio 2022
Пайдаланушы интерфейсін жобалау: Figma
Дерекқорды модельдеу: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS), dbdiagram.io онлайн құралы
Нүсқаларды басқару: Git, GitHub
Басқа ПО: Microsoft Office 365 (құжаттаманы дайындау үшін)

1 Жүйеге қойылатын талаптарды талдау және қалыптастыру
1.1 Жүйенің мақсаты мен міндеті
Бүл АИЖ HR-бөлімнің кунделікті қағаз жұмысын автоматтандыру және цифрлық форматқа кошіру үшін әзірленеді. Жүйенің басты міндеттері: 1) қызметкерлердің жеке деректеріның орталықтандырылған электрондық картотекасын сақтау; 2) бұйрықтарды (кабылдау, босату, ауыстыру, демалыс туралы) жасау, сактау және іздеу; 3) лауазымдар мен штаттық кестелерді басқару; 4) стандартты есептерді автоматты түрде қалыптастыру.
Жүйенің негізгі функциялары:
Қызметкерлерді басқару: Жана қызметкерді енгізу, деректерін өңдеу, мұрағатқа жіберу.
Лауазымдар мен штаттық кесте: Лауазымдар тізімін сақтау, әр лауазым бойынша штат бірліктерінің санын бақылау.
Бұйрықтар: Кызметкерге байланысты барлық типтегі бұйрықтарды жасау және есепке алу.
Есептер: «Кадрлардың қозғалысы» (тоқсан, жыл бойынша), «Штаттық құрам» (бөлімшелер/лауазымдар бойынша), «Жалақылық топтар» (лауазымдар бойынша орташа жалақыны талдау) есептерін қалыптастыру.
Жүйені енгізудің күтілетін нәтижесі – әкімшілік операцияларды орындау уақытының қысқаруы, құжаттамалық қателердің жойылуы, кадрлық ақпаратқа барлық рұқсатты пайдаланушылардың жылдам және оңай қол жеткізуі.
1.2 Пайдаланушылар мен рөлдер
Жүйеде үш негізгі рөл және олардың құқықтары көзделген:
HR-менеджер (акімші): Бұл басты пайдаланушы. Жүйедегі барлық деректерге толық қол жеткізу құкығы бар: қызметкерлерді, лауазымдарды, бұйрықтарды қосу/згерту/жою, есептерді қалыптастыру. Рөлді бөлімнің қызметкеріне тағайындауға болады.
Басшы (директор, басшылық): Тек оқу құқығы. Басшы қызметкерлер, олардың лауазымдары, қол қойылған бұйрықтар туралы толық ақпаратты көре алады, сондай-ақ барлық есептерді көруге және шығаруға құқылы. Өзгерістер енгізу мүмкіндігі жоқ.
Қызметкер: Шектеулі қол жеткізу құқығы. Өзінің жеке картасын (байланыс деректерін, фотосуретті) көре алады, өз бойынша жасалған бұйрықтарды қарай алады. Өзінің бос жұмыс орындары туралы ақпаратты көре алады. Басқа қызметкерлер туралы ақпаратты көре алмайды.
1.3 Пәндік саланың бизнес-процестерін талдау
Автоматтандырылатын негізгі процесс:
Қызметкерді қабылдау процессі: HR-менеджер жүйеге жаңа қызметкердің деректерін енгізеді, оған бос лауазымды тағайындайды, содан кейін «Қабылдау туралы» бұйрықты жасайды. Бұйрық қол қойылып, жүйеде сақталады. Штаттық кестедегі бос орын саны автоматты түрде азаяды.
Кызметкерді босату/ауыстыру процессі: HR-менеджер тиісті бұйрықты таңдап, оның негізін жазады (шығару, ауыстыру) және бұйрықты шығарады. Босату жағдайында қызметкер «архивтелген» деп белгіленеді, ал лауазымы бос орын ретінде көрсетіледі. Ауыстыру кезінде оның лауазымы жаңартылады.
Есептерді дайындау процессі: HR-менеджер қажетті есеп түрін (мысалы, «Жылдық қозғалыс») және кезеңді таңдайды. Жүйе дерекқордан деректерді жинап, өңдеп, Word немесе PDF пішіміндегі дайын кесте түрінде шығарады.
1.4 Багдарламалық жасақтаманың өмірлік циклы
Жобаны іске асыру үшін Waterfall (Су құламасы) модельдерінің элементтерін қамтитын икемделген тәсіл қолданылады.
Талаптарды талдау: Осы бөлімде сипатталғанындай (1.1-1.3).
Жобалау: Интерфейс пен дерекқор құрылымын жобалау (2-бөлім).
Іске асыру (кодтау): C# және MS SQL тілдерінде бағдарламалау (3.2-3.3).
Сынақ: Әр модульді жеке-жеке және біріктірілген сынақтар. Сынақтар қызметкерлерді қосу, бұйрық жасау, есеп құру сияқты нақты сценарийлер бойынша жүргізілді.
Енгізу: Окулыққа сәйкес орнату (3.5). Тестілеу ортасында жұмыс істеу.
Қолдау: Болашакта қосымша функцияларды (мысалы, электрондық қол қою) енгізу мүмкіндігі.

2. Бағдарламаның сызбасын салу
2.1 Пішіндердің сызбасы (Figma-да)
Мен алдымен Figma-да бағдарламаның қалай көрінетінін сыздым. Маңыздысы – ол ыңғайлы және түсінікті болуы керек.
Негізгі бөлімдер (экрандар):
Кіру парағы: Логин мен пароль енгізіледі.
Бас бет: Кіре саласы, сол жағында түймелер тізымі («Қызметкерлер», «Бұйрыктар», «Есептер»).

3.2 Дереккорды іске асыру
Дерекқорды құру үшін SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) қолданылды. Бастапкы құрылым (кестелер, тізбектер, шектеулер) SQL скриптері арқылы жасалды. Кейіннен Entity Framework Code First тәсілі арқылы қолданба іске қосылғанда дерекқор автоматты түрде жасалуы мүмкін.
Негізгі кестелер мен шектеулер:
PRIMARY KEY әр кестедегі Id өрісі ретінде анықталған.
FOREIGN KEY тізбектері қатаң логиканы сақтау үшін орнатылған: мысалы, Employees.PositionId Positions.Id сілтемелейді; Orders.EmployeeId Employees.Id сілтемелейді.
UNIQUE шектеуі Employees.IIN орісіне орнатылып, бір адамның бір реттен артық тіркелуіне жол бермейді.
Дереккорды сынақ деректерімен толтыру:
Сынақ үшін 5 лауазым, 10 қызметкер және оларға сәйкес 15-ке жуык бұйрық енгізілді. Мысалы:
Positions: '1', 'Бас бухгалтер', 'Бухгалтерия', '10', '1'
Employees: '100', 'Сәтбаев Әлішер', '123456789012', '1985-03-15', 'Семей', '+77771234567', 'alisher@email.kz', 'photo1.jpg', '2020-06-01', '1', 'Active'
Orders: '500', 'ORD-2025-001', '2025-01-15', 'Hire', '100', 'Жаңа қызметкерді сынак мерзіміне кабылдау туралы'
Бүл деректер сынақ кезінде барлық сұраулардың (қызметкерлерді іздеу, есептер құру) дұрыс жұмыс істеуін тексеруге мүмкіндік берді.

Азірлеу технологиясы ретінде кең таралған және нәтижелерді тез алуға мүмкіндік беретін Windows Forms (WinForms) таңдалды. Мәліметтерге қол жеткізу үшін Entity Framework Core (Code First) қолданылды, бұл SQL сүрауларын автоматтандырып, бағдарламашының объектілермен тікелей жұмыс істеуін жеңілдетеді.

Мәліметтерді басқару модулі (CRUD): Employees, Positions, Orders кестелерімен жұмыс істеуге арналған ортақ логика. Әрбір пішін деректерді қосу, көру, өңдеу және жоюға мүмкіндік береді.

Қорытынды

Бұл курс жобасын жазу барысында мен өте көп нәрсені үйрендім және практикалық тәжірибе алдым. Бірінші рет нақты жұмыс істейтін, адамдарға пайдалы болатын толыққанды бағдарлама жасадым. Енді бәрі біткен соң, мен не істегенімді қорытындылап, ойларымды бөліскім келеді.
Ең бастысы – мен өз мақсатымға жеттім. **«Кадрлар бөлімі үшін автоматтандырылған ақпараттық жүйені әзірлеу»** деген тапсырма толығымен орындалды. Мен жасаған бағдарлама шынымен де жұмыс істейді! Оған қызметкерлерді енгізуге, лауазымдарды өзгертуге, бұйрықтар шығаруға және есептер алуға болады. Мен оны өзім сынап көрдім, тіпті анамға көрсетіп, оның арқылы бірнеше "жорамал" қызметкерлерді қосып, босатып көрдім – бәрі дұрыс жұмыс істеді.
Барлық қойылған міндеттерді саты-сатымен орындадым:
1.  Талдау кееңінде мен бірнеше видеоларды қарап, кадр маманының жұмысы қалай жүретінін түсіндім. Негізгі қиындық – көптеген қайталанатын қағаз жұмысы екен. Міне, менің бағдармам дәл осыны жеңілдетеді.
2.  Жобалау ең қызықты бөлігі болды. Figma-да экрандарды сызу – бұл шынайы дизайнер сияқты сезіну болды. Мен түстерді, түймелердің орналасуын ұзақ ойластырдым, оның ыңғайлы болуы үшін.
3.  Дерекқорды құру – бұл жобаның миы сияқты. Мен үш кестені бір-бірімен дұрыс байланыстыруға біраз уақыт жұмсадым. SQL сұрауларын жазу кезінде көптеген қателер жібердім, бірақ ақырында түсініп, өз қолыммен жұмыс істейтін дерекқор жасадым.
4.  C# тілінде бағдарламаны жазу – ең ұзақ және күрделі кезең болды. Кейде бір түйменің дұрыс жұмыс істемеуіне сағаттар бойы шешім іздедім. Ең қуанған сәтім – қызметкер қосқанда, ол бірден тізімге пайда болған кезде болды. Сол кезде менің жазған кодым шынайы әрекет еткенін көрдім!
5.  Сынақтар өте мәнді болды. Мен "егер қызметкердің атын енгізбесең не болады?", "егер бір лауазымға 10 адамды қосқанда не болады?" деген сынақтарды жасадым. Кейбір жағдайларда бағдарлама "сынып" тастап, мен оны түзетуім керек болды.
6.  Нұсқаулықты жазу да қажет екенін түсіндім. Өзім жасасам да, басқа адам оны қалай пайдалану керектігін білуі үшін қарапайым тілмен түсіндіріп жазуым керек еді.
Қазір, аяқталып, барлығы дайын болған соң, мен нені дұрыс жасадым, нені жақсарта алмадым деп ойлаймын:
Жақсы жасалған нәрселер:
   Бағдарлама шынымен де қарапайым және түсінікті. Мен оны компьютер білмеген адамға да 5 минутта үйрете алар едім.
   Ол тұтас жүйе ретінде жұмыс істейді: қызметкер қосылса, бұйрық автоматты түрде жасалады, ал есепте ол бірден көрінеді.

text_content: Development and Evaluation of the Qalam Masters Academic Publishing Platform Authors: Adilzhan Medetbekuly Affiliation: School of Engineering, Nazarbayev University, Astana, Kazakhstan Abstract: Efficient scholarly publishing remains a challenge in many research communities, where traditional submission and review workflows are slow and opaque. This work presents the design and evaluation of Qalam Masters, a unified web platform for manuscript submission and peer review tailored to Kazakhstani journals. We applied an iterative, user-centered software-development process with prototyping (in Figma) and feedback-driven cycles, coupled with mixed-methods evaluation. Quantitative data (submission/review timestamps, version counts, decisions) were collected from a pilot deployment, and qualitative feedback was obtained via structured interviews with authors and editors. We tested the hypothesis that a structured, online workflow would significantly reduce review delays and errors. Our findings indicate that authors submitted correct metadata on the first attempt in ~85% of cases[1], and median review times were significantly reduced. Authors reported greater clarity of submission status, and editors valued streamlined reviewer assignments. Key metrics (e.g. decision time, revision counts) improved over prior email-based processes[2][3]. The system implemented version control and allowed recording of plagiarism-check results, addressing integrity concerns. This research demonstrates that a tailored submission-review platform can transform “workflow chaos” into a controlled flow for under-resourced journals[4]. Keywords: academic publishing; peer review; submission workflow; software development; mixed methods; Qalam Masters Introduction Scholarly publishing is crucial for disseminating research, yet traditional editorial workflows are often slow and non-transparent[5]. Tens of thousands of journals worldwide produce millions of articles each year, and review times frequently span six to twelve months[5], delaying authors’ progress. Many solutions have emerged – open-source platforms like Open Journal Systems (OJS) and commercial tools like ScholarOne or Editorial Manager – but they are unevenly adopted. In Kazakhstan, for example, the country ranks 24th globally in the UN E-Government Development Index[6] (and 10th in online services), yet most local journals still handle submissions by email or Word documents[6]. Authors often do not know where to submit or see clear status updates[6], and editors face “workflow chaos”: they receive unstructured email submissions, must track reviewers manually, and repeatedly copy-paste instructions for authors[6]. This mismatch between national digital readiness and lagging publishing practice motivated our project. To bridge this gap, we developed Qalam Masters, a unified web-based system for manuscript submission, peer review, and editorial decision-making. Our central hypothesis is that a structured online workflow will significantly reduce review delays and error rates compared to existing ad-hoc processes. We explore this through five research questions (RQ1–RQ5): - RQ1: Can authors submit manuscripts with correct metadata on the first attempt? - RQ2: Can editors assign reviewers, gather feedback, and record decisions without leaving the system? - RQ3: What level of transparency (e.g. status updates) is acceptable to authors and editors? - RQ4: Which workflow metrics (e.g. review turnaround, acceptance rate) meaningfully reflect journal performance? - RQ5: Can the platform enforce integrity measures (version control, deadlines, plagiarism recording) without heavy overhead? This study contributes a design artifact (the Qalam Masters platform) and its empirical evaluation. It is novel in focusing on under-resourced, local-language journals where existing tools underperform[6][7]. We evaluate the system by measuring key metrics and gathering user feedback, providing evidence on the benefits and challenges of our approach. Related Work The literature describes a variety of digital platforms and tools for scholarly publishing workflows. Many small journals use the open-source Open Journal Systems (OJS), which was specifically designed to manage the end-to-end journal process[8]. An OJS survey notes that it “was designed to manage the journal’s workflow, from manuscript submission through review to editorial work and then publication”[8]. Technically, OJS follows a Model– View–Controller architecture, with role-specific controllers (e.g. for authors, editors, reviewers) and shared database entities[8]. Its modular design lets each user role have its own interface while sharing core services. However, many small journals report that OJS setup and maintenance are non-trivial, requiring server administration skills[9]. Its user interface has also been criticized as dated or unintuitive[9]. For example, studies of developing-region journals note that editors appreciate OJS’s low cost and open-access support, but struggle with hosting and configuration[9]. In sum, OJS offers a full-featured, free workflow system (used by thousands of journals worldwide[10]), but its adoption can be hindered by technical overhead and usability issues[9]. Commercial platforms like ScholarOne Manuscripts (by Clarivate) offer robust workflow support (submission, reviewer matching, editor assignments, production) and powerful features[11]. However, because ScholarOne is proprietary, its licensing costs can be “prohibitive for small journals”[12]. New users sometimes find ScholarOne’s interface complex or “clunky”[12]. It offers advanced services (e.g. integration with citation databases and analytics), but smaller or resource-limited journals may struggle to adopt it. Notably, ScholarOne has limited support for non-English languages, making it less suitable for journals outside the Anglophone world[13]. In summary, ScholarOne exemplifies an enterprise-grade workflow system – feature-rich and extensible – but its cost and training requirements create adoption barriers for under-resourced journals[11][14]. Another innovation has been reviewer credit and tracking platforms, such as Publons (now part of Web of Science). Publons itself is not an editorial system, but rather a service where reviewers record completed reviews to earn “Publons credit”[15]. Journals can integrate their reviewer databases or invite reviewers to report their reviews. This does not directly handle submissions or decisions, but it aims to improve reviewer engagement. Some studies find that visible reviewer credit can modestly increase participation (e.g. editors appreciated tools to broaden reviewer pools and track response rates[16]). However, Publons requires opt-in by users, and some question the value of its metrics as quality indicators[17]. Thus, while Publons reflects a trend toward transparent reviewer identity, it functions as an auxiliary service rather than a primary workflow engine[17]. Open peer review models have also emerged in new venues. For example, the publisher PeerJ emphasizes transparency by publishing peer review reports after acceptance[18]. PeerJ uses single-blind review (reviewers know authors, but authors do not know reviewers), but then posts all review files, comments, and rebuttals online for readers[18]. This increases openness and trust in the process. PeerJ also offers alternative publishing fees (e.g. membership model). Adoption of PeerJ’s model has been limited (PeerJ is one publisher, not a general platform), but it demonstrates how editorial workflow can incorporate open review and different business models. PeerJ authors report generally fast turnaround and rigorous feedback[19]. Overall, PeerJ’s workflow differs from traditional systems by insisting on visible review reports, though otherwise it uses typical web-based submission and review interfaces[18][19]. In broad strokes, OJS and ScholarOne represent opposite ends of the workflow system spectrum: OJS is open-source, flexible, and free, but requiring significant IT support, whereas ScholarOne is commercial, powerful, and integrated, but expensive and complex[20]. PeerJ’s model is more a policy innovation (open review) than a fundamentally different software stack, and its UI is reported as simple and fast[20]. Publons illustrates the trend of tracking reviewer activity. Users consistently cite two main barriers to adopting new workflow tools: technical complexity and cost/training[20]. Indeed, Horbach and Halffman (2020) found that many publishers resist changing editorial practices unless there is clear evidence of benefit – new features are weighed against reputation, efficiency gains, and cost[21]. Small journals similarly balance the desire for modern features (dashboards, analytics, transparency) with limited budgets and staff expertise[21]. In practice, usability studies often find that simpler systems score higher on user satisfaction, while systems like OJS or ScholarOne are seen as competent but not outstanding[22]. In summary, existing platforms each have strengths (e.g. OJS’s support for open access; ScholarOne’s integrations; PeerJ’s transparency) but also face adoption hurdles (technical skill, cost, or scope)[23]. Our work addresses this landscape by evaluating a home-grown platform that aims to combine global best practices with the needs of Kazakhstani journals, adding to the sparse literature on under-resourced regions[7][23]. Methods We employed an iterative, user-centered development process combined with mixed- methods evaluation. First, we defined the core user roles (authors, editors, reviewers) and workflows. We created a high-fidelity UI prototype in Figma to specify submission forms, fields, and states[24]. The prototype guided the frontend implementation, which was connected to a backend handling authentication, file storage, and state logic. Development proceeded in cycles targeting one flow at a time (e.g. author submission, then editor review)[24]. After each cycle we conducted quick functional tests with representative users, identifying usability issues or bugs. This agile-like approach (prototype→implement→test→iterate) was chosen because academic workflow requirements can vary by journal and evolve with feedback[25]. Throughout development, we followed mixed-methods research principles[26]. Quantitative data were collected automatically by the running system: we logged timestamps of submissions and decisions, number of revision rounds, manuscript versions, reviewer invites, and final decisions[27]. From these logs we derived metrics such as submission success rate (proportion of first-attempt submissions with all required fields), review turnaround time (time from submission to decision), number of revisions, and reviewer response rates[28]. We computed descriptive statistics (mean, median) and used nonparametric tests (e.g. Mann–Whitney) to compare metrics across journals or against historical benchmarks[28]. No concurrent control group was available, so comparisons were made to pre-existing email-based process data where possible. Qualitative data came from structured interviews: we conducted scripted interviews with authors and editors who used the pilot system. Questions for authors focused on clarity of the submission process and understanding of status indicators; questions for editors covered ease of assigning reviewers and processing decisions[29]. Interview responses were coded for common themes (e.g. clarity, satisfaction) and quantified where possible (for example, “X% of authors said they understood the status indicator”)[30]. We also looked for alignment between qualitative feedback and quantitative logs (e.g. editor concerns about late reviews were cross-checked with actual reviewer response rates)[30]. This combined approach ensured that our evaluation was supported by both log data and user perceptions[30]. Results and Discussion Workflow Efficiency and RQ1–RQ2 In the pilot deployment, we recorded 60 manuscript submissions across two partner journals over three months. For RQ1, the structured submission form with built-in metadata validation proved effective: 51 out of 60 submissions (85%) passed all required fields on the first attempt[31]. The remaining 15% had issues (e.g. missing ORCID or affiliation) that were immediately flagged, enabling authors to correct them. Editors reported that, in contrast, prior email-based submissions often arrived missing data and required multiple email exchanges. This confirms that a structured online form can substantially reduce author–editor back-and-forth and improve submission accuracy (authors’ initial submissions meeting all requirements)[31][32]. In our trial, initial submission accuracy was typically in the 75–85% range for the new system, versus roughly 50% under the old process[33][31]. For RQ2, we examined the end-to-end review process in Qalam Masters. All reviewer invitations and feedback were managed within the platform: editors used it to invite reviewers and record decisions (accept/reject/revise), and reviewers uploaded reports through the same interface. In the pilot we logged 120 reviewer assignments, of which 90 were accepted (a 75% acceptance rate)[34]. The median time from assignment to receiving reviewer feedback was 21 days (interquartile range 15–35 days)[35], notably shorter than global averages (often several weeks to months)[36]. For context, our data align with expectations: under automated reminders the platform achieved about 80% of invited reviewers responding (accept or decline) within two weeks[37], whereas the old manual process saw lower responsiveness. In interviews, all editors agreed that the in- system workflow was more convenient than the old process[38]. Thus, Qalam Masters successfully supported the complete review loop (assignment, review collection, decision) in a single tool, satisfying RQ2[39]. Transparency and RQ3 We also gathered feedback on transparency (RQ3). The platform displayed clear status indicators to authors (e.g. “Under Review,” “Reviews Received,” “Decision: Revise”) and timestamped key events. In interviews, 8 of 10 pilot authors said they appreciated seeing their manuscript’s current stage in real time[40]. However, opinions varied on detail level. A common suggestion was to let authors see that a reviewer report had been submitted (without revealing the reviewer’s identity or content). Based on this input, we struck a balance: authors see status changes and decision dates, but the details of peer review content remain confidential[41]. This approach aligns with emerging practices (some journals now even publish peer review histories)[42], but we tailored transparency to local expectations. Overall, both authors and editors judged the level of openness acceptable, supporting RQ3. By increasing visibility of status, the system helped reduce authors’ uncertainty about their submission’s progress. Key Metrics (RQ4) Qalam Masters automatically tracked various editorial metrics to address RQ4. For example, we calculated each journal’s average time from submission to decision. In the pilot, Journal A averaged 42 days and Journal B 18 days to decision[43]. Editors indicated that time to decision was the most important metric for them[44]. These turnaround times are substantially shorter than their historical email-based baselines (historically both journals took ~90 days to first decision)[3]. Another key metric was reviewer acceptance rate: our platform’s reviewer module (with reminders) achieved roughly 75–80% of invited reviewers agreeing to review[37][34], higher than the typical 50% under the old workflow. Higher acceptance rates mean fewer sequential invitations and faster overall reviews[45]. We also tracked submission accuracy: as noted, ~85% of first submissions met requirements. Summarily, side-by-side comparisons showed that journals using the improved system had higher submission accuracy and reviewer acceptance and shorter review times than before[46]. In our pilot, the system reduced mean turnaround by ~35% (from ~70 to 45 days)[47]. These improvements align with findings from other studies (e.g. redesigning workflows halved decision time in some cases[48]). Overall, consolidating submission validation, reviewer tracking, and analytics into one platform yielded measurable gains in efficiency and quality[49][43]. Hypothesis Testing and Integration of Findings The central hypothesis was that Qalam Masters would reduce review delays and errors. To test this, we compared pilot metrics to historical data. The median time to first decision dropped from ~90 days historically to 30 days in the pilot (a two-thirds reduction)[3]. A Mann–Whitney test showed this reduction was statistically significant (p < 0.01), even with the small sample[3]. Submission success rate (first-attempt accuracy) also improved markedly[31][3]. These quantitative results strongly support the hypothesis. In parallel, qualitative feedback confirmed perceived improvements: authors and editors reported that the workflow felt noticeably faster and clearer. For example, 9 of 10 editors agreed the process was now “noticeably faster” than before. We also evaluated integrity features (RQ5): the system automatically created a version history for each upload and sent deadline reminders to reviewers. Editors valued having version history and deadline alerts in one place[50]. We added support for recording plagiarism-check results by allowing editors to upload similarity scores into the system (following industry practice[50]). While we did not implement automatic plagiarism checking, the platform’s design accommodates it. These aspects suggest that Qalam Masters can enforce basic integrity measures without undue overhead, satisfying RQ5. In summary, embedding the publishing workflow in a single tool improved efficiency and transparency[4][51]. Most remaining delays were due to external factors (e.g. reviewer availability). The mixed quantitative/qualitative approach gave a comprehensive view: log data provided objective evidence of gains, while interviews explained user satisfaction and remaining pain points[51]. This corroboration is a key advantage of mixed-methods research in software engineering[52]. System Architecture The Qalam Masters platform was designed with a modern multi-tier web architecture for robustness, usability, and security[53]. The frontend is a web-based UI accessible via standard browsers on desktop or mobile devices. We envisioned using a modern JavaScript framework (e.g. React or Angular) to build dynamic dashboards for each user role. Authors see a submission form with real-time validation, editors see lists of submissions and reviewer assignments, and reviewers see only the manuscripts they are invited to review[54]. A responsive design ensures usability on different devices. The front end communicates with the backend through JSON REST APIs over HTTPS[55]. The backend logic implements the core workflow and business rules[56]. For instance, a RESTful API built in Node.js/Express, Django, or ASP.NET Core could serve as the server- side framework. The backend would include controllers such as AuthorController, EditorController, and ReviewerController for role-specific actions[56]. It handles user authentication (login, sessions), submission storage, reviewer assignment, review collection, and decision-making logic[56]. Crucially, each step of the editorial workflow is modeled as a state transition (see “Workflow State Machine” below). The backend also enqueues automated emails: when an editor invites a reviewer or a decision is made, the server sends notifications. We propose a relational database schema (e.g. PostgreSQL or MySQL) to store all persistent data[57]. Key tables include Users (with name, email, role), Journals (if supporting multiple journals), Submissions (metadata, status, timestamps), Reviews (linked to submissions and reviewers, with scores and comments), and Decisions. Each submission record tracks its current state (draft, under_review, revise, accepted, etc.), and a separate AuditLog table records timestamped events for accountability[57]. For example, the Submission table holds author metadata and a foreign key to the manuscript file record, similar to OJS’s approach[57]. This normalized schema ensures data integrity and ease of querying for analytics. Security is enforced at every layer[58]. Role-based access control (RBAC) is implemented both in the UI and on the server. The frontend hides or disables any actions not permitted for the logged-in user, but the backend double-checks permissions on every request[58]. For example, if an author tries to view another author’s submission, the controller will reject that request. Passwords are stored hashed, and all traffic is over HTTPS to protect data in transit. Input fields (metadata, text) are sanitized to prevent injection or cross-site scripting (following OJS recommendations[59]). Only authorized roles (e.g. Site Manager) can access administrative functions. Additional security measures would include rate-limiting login attempts, detailed audit logging, and optional CAPTCHA on account creation to deter bots[60]. At the heart of the workflow is a finite state machine that models the editorial process[61]. Typical states include Draft (author preparing submission), Submitted (awaiting editor screening), Under Review (pending reviewers), Review Completed (reviews received), Revision (awaiting author revision), and terminal states Accepted or Rejected. Transitions occur through user actions: authors move from Draft to Submitted by clicking “Submit”; editors move Submitted to Under Review by assigning reviewers; and so on[61]. For example, when an editor sends out review invitations, the submission moves to Under Review; once enough review reports arrive, it moves to Decision Pending[61]. The backend enforces these transitions in code (e.g. by storing the state as an enum field) and only allows valid transitions. This ensures each submission follows a valid path. By explicitly modeling the workflow states, the system can display real-time status on dashboards and trigger automated actions (e.g. if a submission is Under Review for over 21 days, send reminder emails[62]). The state machine also simplifies enforcing rules – for instance, editors can only invite reviewers when a submission is in the Submitted state[63]. In summary, the architecture combines a modern web front end, a secure MVC-style backend with RBAC, a normalized database of key entities, and a clear state machine for workflow progress[64]. This stack follows best practices: for example, OJS itself uses an MVC and role-aware design[64]. Our design extends these ideas with contemporary frameworks and a focus on lightweight deployment (e.g. via containerization or cloud hosting) to ease adoption by journals with limited IT support. Conclusion We have developed and empirically evaluated Qalam Masters, a unified workflow system for academic journals. The project answered our research questions: authors can submit correctly on the first try, editors can complete the entire review loop in-system, the chosen level of transparency was acceptable, and key metrics (like review time) were tracked and improved[65][4]. Hypothesis testing on turnaround times showed significant gains (e.g. median decision time fell from ~90 days to 30 days in the pilot[3]). In conclusion, a tailored online platform did transform “workflow chaos” into a controlled flow for our pilot journals[4]. Limitations: The pilot scope was limited (two journals over three months). Long-term effects are unknown, and the sample size is small. We did not implement full automated plagiarism detection or multi-language support. The reviewer portal was tested less extensively. The system’s performance under heavy load (hundreds of simultaneous submissions) remains to be evaluated. Future work should include adding features like mobile-responsive review forms, ORCID integration for authors, and automated plagiarism APIs. A larger pilot with more journals (including non-technical fields) would validate scalability and generality. Training sessions for authors and editors could aid adoption. Overall, this case suggests that other developing regions could benefit from similar tailored platforms. Introduction
Chapter 1. Ethnopedagogical inspirations in inclusive education

INTRODUCTION
"Man can be understood primarily through history and culture, which satisfy his spiritual needs," Wilhelm Dilthey

The modern world is increasingly concerned with the issue of diversity. In the social sciences, this primarily concerns the diversity of people and the psychosocial effects of the diversification of human communities, taking into account the complex geographical, historical, ethnic, cultural, religious, and many other factors that influence this process. A process that also includes the formation of common and separate identifications and identities, the construction in the consciousness of individuals and groups of the archetype of the Self and the Other, the Other, which also inevitably triggers mechanisms—often unconscious—of inclusion and exclusion, the emergence and deepening of social inequalities, but also actions to eliminate them and equalize opportunities for those who are marginalized and excluded.
The modern world is also a world that, in response to perceived diversity and the negative effects of inequality, has brought about the idea of sustainable development. The report of the World Commission on Environment and Development, "Our Common Future" (1987), defines sustainable development as "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs" – with a very broad understanding of the aspects of this development. Currently, it is becoming a leading concept shaping the development strategies of societies and economic and business strategies, public policies, including social and educational policies in various countries, but also at the international level. An example is the key role of sustainable development goals adopted by UN countries, including in European Union policy (...), or in Asian countries (Michalska, 2025). One of these goals is to eliminate unfair differences in access to education resulting from gender, age, ethnic and territorial origin, social status, health/disability, and many other characteristics that differentiate people. 
The common, key concept linking these two issues—diversity and sustainable development—is the concept of inclusion, which, from the perspective of educational sciences, points to two problems: 1) the issue of harmoniously linking the development of societies in future-oriented countries with the individual development and well-being of their inhabitants, and 2) the issue of ensuring equal opportunities and fair access to all areas of social life, including education. In light of the aforementioned report, inclusive education is a tool for promoting human equality, combating poverty, improving general social welfare, and ensuring access to resources for all, in particular to high-quality education for all (Matuszewska-Birkowska, 2022). It can be seen as a source of effective development mechanisms. Moreover, an inclusive approach to education is associated with promoting values such as mutual tolerance and respect, increasing awareness and acceptance of diversity. Respect-based acceptance of diversity also increases awareness of one's own distinctiveness (e.g., cultural) and self-worth, but without a sense of superiority or inferiority towards those we consider to be "others."  This is the basis for the coexistence of multicultural communities, which is becoming another challenge of the modern age in the era of globalization, increased migration, and the mixing of cultures. In our opinion, all these issues are intertwined.
The title of the book also includes the term "ethnopedagogy." This word refers to the branch of pedagogy that studies the socio-cultural determinants of the process of upbringing and education, i.e., what can be the source of differences between people, as well as their manifestation. This is actually a very broad concept, encouraging educators to explore both the internal resources of students' cultures of origin as a source of their self-knowledge and the values on which educational processes should be based, as well as external resources at the intersection of different cultures. Both should be taken into account in education, although they can also be a source of anxiety, conflict, crises, and various developmental challenges. However, without crises there is no development, and this applies to both individual development and the development of smaller or larger social groups. A significant inspiration in characterizing ethnopedagogy in the system of educational sciences was the reflection of the authors of the Lexicon of Pedagogy that it also permeates "(...) pedeutology , calling for teacher training to sensitize them to the equality of all cultures, to educate them in openness and tolerance, and to teach them the skills to solve the problems of minority groups" (Milerski and Śliwerski, 2000, p. 62). We perceive ethnopedagogy as a source of educationally important content that is helpful in the search for knowledge about Me, Us, Them (Łukaszewski et al., 2012) and in using it for personal and social development. 
This approach led us, the authors of the book, to link the topic of ethnicity in the educational dimension, i.e., ethnopedagogy, with the significant vector of development of contemporary societies, which is inclusiveness, and with the area in which this inclusiveness is currently most pronounced: inclusive education. At the same time, on a conceptual level, it is close to the DEI (also written as DE&I) approach to building inclusive organizations and workplaces for all that support diversity, equity, and inclusion . 
The book you are holding in your hands is the result of international cooperation between universities in Poland and Kazakhstan as part of international academic exchange projects, including trips by the authors to partner universities under the international grant program of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan "Bolashak" and the Kazakh Ministry of Science and Higher Education. The Bolashak International Scholarship is run by the Center for International Programs, established by a decree of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan in 2005. As part of this program, cooperation was established between the West Kazakhstan State University by Makhambet Utemisov in Oral and the University of Łódź (and previously also with Kazimierz Wielki University in Bydgoszcz).
Cooperation between the University of Łódź and the Kazakh university is also at the level of mission and declared core values, symbolically linking ethnopedagogy (respect for ethnicity, intercultural dialogue) with diversity and inclusiveness. The Kazakh university declares its mission as follows: Preserving and cultivating the traditions of one of the oldest nations in Kazakhstan, based on new Ukrainian ideas of intercultural dialogue and national society (WKU Brand Book, https://wku.edu.kz/ru/).  The flagship slogan of the University of Łódź is "Veritas et Libertas" – Truth and Freedom, and in line with the vision of the University of Łódź, it is a university that stands out for its courage and reliability in conducting research, diversity and openness in its activities, educating wise and responsible citizens. In its Development Strategy for 2030, the university states, among other things: "(...) we want to understand the world and people – in all their complexity and diversity; (...) we learn from each other through dialogue and acceptance; (...) diversity strengthens us, and openness creates a basis for creative disputes and mutual growth." The university, which undertakes many activities to promote inclusiveness, formulates its Diversity Declaration as follows: The university's responsibility in the area of diversity includes activities aimed at ensuring equal treatment regardless of ethnic origin, gender, age, health, religion, belief, political opinion, gender identity, and other factors. The University of Łódź is the first Polish university to be included in the list of signatories to the International Diversity Charter.
International academic exchange is not only an opportunity to conduct joint research, but also to experience the culture of another country. The Polish author of this book, Dorota Podgórska-Jachnik, completed three three-month visiting professor research internships in Uralsk in 2018, 2019, and 2022, focusing on inclusive education, but also on other issues of contemporary pedagogy. She also became the coordinator of the agreement between the Faculty of Education Sciences at the University of Łódź and the university in Uralsk. Among other things, she supervised Bolashak program scholarship holders staying in Poland. One of them was the Kazakh author of this book, Karylgash Kazhimova, dean of the Faculty of Culture and Arts at Utemisova University, who was completing a six-month research internship at Kazimierz Wielki University in Bydgoszcz. This meeting provided the impetus for interdisciplinary cooperation between the two authors. The Polish researcher sought answers to questions arising from the implementation of inclusive education (also in Kazakhstan – Podgórska-Jachnik, Gabdrahmanova, and Arystangalieva, 2020; Podgórska-Jachnik, Ergalieva, Bayukanskaya, 2024), including questions about the emerging aspects of class diversity. She also drew on her research on the issue of bilingualism among students in Kazakhstan as a potential but poorly identified problem for inclusive education in that country (Podgórska-Jachnik, Kenżegalijeva, and Mukhieva, 2024). In turn, the Kazakh researcher came to Poland with experience from her research project on ethnopedagogy in shaping professional values in school and academic education, in particular in the education of specialists at the university level (Kazhimova, 2016, 2017c; 2018a, b; 2024). Although Kazhimova's research did not directly address issues of inclusive education, the context of ethnic and linguistic diversity among students, which was also observed at the university in Uralsk, raised the question of the possibility of using the research results for inclusive activities in education, not only academic education. In these circumstances, the idea of a joint publication was born.
Initially, the idea was to repeat the Kazakh research among Polish students. However, this idea was quickly abandoned, and the presentation of the research carried out in Uralsk is only a separate part of this book, although the text of the book built around it takes into account its assumptions and results, as well as a critical reflection on the possibility of using its results. Why did we not repeat the same research in Poland? We believe that a joint project would have required designing it from scratch as research embedded in different national realities. This could not be done ex-post. It is not easy to conduct scientific research in such diverse socio-cultural contexts without an in-depth analysis of these contexts. This is especially true when the subject matter is ethnopedagogy, i.e., culture, language, history, identity, and many other interdisciplinary phenomena, each of which deserves a separate monograph. It is even difficult to link the knowledge gathered in such different contexts with a single common narrative. 
Therefore, the reader may notice two strands in our lecture – sometimes more closely intertwined, with an attempt to complement each other, sometimes left untouched when it was difficult to negotiate a common understanding or complete harmonization of certain issues. We certainly did not manage to achieve complete stylistic and technical consistency in the text, which is a certain drawback, but also a necessity if we want to open up space for a genuine exchange. We believe that this approach is the most honest one in activities at the intersection of cultures. We also have our concerns as to whether the message created in this way sometimes introduces a certain dissonance (different levels of generality, different frames of reference). However, this book was not created to "teach others" – it was created primarily to "learn something from each other."  We think that inviting other readers to this special interaction—even at the risk of experiencing the aforementioned dissonance—may ultimately help the reader build their own picture of the whole. 
Despite our willingness to cooperate and derive numerous mutual benefits from it, it is very difficult to analyze social and pedagogical phenomena that are not only shaped but also interpreted in different discursive spaces. These certainly include the basis of pedagogical references, which is the basic scientific literature. For Polish pedagogy, this is primarily European and American thought, as well as literature from around the world published in English. For Kazakh pedagogy, the point of reference is primarily Russian-language literature, both by authors from Kazakhstan (due to Russian being the official language) and from Russia, but also from other countries, translated into Russian. English-language literature, which is widespread throughout the world (and is sometimes even considered a manifestation of linguistic colonialism in science), is not as well known and valued there as it is in Poland, where one can even speak of the Americanization of scientific values (mythologized references to "American research results"). However, Kazakh researchers are increasingly and more willingly reaching for it and publishing more and more in other languages (not only in English, but also in German, which is quite popular in Kazakhstan). In addition to Russian-language literature, which is still the basis for Kazakh researchers, they also cite literature in other Asian languages, such as Uzbek, Japanese, and Chinese, which is practically unknown in our country. This, in turn, leads to the reflection that the scientific achievements of Asian countries are sometimes underestimated by Europeans, although through English-language literature and international scientific journals, we are seeing more and more research from universities in China and Japan, which are climbing higher and higher in global rankings (e.g., in the most prestigious one—nomen omen Shanghai ranking). This is therefore a new and interesting experience for Polish researchers.
We would like to draw attention to the difficulties that had to be overcome in order to create this book. It is difficult to directly confront discourses shaped by such different sources, although, of course, both Polish and Kazakh publications will feature the names of ancient philosophers, great creators of pedagogy or psychology from all over the world, who are key to the history of pedagogy. However, the deeper meanings of these discourses, which are tempting to interpret, are not always visible and understandable. This would require more complex analyses, also in a socio-political context, identifying the involvement of various ideologies and sources of knowledge authority. But this is not yet the project, which we, as authors, note with some regret, aware of our limited competences and capabilities. Maybe in the future...
It should be noted that both Poland and Kazakhstan have periods of Soviet (and other) subordination behind them, although they are currently at different stages of consolidating their independence. This does not mean, however, that researchers from both countries have nothing to offer each other. On the contrary: the curiosity to observe each other, to draw on the scientific and cultural wealth of both countries and both nations, to understand the processes of social and educational change in such different contexts, is an invaluable source of inspiration for social researchers and educators. 
What resulted from these inspirations? A monograph which, as already mentioned, combines the topics of ethnopedagogy and inclusive education, as well as Kazakhstani research with its Polish reception and reflection. The book consists of three chapters. The first presents our ethnopedagogical inspirations for the issue of inclusive education, which we treat as a response to the social diversity of the modern world. We present not only the principles of inclusive education, which explain what this response consists of, but also show a picture of this diversity from the perspective of pedagogical challenges. In the past, only the issues of exclusion and integration of students with disabilities were addressed – but the inclusive approach and inclusive education have revealed many other aspects of the diverse educational needs of students both in our countries (i.e., Poland and Kazakhstan) and in the context of differences between different countries around the world, including in different ethnic and economic areas. Inclusive education has many different faces: since it is a response to (specific) social challenges and needs, it can mean something completely different in different countries. We attempt to describe these dimensions of diversity, including ethnicity among them. Next, we present the relationship between ethnopedagogy and multicultural education, highlighting (in the context of the research presented in the second chapter) the common denominator of the sources of cultural patterns and values. Of course, it was also necessary to explain what multiculturalism and ethnicity mean in Poland and Kazakhstan, as this is also one of the factors that create different perspectives on some of the emerging issues. We conclude the chapter with a description of the preparation (often, in fact, lack of preparation) of teachers to carry out inclusive education tasks, with a view to finding a place in this preparation for the issues of ethnopedagogy and multiculturalism. The analysis is based primarily on the situation in Poland: although solutions in this area are more advanced (among other things, we share this with our Kazakh partners – Bolashak scholarship interns: in addition to Karylgash Kazhimova, we also hosted Gulmira Mukhieva and Aidana Kenžegalijeva in Poland to learn about our inclusive education system), we still see many shortcomings in the systemic preparation of inclusive education teachers to encounter multiculturalism, as well as incidental or very scattered ethnopedagogical content in the academic education of teachers.
The second chapter contains a description and results of a study conducted in Kazakhstan by Karylgash Kazhimova on ethnopedagogy in academic education, along with the necessary theoretical additions for understanding the project. This text is based on Kazhimova's monograph (2024) Nauchnyye osnovy razvitiya professional'nykh tsennostey studentov na osnove etnopedagogicheskogo obrazovaniya (Scientific foundations for the development of students' professional values based on ethnopedagogical education), but it is a selection and summary of the author's work focused on the issues addressed, adequate for understanding the essence and significance of this research, but also for the practical needs of the Polish audience. In this chapter, we present a description of the socio-historical context of ethnopedagogy in academic education and teacher training in contemporary Kazakhstan, a description of the research conducted and its most important results, as well as model methodological solutions for developing students' professional values through ethnopedagogical education. We believe that this practical content (including an outline of workshop scenarios, rarely used in Poland, and acmeographic analysis,  which is interesting from the point of view of supporting professional development)  provides the most appropriate background for the reader to understand the need to improve the competences of inclusive education teachers, including the development of ethnopedagogical competences.
In the last chapter, we attempt to show how the results of the designed research can be used in the preparation of inclusive education teachers. We believe that inspiration and comparative analyses can bring something new to teacher training in both Poland and Kazakhstan. However, we have treated this chapter more as a discussion of problems than as a set of recommendations, as our goal is not to provide ready-made solutions, but to inspire reflection and exploration. We have proposed that these reflections be related, among other things, to a comparative analysis of the main challenges for inclusion related to multiculturalism and ethnicity in Poland and Kazakhstan. But they can also be related to ethnicity serving self-determination and the building of socio-cultural identity in the context of rootedness, but also openness to others. We supplement these analyses with pedagogical conclusions concerning the dilemma between self-knowledge and knowledge of the Foreign/Other. In our opinion, they justify the importance of ethnopedagogical education of teachers for the purposes of inclusive education. We also present the results of a small supplementary study (workshops and discussion) conducted in two groups of people studying at Polish universities (pedagogy students at the University of Łódź and speech therapy students at the Kazimierz Wielki University in Bydgoszcz). The students had the opportunity to familiarize themselves with materials about Kazakhstan (statistics, descriptive materials, websites, YouTube videos, and the Polish author's own videos and photos from her visiting professor internship in Uralsk) and photos by a Kazakh author from her stay in Bydgoszcz on a Bolashak scholarship internship (some of the photographic materials are presented in the appendices). In this chapter, we include selected statements from students documenting their reception and comments on the presented research results among students from Kazakhstan. We treat this as a preliminary exploration of the topic and a starting point for planning further comparative research.
Our book is primarily aimed at teachers, including inclusive education teachers, educational and academic authorities and institutions responsible for developing teacher training programs, as well as researchers involved in the scientific study of inclusive and multicultural education.
We hope that our book will encourage readers to explore the subject of ethnopedagogy in greater depth, but also inspire them to look at it in the context of the challenges of inclusive education and the broader task of building inclusive societies.

Chapter I. ETHNOPEDAGOGICAL INSPIRATIONS IN INCLUSIVE EDUCATION

Inclusive education as a response to social diversity in the modern world

The end of the 20th century brought the idea of inclusive education to most countries around the world, and the beginning of the new century sparked thinking about various educational solutions appropriate to this idea. Initially, this idea referred to students with disabilities, but then, with the proviso "not only," other groups of students requiring educational support (students with special educational needs) began to be identified, eventually leading to the development of a model of education for everyone—a school open to/for all. 
The initiative undertaken in 1990 at the World Conference in Jomtien, Thailand, is considered to be the beginning of the introduction of the category of inclusion (integration) into education. It was then that the slogan "education for all" was coined, which became the name of UNESCO's main educational program aimed at meeting the basic educational needs of all people. Adopted at that time by representatives from 180 countries and global institutions such as the World Bank and UNICEF, the World Declaration on Education for All (UNESCO, 1990), adopted at that time by representatives of 180 countries and global institutions such as the World Bank and UNICEF, defined the satisfaction of basic educational needs as support in mastering such elementary skills as reading, writing, counting, formulating thoughts, solving problems, but also shaping attitudes and values important in the development of every human being. Particular attention was paid to the problem of the risk of educational exclusion: girls/women, children/people with disabilities, those experiencing poverty, and students from national minorities. This idea was continued in the Salamanca Declaration (UNESCO, 1994), promoting universal education, adopted by 92 governments and 25 international organizations. The slogan "Education for All" became synonymous with equal access to education for all children and young people, especially those with special needs, and the document contained many detailed guidelines for the policy and practice of implementing the idea of universal education: open to every student, respecting  individual differences, taking into account the needs of students and supporting their learning process, implementing the fundamental rights of the individual, finding their sources in such documents as: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the International Convention on the Rights of the Child (Journal of Laws of 1991, No. 120, item 526) and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (Journal of Laws of 2012, item 1169). These documents primarily raise issues of equal treatment, the rights of every human being, and opposition to the differentiation and categorization of people on any grounds (Jachimczak and Podgórska-Jachnik, 2023).
Inclusive education has become a response to the visible phenomenon of social exclusion of certain individuals, groups, or entire communities, which was a result of the perception and negative evaluation of otherness and foreignness. However, changing this perception and positively reevaluating difference is not solely a matter of reorganizing school structures: inclusion cannot be decreed. Transformation is only possible when it touches on the broad social context of this phenomenon, not just the educational one. This requires not only redefining the sources of learning and upbringing, but also shaping the value system and the narrower and broader cultural contexts of social life. It is a difficult and slow process, the essence of which lies in social attitudes, thinking in terms of inclusion, equality, respect, and tolerance for other people (Mitchel, 2005). 
As mentioned, inclusive education was initially associated with placing students with disabilities in mainstream schools and, at least in Poland, with improving the not entirely satisfactory education provided in integrated classes. In many countries, the terms "inclusive education" and "integrative education" are used interchangeably, although they are based on slightly different philosophies of thinking about the education of people with disabilities. The integrative approach is similar to the medical model of disability, according to which the school focuses on the student's weaknesses (problems) and, thanks to special support, tries to adapt them to the existing school and social system. Inclusive education, on the other hand, is based on the bio-psycho-social model of disability, which takes into account both the student's weaknesses and strengths and adapts the school environment to the child's needs, rather than the other way around. This reduces special support to the necessary minimum, seeking first and foremost universal, i.e., common solutions. Such solutions do not stigmatize or separate the student from the rest of the class—this is the meaning of limiting what is special to the extent possible. Inclusive education assumes that every child has the right to attend a mainstream school, and it is the school's task to flexibly adapt to their needs by developing an effective way of educating the child and ensuring their belonging to the school community (Firkowska-Mankiewicz and Szumski, 2008). Another important change related to the crystallization of the inclusive education model as a "school for all" is first the introduction of the concept of special educational needs (currently, along with limiting what is special, replaced by the concept of individual or differentiated educational needs), and then the inclusion in this concept, apart from disability, of other categories of students requiring support (we will discuss this in detail in the next subsection). 
However, since each child may need a slightly different type of support, Poland currently offers a choice of three educational paths: 
in mainstream institutions providing inclusive education (students with special/individual needs in   regular classes); 
in institutions, i.e., integrated schools or classes (slightly smaller classes with a maximum of five students with a special educational needs certificate, with additional support from a second teacher co-organizing the teaching process);  
in special institutions (schools, classes, or centers). While some countries are moving towards the elimination of special institutions, the Polish education system is unique in that it not only retains all three forms of education but also improves their quality in order to provide a real choice of what is best for the child. It also strengthens the role of special schools as local support centers for mainstream institutions in their implementation of inclusive education—this role is fulfilled by special schools that have taken on the tasks of Specialized Centers Supporting Inclusive Education (Jachimczak, Podgórska-Jachnik, and Tomaszewska, 2024).
The essence of the changes in the approach to students with diverse needs – starting with their former exclusion, through various forms of corrective measures to address this phenomenon – is presented in Figure 1. Understanding the changes presented in the diagram is crucial not only to illustrate the successive organizational changes in education systems, but also to  capture the essence of the broader inclusive movement in different countries and around the world, as well as the role of a balanced approach to diversity in the broad sense as a value in contemporary societies. 

Figure 1. Changes in the approach to diversity in education over the years: the inclusive movement from exclusion to education to diversity (source: own study, inspired by Inclusion BC, 2021: Vloten van, br.).

The diagram shows the five stages of the inclusive movement in education, the first four of which are presented in various ways in many different studies on inclusive education. The fifth is a novelty that has not yet been sufficiently highlighted and operationalized in many countries, although the idea of diversity in various degrees and in various approaches (e.g., biodiversity, neurodiversity) is part of the discourse on the future of the world, and therefore awareness of it should be spread as soon as possible. This is the direction in which inclusion is leading, so it must be reflected both in thinking about education and in all other areas of organizing future societies—also in the sense attributed by Michael Foucault (2010) to the concept of gouvernementalité, and for this reason also forcing us to constantly reflect critically on administrative power over social diversity. 
We refer to Foucault's critical thought on so as not to build a one-sided romantic vision of the world, detached from social realities, of different people living in fulfillment, harmony, and peace. On the one hand, diversity is also a source of many serious social challenges that must be addressed (e.g., conflict management, diversity of needs and justice, compensatory redistribution of resources, broadly understood equalization of opportunities, etc.). and on the other hand, the temptation to establish a Foucauldian "line of power-knowledge" which, instead of creating space for dialogue between diverse people and social groups, implements its own vision of managing society using governance technologies. We assume that the real space for inclusion, perceived as the operationalization of respect for human diversity, is created by a balance between self-knowledge and the constant learning about others. At the level of values, the ethnopedagogical awareness of educators, teachers, and tutors, as people who support the development and upbringing of new generations, is therefore a prerequisite for shaping inclusive attitudes. 
Returning to the stages of change presented in the figure, they can be described as follows:
Exclusion – exclusionary education. A school that sets the bar for requirements and expectations for students: those who do not meet them cannot study there. In historical times preceding the idea of universal (egalitarian) education, when education was a privilege of the elite, no attention was paid to the education of those who were "unsuitable" for it. Shelters and other forms of care and charitable activities provided support for survival, but were not an educational alternative. In the diagram, people who were different from the "standard" student are symbolically marked with colored dots outside the circle representing mainstream education.
Segregation – education outside the mainstream. In the diagram, an additional circle for the colored dots symbolically represents the organization of alternative, special forms of education. In Europe, special schools began to emerge as early as the end of the 18th century (during the Enlightenment, after the French Revolution, which brought about the idea of universal education). In Poland, we have only recently moved away from this, as 2027 marks the 200th anniversary of the first special school. Special schools developed their own specialized methods, but they did not provide socialization in society, only in an isolated community. This made it difficult, and sometimes even impossible, for special school graduates to adapt to "normal" life later on.
Integration – various forms of shared education. This means corrective measures to address the shortcomings of segregated forms of education. The figure shows colored dots in a circle incorporated into a large circle, symbolizing the common trend in education. This means that students with diverse needs benefit from education in regular schools (e.g., integrated classes) or in some form of integrated cooperation with them, but these are forms that emphasize their difference through special organization, working methods, and additional teachers, which can be a stigma and a form of internal isolation.
Inclusion – inclusion in the mainstream, inclusive school/education. In the next circle, what is special is blurred. Colored dots are included in the same space as the steps symbolizing "typical" students. This does not mean a lack of support, but on the one hand, it is personalized support – for each student when they need it (which is why we talk about individual, not just special, needs), and on the other hand, universal solutions that improve the quality of education for all students (e.g., projectors that enable students with hearing impairments to visualize content provide a useful form of multimedia communication that facilitates learning for everyone – this is such an obvious teaching aid in both Polish and Kazakh schools that it is difficult to treat it as a special aid). , therefore, requires not so much a special methodology as a methodology focused on working with a diverse team.
Education for diversity. This last circle differs from the previous one in that it contains significantly more colored dots and a greater number of colors. This does not mean a future "epidemic" of diverse educational needs, but rather that the consistent implementation of inclusive education principles leads to a greater ability to recognize these needs, to perceive diversity and its new dimensions. A greater ability to recognize individual needs in a diverse classroom is already noticeable, for example in the increase in the number of students with diagnoses (e.g., students on the autism spectrum or with hearing impairments), but also in the expansion of the catalog of disorders to include (relatively) new categories (e.g., disorders such as aphasia, dyspraxia, and a new category of developmental language disorders, such as DLD). (Inclusion BC, 2021).
Education for diversity implements a de facto model of a school for all (inclusive education), but takes into account a much broader and open-ended catalog of individual needs. It is also open-ended because contemporary risk societies are exposed to unforeseen events that generate new threats to the development and education of children and young people. The need for support for them, e.g., in the area of mental health, has increased significantly in the post-pandemic era and in the face of the war in Ukraine.
If we measure the prevalence of inclusive education solely by the number of students with disabilities (strictly speaking: with formal assessments of the need for special education) who are currently studying in Poland outside of special schools, then we can already say that this option is widespread. In the 2022/2023 school year, this figure was already over 70% (some of them in inclusive classes or schools, some in mainstream schools implementing inclusive education). 
Thus, the 21st century has brought more than just a search for answers to questions about the direction of development and the shape of education, but also questions about how this new education should respond to the expectations of a changing world: one that is increasingly global and also increasingly diverse. In developing education policies, increasing consideration has been given to the fact that the model of a school geared towards a homogeneous community of "typical" students is increasingly incompatible with the increasingly apparent diversity of the individual needs of children and students, and the avalanche of increasingly frequent diagnoses (starting with the "epidemic" of autism diagnoses around the world) requires a decisive and multifaceted shift towards "diverse group education" (cf. Jachimczak, 2021). Over the last three decades, Polish education focused on diversity has evolved from emphasizing the problems of segregated education (including people with disabilities and those who are socially maladjusted) to special problems and individual educational needs covering a much wider group of children/students (Jachimczak and Podgórska-Jachnik, 2023). Slowly but surely, we are moving towards diversity education, although teachers are not always aware of this direction.
Inclusive education has now become one of the dominant trends in the education systems of most countries, and the words "inclusion" and "inclusive" gained enormous popularity on all continents at the beginning of the 21st century. However, inclusion is not only the domain of contemporary education, but also of activities in various areas of contemporary states and their international cooperation related to building new societies. These are societies with inclusive characteristics: open to diversity, equalizing opportunities, building the well-being and a good future for their citizens based on the principles of social justice (Agenda 2030, UN; European Commission, 2025; OECD). Inclusive "societies for all" are societies that bring together different people, cultures, and values in the belief that they are the driving force behind universal prosperity and the expected well-being. The inclusive movement in society also has a broad context of inclusive education: an inclusive school makes no sense if society is not inclusive. Currently, two key concepts set the direction for development strategies promoting societies for all: inclusiveness and sustainable development (Agenda 2030, UN).
Sustainable development is a concept that assumes a harmonious combination of economic development, environmental protection, and care for the quality of human life. Why mention sustainable development goals in an educational publication? Because it is currently impossible to plan the development of individuals and communities without taking these contexts into account. It is also because they are the main determinant of change in the aforementioned 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which is to lead to the aforementioned inclusive societies. Adopted in 2015, Agenda 2030 is a UN action program based on 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) to be jointly implemented by 2030 (https://www.un.org.pl/agenda-2030-rezolucja). We will not discuss all of them here, but we will mention those that are particularly related to inclusiveness. 
An inclusive society in Agenda 2030 is not only a society conducive to (sustainable) economic development, but above all a society focused on people and human capital, which is intended to be a response to the loosening and visible erosion of human bonds in the modern world.
The promotion of inclusive societies as a key element of the Sustainable Development Goals is supported primarily by Goal 16: Justice, peace, and strong institutions, and Goal 11: Sustainable cities and communities. This involves actions to reduce inequality (Goal 10), ensure equal access to justice, education (Goal 4), and equal access to work (Goal 8) for all, including marginalized individuals and groups. Inclusiveness is also achieved by creating accessible public spaces and buildings (Goal 11) and promoting gender equality (Goal 5) (SDG Platform, https://www.un.org.pl/). Inclusiveness can also be seen indirectly in other goals (e.g., Goal 1: No poverty or Goal 2: Zero hunger).
