In summary, inclusive education is a trend in education systems that seems irreversible, as it responds to the challenges of the present and the future. Inclusive education is part of a broader movement to build inclusive societies. This direction is included in the strategic documents of many countries, especially those that identify with the direction of change set out in the 2030 Agenda Sustainable Development Goals. This strategic positioning of inclusive education indicates that it is not an ephemeral, temporary solution, but a lasting transformation linked to national and international social policy.

Ethnicity among the dimensions of diversity and implications for ethnopedagogy and inclusive education
As the analyses presented show, diversity is a concept that is integrally linked to the concept of inclusion. Hence, the key task of inclusive education is to get to know children and students in all their diversity and variety of educational needs in order to optimize their learning in a school that is open to/for everyone. From the point of view of the coherence of inclusive education and the inclusive movement in an inclusive society, recognizing diversity in the classroom, personalizing the education process and providing the necessary support (a way of meeting individual developmental needs) introduces them to the realities of life and work in a diverse community and country that defines its own attitude towards diversity in the context of building and utilizing social, cultural, and human capital for its development. It is therefore a path, and often a condition, for the social participation of various vulnerable groups at risk of social exclusion, including educational exclusion. That is why it is so important to determine how many dimensions of diversity we may encounter at school.
In a positive sense, i.e., taking into account the strengths and the declared treatment of diversity as a resource in inclusive education, working with a diverse group means working with a class full of individuality, unique students, and their diverse experiences, in which the family environment and ethnic and linguistic roots play a fundamental role. 
Socially vulnerable groups (requiring support due to the risk of social exclusion) in Kazakhstan include pupils and students with disabilities, but not only. They also include people from low-income families, orphans and children left without parental care, pupils with immigrant status, and those living in rural areas. These situations are identified as causes of lack of support, social isolation, and other forms of alienation, discrimination, and marginalization (ERI, 2020).
In Poland, the list of students requiring slightly more support due to their individual educational needs is specified in the Regulation of the Minister of National Education. According to its content, the need to provide a student with additional support results in particular from: 
disability;
social maladjustment;
risk of social maladjustment;
behavioral or emotional disorders;
special talents;
specific learning difficulties;
competence deficits and language disorders;
chronic illness;
crisis or traumatic situations;
 educational failures;
 environmental neglect related to the living conditions of the student and their family, how they spend their free time, and their social contacts; 
 adaptation difficulties related to cultural differences or a change in the educational environment, including those related to previous education abroad.
This long list is important in terms of sensitizing teachers to the diverse needs of students, and it is not complete, because, as a rule, psychological and pedagogical assistance and basic educational support should be provided to every student who needs it (even on a situational basis). The title issue of this subchapter – the positioning of ethnicity in terms of student population diversity – is included in the last point of this list, although no ethnic or national groups are explicitly mentioned in the description. However, this catalog can ultimately only be of an indicative, auxiliary nature, as in the Polish education system, the basis for the support provided is ultimately to be a functional assessment, rather than a categorical assignment to any group, including the nosological label of a disorder. Nevertheless, the teacher's awareness of factors that pose a potential threat to meeting needs builds their social imagination and sensitivity to the diverse needs of students. It is for this purpose that the various categories of students requiring greater support in inclusive education, and even more: simply life support, have been compiled below, selected from several annual UNESCO reports on inclusive education in the world (Global Education Monitoring Reports – UNESCO). They show that among children with special needs, the following can and should be distinguished:
children living in remote or underdeveloped areas; 
tribal and nomadic children;
children who are victims of natural and social disasters, experiencing discrimination due to poverty, skin color, gender, race, language, culture, religion, place of residence, or their parents'/families' political affiliations;
children with specific socialization experiences (e.g., those subject to certain stereotypes that require support in overcoming them and compensating for the limited opportunities they present, such as "country girl," "city boy," or "street children"); 
children with specific identity experiences (those who do not know their father or parents, twins, transgender children, etc.);
orphans, stray orphans, abandoned children, expelled children, homeless children – children living outside the home and without adult care; children in conflict with the law, addicted, living by theft, begging, prostitution;
children infected with HIV, falling into the category known in the literature as PLWHA (People Living with HIV/AIDS).
Most of these categories are not particularly prominent in Poland or Kazakhstan (some certainly are, but these are often isolated cases where the need for support only becomes apparent after closer examination of an individual, sometimes more complex situation. As can be seen from the overview, although the words ethnicity or nationality do not appear explicitly here either, it is precisely the experiences related to the environment of origin that in many cases can be a burdening factor in the development of these children (see points 2, 3, and 5) and, when included in support programs, a source of much-needed roots, strength, and resilience. It is worth taking this type of possible diversity into account when creating ethnopedagogical experiences, which will be discussed later in this book.
Diverse groups in education in the broad sense are becoming commonplace and form the basis for theoretical concepts and practical solutions for inclusive education, often referred to as education for all. It was precisely the observation of a change in the perception of the group as maximally diverse, with its potential in areas of interest to educators and special educators, that was the catalyst for bringing together in one volume different perspectives on the common and specific challenges of "separate" groups, as well as their co-functioning in heterogeneous groups. The first part of the monograph consists of texts on the theoretical contexts of the conditions for the education of diverse groups, ranging from the conditions of educational inequality, through the creation of boundaries and differences in education, to cooperative teaching and learning in a diverse group.
Beata Jachimczak (2021), the initiator and scientific editor of a monograph on diverse classes through a catalog of diverse needs, abilities, and origins, conceptualizes the notion of a diverse and maximally diverse group. Students who stand out in such classes due to their educational needs are most often those with specific learning difficulties (e.g., dyslexia, dyscalculia), students with special educational needs, gifted students, and children from different backgrounds, but the author also mentions age-diverse groups. 
Many such lists can be created, also delving into various categories of disorders or functional diversity (e.g., following the current trend of distinguishing neurodiverse students—those on the autism spectrum, with dyslexia, ADHD, but also including new individuals in this category, e.g., SLI/DLD, FASD, motor coordination disorders – dyspraxia, etc.). This may also apply to a catalog of special abilities. However, it is more important to organize the list than to constantly extend it, creating a never-ending list. Katarzyna Szczepkowska-Szyszko (2023) has done this, listing the following issues of diversity in the classroom: 
Differences in skill levels: individual differences in knowledge, skills, and experiences;
Differences in learning styles: unique learning styles resulting from individual physical, personality, and environmental characteristics, as well as previous educational experiences;
Differences in educational needs: the need for additional support, e.g., due to learning or developmental difficulties, or additional challenges due to greater abilities or working at a higher level than peers;
Cultural and socioeconomic background: different cultural and socioeconomic environments, bringing diverse experiences, values , and perspectives to the classroom, which influence the diversity of individual learning processes;
Language: the presence in the classroom of foreign-language children whose first language is different from the language of instruction;
Emotional and social factors: different emotional and social needs of students, including those resulting from personal traumatic life experiences or family dysfunction (Szczepkowska-Szyszko, 2023, pp. 7-8).
This is an important clarification, which reminds us that there are no truly homogeneous classes or groups of pupils or students, but that each is a diverse group. Outlining the scope of the real challenges for inclusive education teachers, in Poland there is talk in this context of a "maximally diverse group" (Jachimczak, 2021, passim). This is an interesting proposal, but the use of such a broad quantifier may raise questions about the criteria: what does "maximum" mean and how can we operationalize the distinction between a diverse class and a maximally diverse class? Dorota Podgórska-Jachnik (2022), accepting the universality of inter- and intra-individual differences in school classes, adopts a pragmatic definition from a methodological perspective, recognizing that a diverse class is a class: 
in which the teacher recognizes and takes into account diversity;
in which the diverse needs of students (including those requiring greater psychoeducational support) are recognized, and educational requirements are adapted to them in order to make optimal use of their individual potential.
By comparing the areas of diversity listed above by Szczepkowska-Szyszko (2023) in the following diagram (Figure 3), we present the positioning of the category of ethnicity among these areas in response to the problem highlighted in this subsection. It can be said that it lies at the intersection of areas related to different cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds, linguistic diversity, and diversity of individual emotional and social factors. In our opinion, the connection with the latter area results from the strong potential of ethnicity in shaping attitudes—often the most important attitudes in life, involving identity and values, and thus guiding lifelong choices and actions. This is also an important area that should be taken into account in educational activities in the field of ethnopedagogy.

Ethnicity in terms of class diversity is associated with the presence of children with a specific ethnic identity who identify with members of their reference group on the basis of perceived common characteristics that distinguish them from other groups. The characteristics that are considered common to ethnic groups include language, culture, common origin, traditions, society, religion, history, but also social treatment by others. This can be a source of pride and strength, but it can also cause feelings of insecurity, inferiority, and sometimes a worse social position (fewer opportunities, sometimes even discrimination and persecution). They certainly deserve respect and cannot be overlooked in the education and professional training of pupils and later students.
This opens up space for ethnopedagogical considerations – the sources of cultural patterns, values, and attitudes that will play a key role in education and supporting personal development. We will explore these issues in more depth in the next chapter, providing here only general guidelines for use in designing pedagogical activities that take into account the needs of a diverse group and its teacher. In our opinion, the general pedagogical context for ethnopedagogy, as well as the closely related intercultural pedagogy, is the pedagogy of encounter and dialogue. This term has a broad meaning and scope that fits into a personalistic approach, but for analytical purposes we narrow it down to the concept of educational dialogue (Al-Khamisy 2013, 2020), the main components of which are presented in Figure 4.

Both inclusive education and ethnopedagogy, as pedagogical subdisciplines, but also as distinct interdisciplinary areas of research in the social sciences, are a response to the challenges of the modern world, including the multifaceted diversity of contemporary societies and the processes of globalization. In his fundamental Polish monograph on ethnopedagogy, Jerzy Nikitorowicz attempts to draw the reader's attention to:
human functioning in conditions of cultural diversity and constantly evolving multicultural societies, the need to notice cultural differences, learn about them, understand them, cooperate and interact, and support each other symmetrically in the process of development (Nikitorowicz, 2018, p. 9).
Although Nikitorowicz's monograph has been described as "fundamental," the author has come a long way in his work, marked by other monographs leading to the development of Polish ethnopedagogy principles, which we would like to present before giving the floor to Kazakh ethnopedagogues in the next chapter. This is not because we assign any hierarchy of importance to these publications, but because we recognize their differences (despite many common issues). 
Nikitorowicz began his research work with the issue of creating a child's identity (Nikitorowicz, 2005, 2008), which only subsequently led to the emergence of the themes of culture and multiculturalism as the context for the formation of this identity (Nikitorowicz, 2008, 2009). Subsequent works linked the topic of multiculturalism with the issues of regionalism (Nikitorowicz, 2009) and ethnicity (Nikitorowicz, 2010), although the problem of identity formation does not disappear, but remains in all these (and other) publications by the author as a common pedagogical denominator of the analyzed issues. In 2014, the author published a book with a title that sooner or later must be asked in the context of ethnic and national issues: the question of patriotism and nationalism, or what cultural identity are we moving towards? (Nikitorowicz, 2014). It is only after following this line of thought that the cited monograph emerges: Ethnopedagogy in the context of multiculturalism and constantly evolving identity (Nikitorowicz, 2018). Later still, the conceptual model developed in this way is used to study educational and social problems in the Polish borderland (Nikitorowicz, 2024), which symbolically closes the loop: from detail to the crystallization of a general concept and a return to specific problems with the developed theoretical tools. 
The path taken by researchers from Kazakhstan is different, which results both from the history of our countries and the stage of their development at which these issues began to emerge, as well as from completely different geopolitical and ethnic experiences (which we will outline in more detail later in this paper). 
Of course, although ethnopedagogy as a science emerged in Poland relatively recently thanks to Jerzy Nikitorowicz, there is no shortage of authors in Poland who have dealt with this issue in the context of nation and nationality (e.g., Dyczewski, 1996). multi-, inter-, and transculturality (Korporowicz, 1997; Grzybowski 2007; Zalas, 2021), issues of relations and dialogue in encounters with the Other and the Foreigner (Korporowicz, 1997; Chromiec, 2004; Cudowska, 2011), which are so important in the era of globalization and the clash of different cultures in the process of its intensive development (Gnitecki, 2002). It is also worth mentioning the work of authors who prepare coherent scientific materials supporting researchers and teachers in the implementation of the above-mentioned interrelated issues into educational practice, such as the team of authors who developed the Lexicon of Ethnopedagogy and Transculturalism (Guziuk-Tkacz, Siegień, and Matyjewicz, 2015; Guziuk-Tkacz, Matyjewicz, and Siegień, 2017).
Ethnopedagogy as a defined science may not be as widely represented as among Kazakhstani researchers, whose views we will present in the second chapter, but it has its solid foundations in multiculturalism research, ethnology, and cultural anthropology. 
Jerzy Nikitorowicz defines ethnopedagogy as:
a branch of pedagogy that observes and emphasizes the connections and dependencies between the functioning of people who identify with ethnic, national, and religious groups, the processes of socialization and enculturation that take place in these groups, with pedagogy that points to the possibilities of human development, supports it in the process of upbringing, education, and self-education throughout life, shapes dialogical attitudes towards cultural diversity, and ensures the continuous formation of identity. (...) Analyzing ethnic, national, and religious cultures. Problems of adaptation, acculturation, transculturation, and assimilation, it directs upbringing, education, and self-education towards dialogue in order to create a paradigm of coexistence of different cultures on the globe (Nikitorowicz, 2018, pp. 16-17).
According to the author, by taking into account and emphasizing the diversity of experiences and cultural values in the development and shaping of human identity (Nikitorowicz, 2005, 2008), ethnopedagogy sensitizes people to cultural heritage, understood on a micro, meso, and macro scale, to attitudes shaped towards family culture and towards experienced/revealed multiculturalism, to the orientation of attitudes built on this basis towards ethnocentrism, patriotism, or nationalism (Nikitorowicz, 2014; 2018). The repertoire of these attitudes can be further expanded to include chauvinism, fanaticism, racism, megalomania, and xenophobia (Chromiec, 2014; Nikitorowicz, 2018), which may pose a threat both to individual personal development and to the coexistence of diverse groups. After all, these are attitudes responsible for conflicts, wars, and ethnic cleansing. Concern for the peaceful, harmonious coexistence of different nations and ethnic groups is concern for the good future of the world. 
The common denominator for most new phenomena and vibrant social categories resulting from globalization and the rapid social changes of the modern world, while maintaining an inclusive approach as the horizon of thinking about modern society and the world, should be the area of issues related to intercultural and transcultural education, education for acceptance and tolerance of otherness, difference, and foreignness, as well as the issue of the dynamic formation of cultural identity. Developing and expanding knowledge about the cultures of the world, their ethnic origins, and cultural heritage, including their axiological legacy, seems to be the best way to build an inclusive society: one that is open but retains its own identity, tolerant but aware and proud of its own achievements and demanding respect for them, prepared to co-create a living space in a transcultural and transnational dialogue with "others" (Guziuk-Tkacz, Matyjewicz, and Siegień, 2017).
Ethnopedagogy thus allows us to shape harmonious individuals who are rooted in their own culture and capable of encountering the Other and their culture on the basis of respect and reciprocity. It also allows for the formation of peaceful and creatively oriented communities and entire societies that draw on differences and accept them, rather than treating them as threats that must be destroyed. This also applies to differences perceived in education as a cause of unmet specific (special) educational needs. Differences and diversity among people are therefore at the intersection of ethnopedagogy and inclusiveness, including inclusive education. It is precisely in this area of scientific transdisciplinarity and transversality that we will seek inspiration for increasing the potential of schools and education in terms of equal opportunities. Opportunities for all, because that is the essence of inclusion and inclusive education.
One of the main sources of anxiety when encountering the Other/Stranger is the fear of a threat to one's own values, distinctiveness, and above all, autonomy. Attempting to reconcile two opposing vectors: "towards other cultures" and "away from other cultures" is possible, but it must involve some kind of axiological strategy. One such strategy is to discover and strengthen one's own culture and sense of belonging to it. This is where ethnopedagogy comes in. 
One of the fundamental aspects of ethnopedagogy—a potential source of models and values, the basis for pride in one's roots—is learning about national and folk culture. These played an important role in the project carried out by Karylgash Kazhimova with her Kazakh students. Let us therefore take a closer look at this concept in Polish literature before we turn to its exploration by Kazakh researchers:
Folk culture is part of national culture, a common good created over many generations, translating into a way of understanding the traditional world, enclosed in words, memory, and imagination. It is a heritage that defines the specificity of a region, interwoven with cultural diversity and richness, passed down from generation to generation. Folk culture grows out of tradition and is a permanent part of it, embedded in the global and regional vision of the world and man, which includes the language, customs, traditions, rituals, and beliefs of rural inhabitants. At the same time, it is a close relationship between man and nature, respect for places and people, as well as fidelity to the past, without which neither the present nor the future can be built. (…). There is another aspect. In a global world, people need something close to them, their own place on Earth, and this is what folk culture becomes (Pelc, as cited in: Wołoszyn-Mróz, 2023, bns).
These concepts and the way of thinking consistent with this description are shared by our Kazakh partners, which will be revisited in the second chapter. It became the basis for thinking about the research project presented later in this paper.

What do multiculturalism and ethnicity mean in Poland and Kazakhstan?

Although the concepts of ethnicity and nationality have their dictionary definitions (denotations), their connotative meanings, as well as their use in managing a country's ethnic diversity, can construct a completely different picture of what lies behind these concepts. The clarification of the concept is already expressed in the provisions of the law, which defines quite precisely who can and who cannot be recognized as a member of a national or ethnic minority (Figure 5).

Figure 5. National and ethnic minorities as defined by Polish law (own study based on: ACT of January 6, 2005 on national and ethnic minorities and regional languages, Journal of Laws 2005 No. 17 item 141).

There are nine national minorities in Poland: Belarusian, Czech, Lithuanian, German, Armenian, Russian, Slovak, Ukrainian, and Jewish. There are also four ethnic minorities: Karaim, Lemko, Roma, and Tatar. However, other nationalities and ethnic groups represent a small proportion of the total population of Poland, as according to the National Census of Population and Housing, they account for a total of approximately 3.5% (GUS, 2021). Although multiculturalism is present and increasingly emphasized in scientific and public discourse, mainly due to migrants, who do not have citizenship status , this is still a much lower percentage than in other European countries, as well as in Kazakhstan.
In terms of multiculturalism, it is a unique country. Kazakhstan does not officially use the term "national minorities," but the country is considered a global ethnic and national phenomenon, as representatives of over 130 ethnic groups live on its territory. Therefore, unlike in Poland, it is difficult to list them all. In addition, representatives of ethnic minorities constitute approximately 37% of the country's population, which means that more than one in three inhabitants of Kazakhstan is not of Kazakh origin. In Poland, taking into account the above-mentioned rate of 3.5%, less than one in thirty inhabitants is not of Polish origin. The scale of the phenomenon in Kazakhstan is therefore ten times greater. This is a diametrically different situation in both countries, even after a preliminary assessment of the problem, which may become a real social and political confession. Such complex multi-ethnicity determines a completely different way of managing such a common difference.
The most numerous nationality in Kazakhstan is, of course, Kazakh (63.1% of the population – data for 2009), followed by Russians (23.7%). Apart from Kazakhs and Russians, there are also Uzbeks (2.8%), Ukrainians (2.1%), Uyghurs (1.4%), Tatars (1.3%), Germans (1.1%) and 4.5% of representatives of other ethnic groups (including Koreans, Turks, Azerbaijanis, Belarusians, Dungans, Kurds, Tajiks, Poles, Chechens, Kyrgyz, Bashkirs, Ingush, Moldovans, Chuvash, Armenians, Greeks, Bulgarians, Turkmen and Jews. (Kalizhanova and Almaniyazova, 2009, bns,).
Until recently, two languages were commonly used in Kazakhstan: Kazakh (from the Kipchak group of languages in the Altaic-Turkic language family) and Russian, and in addition, many other languages, such as Turkish, Ukrainian, Uzbek, and even German, were used locally by a significant number of residents. Kazakh is currently the official state language, but Russian is treated as the de facto official language due to its widespread use. It is still used almost universally, which is further reinforced by the fact that most Internet users use Russian-language resources, often as their main source (the Russian-language Internet is seen as an attractive source of access to online culture, especially music for young people). In addition to Kazakh-language schools, Russian-language schools continue to operate, and university courses are also available in these two languages. Although Kazakhs currently make up the majority of the population, with Russians accounting for only 15.5%, Russian is spoken by about 70% of the population, and Kazakh by over 92%. According to the 2021 Census, 44.9% of the population (over 5 years of age) speaks two languages. Another 28.6% speaks three languages, 1.7% speaks four, 0.2% of the population knows 5 languages, and 0.1% knows as many as six (2021 Census, https://stat.gov.kz ). Bilingualism may be a certain unidentified problem in Kazakhstan. Until recently, the coexistence of two official languages (Kazakh and Russian) meant that many children grew up in a bilingual environment, which, according to our previous research, is most often considered beneficial for development (enriching bilingualism). However, in some cases, the overlap of two languages can interfere with development (impoverishing bilingualism), which can only be determined by monitoring the level and course of language acquisition. It seems that some of the reading difficulties experienced by children in Kazakhstani schools may be due to unconscious language difficulties resulting from bilingualism (Podgórska-Jachnik, Kenżegalijeva, and Mukhieva, 2024). In addition, additional difficulties may arise in the near future due to the Kazakh government's planned transition from the Cyrillic to the Latin alphabet.
In Poland, the language situation is slightly different, although according to the Education Information System, in recent years Polish schools have had students who bring more than 140 languages to the school environment, which they use as their first languages (SIO, 2024). In many cases, this entails the need to support the student (e.g., an adaptation year with a language assistant who speaks the child's language).
There are currently two official languages in Poland: Polish and Kashubian, the latter being so limited in area and scope and so recent that most Poles are unaware of the official status of the Kashubian language. The Polish language, or Polszczyzna (a Lechitic language from the West Slavic group, which is part of the Indo-European family), is not only the official language of Poland, but also one of the official languages of the European Union. 
The second official language, Kashubian, is a minority language of local importance. The Kashubian language, or Kashubian – and in Kashubian: Kaszëbskô Mòwa (a Lechitic language from the West Slavic language group, closely related to Polish, Czech, Slovak, and Sorbian), used to be treated as a local dialect, but there are linguistic arguments for its status as a separate language (including a separate alphabet and grammar). It is spoken by Kashubians in Poland and Kashubian emigrants. The language was legally recognized as a regional, i.e., official language: an auxiliary language of an ethnic minority in 2005. Currently, about 20,000 children are taught in Kashubian, and it is possible to take the high school final exam in Kashubian. 
Against this background, it is worth noting that a much larger group than the Kashubians, namely the Silesians (inhabitants of Lower Silesia, but also, more broadly, people who identify with the Silesian nationality, which is declared as their first or second nationality in censuses), has been seeking a similar linguistic status for years. In 2004, the Polish Sejm even included Silesian as a regional language in the law. This would pave the way for the recognition of the Silesian national minority, but this is strongly opposed by some political circles. The law was rejected by the President of Poland - the decision was motivated, among other things, by insufficient distinctiveness, but it must be agreed that in the process of emancipation of languages and ethnic groups (not only in Poland), political arguments are actually more important than linguistic ones. The Silesian language is currently treated as a dialect. However, its presence in the tradition and culture of the region is very strong, and it is also promoted in the country, among others, by popular film and stage artists. 
Another factor that differentiates the two countries—Poland and Kazakhstan—both internally and between themselves is the religiosity of their citizens. According to current research on the religiosity of Poles (CBOS, 2024, as cited in Bożewicz), members of the Roman Catholic Church (88.8%) clearly dominate in the country, to which can be added followers of other Catholic rites (approx. 0.2% of the population). Orthodox Christianity is professed by 0.5% of Poles, Protestantism by 0.4%, other Christian denominations by 0.5%, Jehovah's Witnesses	0.5%, other religions, other denominations and other churches - only 0.1%. Atheists account for 7.3%. Despite the separation of church and state enshrined in the Polish Constitution (a legacy of post-Enlightenment thinking, but also recognized by the Catholic Church at the Second Vatican Council as the most appropriate model for the functioning of the Church in the modern world), Poland is one of the most Catholic countries in the world. It is not a religious state, but the majority of its citizens are declared Catholics. The state and the Church are independent and sovereign in their activities. The Concordat between the Republic of Poland and the Vatican, like the Polish Constitution, states: 
The Republic of Poland and the Holy See confirm that the State and the Catholic Church are independent and autonomous in their respective spheres, and undertake to fully respect this principle in their mutual relations and in their cooperation for the development of the human person and the common good (Concordat, 1993, Art. 1).
In practice, the existence of religious services in certain closed institutions, such as hospitals or prisons, depends on the will of citizens. On this basis, state-funded religious education was also introduced in schools. The "fight for crosses" in public places – at work, at school, in the Polish Parliament – is considered part of the process of decommunization of the country, of promoting Catholic values as an important part of Polish identity. Sometimes, however, certain boundaries were crossed, such as street demonstrations by the school superintendent, a representative of the local education authorities, with a rosary in her hand on the streets of the city (School Superintendent..., 2019). In the religious sphere, it is very difficult to find this clear boundary, which on the one hand can lead to discriminatory practices, and on the other to excessive mixing of public issues with the private sphere of religiosity. This is particularly difficult in a country such as Poland, which is strongly divided politically. Unfortunately, religious views, including views on the place of religion in schools, divide Poles, and this is undoubtedly also an area of diversity that should be taken into account in the context of inclusive education (primarily in the context of educating people to live in a society that does not discriminate against other religions and other people because of their religious views). The recent change from a conservative to a democratic government has led to restrictions on the favoritism shown to the Catholic Church in the state funding of its activities and to measures by the Ministry of National Education to reduce the number of hours of religious education in schools. Despite such clear pro-religious and pro-Catholic actions in Poland, there is a visible secularization and a decreasing participation of students in religion classes (it is not a compulsory subject). The Covid-19 pandemic was a turning point, but the Church's politicization in recent years is also cited as a reason for the shift away from the Church (Zielińska, as cited in PAP, 202.09.11). Without going into the details, it should be noted that international statistics indicate Poland, known as a "bastion of Catholicism," as the fastest secularizing country in the world after 2016 and a country of "axiological revolution," showing the world's largest intergenerational differences in religiosity (Stolz, as cited in PAP, 2025.09.11).
In terms of religious diversity in Kazakhstan, it is worth noting that there is no official religion in this country, and religion is separated from the state by the Constitution, as is the case in Poland. This does not mean, however, that there are no followers of different religions, especially Islam. Kazakhstan is characterized by its established ideological neutrality, which means that the state does not favor any religion or require citizens to disclose their beliefs. These rights may only be restricted by law and only to the extent necessary to protect the constitutional system, public order, human rights and freedoms, and the health and morality of the population. 
The Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and belief, including the right to renounce religious affiliation, although the right to practice one's beliefs and participate in religious practices applies to registered religious groups, especially those considered traditional in Kazakh society (this usually refers to Sunni Hanafi Islam, Russian Orthodoxy, Greek Catholicism and Roman Catholicism, Lutheranism, and Judaism). 
Muslims are the largest religious group in Kazakhstan: 70.4% of the population professes Islam. In second place are Orthodox Christians, accounting for 21.4% of the population. Some sources also mention a fairly large Jewish community. Contrary to what Poles might think, Catholics account for only about 2.4% of the total population. The only Catholic church in Uralsk serves a small but active community of people of various nationalities. Currently, there is a Polish parish priest (Fr. Łukasz Niemiec) and Polish Elizabethan sisters, although it is emphasized that this is not a "Polish church" but a "Roman Catholic church." The Protestant population is similar in size to the Catholic population, accounting for slightly less than 2.0% of the population (mainly: Evangelical Baptist Church, Lutheran Church, Pentecostals, Presbyterian Church, Seventh-day Adventist Church). In addition, 0.2% of the population are Buddhists and 0.11% are Jehovah's Witnesses (Kalizhanova and Almaniyazova, 2009, bns.).
Statistics also indicate that 0.3% of Kazakhs are followers of traditional ethnic religions (Kalizhanova and Almaniyazova, 2009, bns.), but this phenomenon seems to be more complex.
What distinguishes the religiosity of Poles and Kazakhs at first glance is the visibility of the former's religious practices, which also permeate schools and workplaces, while in Kazakhstan they are strictly limited to the private sphere. Of course, on the streets of Uralska and other cities in Kazakhstan, you can hear the muezzin singing, you can see the faithful going to church, sometimes women in hijabs, but there are no prayers in the public sphere, no public preaching of religion (except for the possibility of receiving religious services in the media, e.g., on the radio or television), let alone public forms of religious agitation. However, certain elements of the intermingling of different beliefs and traditions are inevitable, such as the beautiful custom of sitting down together at the table at the end of the week – also in work teams. Sharing tea, small snacks, sweets, and fruit, expressing affirmation (gratitude to others) – this is a charming tradition that integrates a team of colleagues, but also an opportunity to encounter fragments of old beliefs, as expressed, for example, in the Kazakh pancakes called borsaks/baursaks, prepared every Friday:
In Kazakhstan, it is believed that the smell of oil during the frying of baursaks rises high into the sky and deceased relatives and loved ones can feed on the aroma and enjoy themselves together with the feasters. That is why baursaks were prepared for weddings and important family celebrations or meetings (Szczun Na Śląsku...2017.12.17). 
These and other beliefs and traditions, full of references to the spirits of ancestors – also very important to the modern inhabitants of Kazakhstan – also refer to the ancient beliefs of the steppe peoples of Central Asia, who developed a slightly different variant of Islam than the orthodox one. A special role was played here by the belief in Tengri, the all-encompassing god and personification of the universe, which has been present among nomadic peoples for thousands of years. 
Tengri lives in the Kazakh soul. Contemporary Kazakhs have one foot in modernity, but they still cultivate traditions from the time when Tengri was a god. The most striking example is the main axis of the capital of Kazakhstan – Astana. The main boulevard of this ultra-modern city runs along a sacred road, and in the middle, a tower has been erected, referring to the shamanic tree of life (Bronikowska, 2025).
This shamanic, mythical "tree of life" with a golden ball at the top, representing the egg of the Samruk bird, is Bajterek, a traditional Kazakh symbol of happiness, but also a symbol of the contemporary connection between tradition and modernity. The meaning that Kazakhs themselves attach to these oldest traditions is important, as it is these deeply rooted religious elements that arouse interest around the world, giving the Kazakhs a unique socio-cultural identity. This is evidenced by the interest in exhibitions devoted to Tengriism and traditional crafts of Kazakhstan at the Smithsonian Museum in Washington (Smithsonian Folklife Festival and the Soul of Tengri project – T. Álemi, 2023), but also in Poland (Bronikowska, 2025). 
With such strong roots, it seems obvious that the Muslim religion in Kazakhstan was steeped in pre-Islamic traditions and rituals, which, together with the clash with the so-called high Islam, professed by the mullahs, and later with attempts to eradicate all  religions in the Republic of Kazakhstan during the existence of the USSR. In practice, this has led to the heterodoxy of Kazakh Islam (Charatańska, 2026). The 20th century and Soviet oppression ended the nomadic period in Kazakhstan, but despite repression, it did not destroy the religiosity of the Kazakhs, even despite the formation of a new relationship between the state and religion.
In the mid-20th century, two variants of Islam coexisted in Central Asia: the official one, supported by the authorities [the so-called "licensed" Islam, promoted by the Central Asian Muslim Spiritual Administration (SADUM), established in Tashkent in 1943 – authors' note] and the folk variant, oppressed by the authorities. The persecution, repression, and deportation of followers and representatives of the folk Islamic clergy continued unabated. However, it was not uncommon for people holding important state functions, who officially renounced Allah, would pray when they returned home, and even (in extreme cases) were themselves mullahs or ishans [which was very reminiscent of the post-war situation in Poland, when the communist authorities tried to eradicate the religiosity of Poles – authors' note]. The 70 years of the Soviet Union's existence undoubtedly left a mark on the consciousness of the people who lived during that period. Mass unification was intended to create a society without ethnic, cultural, and linguistic differences. Therefore, the collapse of the colossus came as a huge shock. A void was created that had to be filled. The end of the USSR meant an ideological vacuum. The construction of new states had to be based on ethnic and religious issues. The presidents of the newly formed republics were well aware of this, and they redefined the concepts of "common good" and "national interest" as "state interest" (...). Although the constitutions of each of these countries include a provision on secularism, a strong connection between the state and religion could be observed, as well as significant, though often only declared, assistance in rebuilding faith. Financial assistance consisted in the construction of mosques and religious schools. In Kazakhstan, there were 25 mosques in 1965, while in 2001 there were already over 1,400 registered . (Charatańska, 2016, bns.).
Despite changing attitudes towards religion, it should be emphasized that religion is an important element of the spiritual strength of individuals and nations, strongly linked to ethnicity and ancestral values, and therefore tends to revive, despite repression and attempts to eradicate it. Therefore, when it comes to contemporary trends in religion in Kazakhstan, as in other Asian countries, there is a progressive Islamization, with more young people on the streets wearing traditional clothing. However, the complex history of religion  in Kazakhstan and Central Asia, as well as the centuries-old history of the local peoples, mean that Islam in this region of the world today
a syncretic combination of many beliefs: Christianity, Islam (in its more "orthodox," "pure" sense), and above all, shamanism. (...) People often do not realize that they are violating certain prohibitions or commandments of "Koranic" Islam [e.g., by wearing amulets or referring to the established traditions of shamanic practices – authors' note]. (...) The Muslim religion has not completely supplanted shamanism; it can be said that these two religious systems have merged to form a syncretic image. (Charatańska, 2016, bns.).
It is worth adding that in the face of progressive Islamization, which also raises fears of  radical Islam, as well as the inviolability of the principle of separation of state and religion, the Kazakh authorities issued a ban on wearing the hijab in schools in 2023. Thus, on the one hand, there is acceptance of the religious needs of Kazakhs, while on the other hand, there is a visible continuation of the government's secularization policy, which believes that education should be religiously neutral. However, we should remember that religiosity is another characteristic that strongly differentiates people, which cannot be overlooked in the context of observing social processes of exclusion and inclusion. The image of religious beliefs and practices that has developed in different regions of the world is also part of the image of peoples and nations as seen from the outside, as features of local folklore. 
These few key historical and social facts and the statistical data cited show that the situation in terms of ethnic, linguistic, and religious diversity in Poland and Kazakhstan is very difficult to compare, let alone manage such diversity. In such different social and geopolitical situations, the answers to such difficult questions are completely different:
How to reconcile the education of nation states with the idea of multiculturalism, national patriotism with civic patriotism, the rights and norms of hosts with the expectations and needs of newcomers , how to create a space in constantly evolving multicultural societies where different communities and cultures would interact and enrich each other in the process, implementing specific development strategies, guided by the principles and norms of respect and recognition of the law that unites a given society, how to organize situations that stimulate the development of value systems supporting human development in multicultural conditions, how to create bonds and a sense of community, responsibility for human behavior in the socio-cultural space shaped by them? (Nikitorowicz, 2018, p. 10).
The difficulty of ethnic comparisons between Poland and Kazakhstan stems, first of all, from the very different scale of the minority phenomenon. Secondly, it is due to the complex history of the country and personal histories, which are only outlined here, translating into experiences of current minorities that are difficult to integrate, often associated with the traumatic experience of forced displacement from their country of origin. Their scale in Soviet times was truly significant:
The reason for both the large number of nationalities and multilingualism in Kazakhstan is the fact that it was a country to which the communist authorities sent people en masse to labor camps (lagers), and it was also a place of mass deportations of people, most of whom never returned to their homelands. (Kalizhanova and Almaniyazova, 2009, bns.).
These are experiences of cultural adaptation in conditions that force people to write their personal and family histories in a new place, which for some becomes a new homeland, while for others remains a place of exile forever. It is difficult to make clear generalizations here. These different patterns of adaptation are certainly not without significance for the formation of a new identity/reconstruction of the existing one in new conditions. Humans have rich resources of adaptability and resilience, but reconstructing life in new conditions, or rather constructing it anew, means writing a different, personal history in each case.  But this does not only apply to migrants and displaced persons.
The inhabitants of Kazakhstan are also rewriting their history after regaining independence, just as the Poles began to do after the period of partition, and then – its next volume – after the political transformation of the 1990s. These are not just changes in scenery, but a social and axiological space to be filled.
Regardless of the weight of these experiences (the personal effects and meanings attributed to the changes in the world we live in), it is worth remembering the key thesis of Polish ethnopedagogue Jerzy Nikitorowicz (2018) about the constantly evolving identity – regardless of whether a person experiences mild transformations or extreme trajectories of fate. It is a constant life task, and we do it in different ways and under different conditions – but always based on subjective heuristics related to the integration of personal histories. Personal histories are collections of mirrors reflecting the surrounding reality – family, local, and national.

Preparing Polish teachers to implement inclusive education tasks, taking into account educational and pedagogical resources

The role of inclusive education in a world full of change and incompleteness is gradually becoming more and more important. One of the main challenges associated with the implementation of inclusive education is the adequate preparation of teachers: this is associated with preparing to meet the special educational needs resulting from various disabilities, but not only from them. It also involves preparing to cope with the complex and often underestimated diversity of the classroom. Preparation at both the attitudinal and professional competence levels.
Inclusive education is being implemented in education systems in both Poland and Kazakhstan. However, Poland has a much longer tradition of special education, which dates back to the establishment of the first schools for deaf children, followed by blind children, more than 200 years ago. UNESCO's activities in the field of promoting inclusive education indicate that each country must find its own path and its own model of inclusion, but international exchange of experiences is very valuable in this regard. Hence, among other things, the interest of Kazakhstani educators in exchanging experiences on inclusive education with Polish partners, as well as exchange internships for both authors and other educators from both countries (including an internship in Uralsk for Agnieszka Kamyk-Wawryszuk from Kazimierz Wielki University in Bydgoszcz and internships at UKW in Bydgoszcz for Gulmira S. Mukhievej and at the University of Łódź for Aidana Zh. Kenżegalijeva). Given Poland's greater experience in this area and the direction of the transfer of this experience, when discussing the preparation of teachers for the implementation of inclusive education tasks, we will therefore refer to what has been developed in the Polish system to date.
Analyzing the experience to date with inclusive education in Poland, it must be acknowledged that many of the organizational changes made to promote the education of students with disabilities, but also those with greater educational needs for other reasons, have outpaced the efforts to prepare teachers for this. This is a peculiar paradox, as it seems that should be the obvious first step. Meanwhile, schools were opened for these students before real steps were taken towards the systematic preparation of teachers in mainstream schools: both in terms of substantive preparation and mental preparation for change. Admittedly, more than two decades ago, numerous conferences and seminars for educational staff began to "roll out" across the country, preparing them for the new idea of educational inclusion. Various types of training courses also began to be organized – at the Center for Education Development, in teacher training institutions, in schools and kindergartens (training for teaching staff). However, it is difficult to consider these as systemic changes, as they do not translate into the preparation of EVERY teacher to carry out inclusive education tasks in EVERY school, which is the only way to determine the readiness of staff. 
In addition, after several years of implementation, the system of disseminating knowledge in the form of conferences and training courses dedicated to successive groups of teachers gives the false impression that "everything has already been said." Meanwhile, knowledge that arrives in a cascade (if the knowledge transfer system is organized in some way) or randomly (when it creates an educational offer based on interest, motivation, and commitment, i.e., the goodwill of individual teachers to pursue additional education) does not necessarily reach everyone it should. 
Agata B. Jardzioch points to 2006 as the beginning of inclusive education in Poland, as it was then that Poland became a member of the European Agency for Special Needs and Inclusive Education. The author notes that this topic had already appeared in the literature and research on the inclusion of students with disabilities in mainstream schools (in addition to the already developed classes referred to as integrative), but it was 2006 that brought an increase in interest in the inclusive trend (Jardzioch, 2017). However, significant organizational changes in the education system came in 2010, when a whole package of interrelated regulations of the Minister of National Education came into force, comprehensively regulating various aspects of organizing education, upbringing, care, and psychological and pedagogical assistance for children and young people with special educational needs (including those resulting from disability and social maladjustment or the risk of social maladjustment). Only one thing was not taken into account: preparing teachers to work with such children. What is more, when, a few years later, in 2019, a new standard of education preparing for the teaching profession was introduced by the Regulation of the Minister of Science and Higher Education (Journal of Laws 2019, item 1450, consolidated text Journal of Laws 2024 item 453), apart from a few provisions at the level of expected learning outcomes, which may give the impression of equipping teachers  in mainstream schools with the competences to work with students with diverse educational needs, the anticipated manner of achieving these outcomes – in particular the number of hours allowing for preparation for inclusive education, especially for teachers of school and vocational subjects – leaves no doubt that these expectations are unrealistic. 
In addition to substantive and didactic preparation in the subject taught , the standard provides for a block of so-called psychological and pedagogical preparation of 180 hours (90 hours of psychology and 90 hours of pedagogy) plus 30 hours of practical training. This is supplemented by 60 hours of teaching basics and voice training, but let's not kid ourselves that in a 90-hour block devoted to various issues from different key areas of pedagogy (e.g., theory of education, social pedagogy, care pedagogy), it is possible to develop the expected (and necessary in inclusive education) skills of diagnosis (including functional assessment, designing personalized developmental, therapeutic, and didactic support, including universal design, communication and didactic adaptations, and working with methods adapted to the conditions of a diverse group).
The possibility of preparing school and vocational subject teachers for inclusive education tasks looks particularly "poor" when compared to the preparation of special education teachers (and it should not be forgotten that the choice between a mainstream school and a special school will also be a choice between teachers prepared in this way for the parents of the child or student). In the case of special educators – in addition to the same 180-hour block of psychological and pedagogical preparation (90 hours of general preparation in psychology and 90 hours of general preparation in pedagogy) plus 30 hours of professional practice, the following is provided for: 790 hours of specialized education (and 60 hours of practical training in this block), 640 hours of preparation  in a selected area of special pedagogy (and 120 hours of practical training in this block), as well as a separate block of 390 hours of inclusive education (plus 120 hours of practical training in this block). We will omit other blocks from the description, but in the context of comparisons with the preparation of subject teachers, it is worth noting what is provided for special educators in the Inclusive Education block. The topics covered are as follows: 
60 hours: Theories of integrative and inclusive education;
90 hours: Diagnosis of special educational needs, planning, implementation, and monitoring of support measures;
120 hours: Methodology of teaching in diverse groups;
60 hours: Educational programs in inclusive and integrated education;
60 hours: Organization of inclusive education (Journal of Laws 2024, item 453).
The comparison presented shows how big the difference is in the preparation of different teachers for inclusive education: special educators, in addition to acquiring extensive knowledge in their field of specialization (according to the type of disability or other developmental disorders), are prepared much more comprehensively and thoroughly than teachers of any school or vocational subject taught in a mainstream school .
In this respect, the standard of education preparing for the profession of kindergarten and early school education teacher (grades 1-3 of primary school) is more realistic. In the psychological and pedagogical preparation block, the standard assumes, among other things, the following subject areas: 300 hours of Fundamentals of Pedagogical Activities, 180 hours of Preschool and Early School Pedagogy, and 180 hours of Fundamentals of Psychology for Teachers (Journal of Laws 2024, item 453). Each of these blocks can include content that is useful from the point of view of inclusive education. However, that is not all, as separate specialist blocks are provided for , allowing for the inclusion of curriculum content in this area (the standard leaves a lot of autonomy to universities here), namely: 
400 hours: Supporting the development of children  in preschool  and early school age (it must be admitted that this is a very modern, comprehensively planned thematic block, exceptionally suited to the principles of inclusive education: from diverse models of the development support process in behavioral, constructivist, and emancipatory terms – through the basics of knowledge about the organization of an optimal educational environment, also taking into account the diverse needs and abilities of children – to the design of personalized educational strategies),
120 hours: Children or students with special developmental and educational needs in kindergarten and grades 1–3 of primary school;
60 hours: Organization of kindergarten and school work with elements of education law and children's rights, as well as kindergarten and school culture, including the education of students with special educational needs and disabilities;
60 hours: Basics of educational diagnostics for teachers (which includes developing the ability to recognize children's needs and interests and to assess them in order to support their development) (Journal of Laws 2024, item 453).
Of course, we are not discussing here the scope of substantive and didactic preparation for teaching classes and other elements of pedagogical preparation (the entire standard provides for a minimum of 2,800 teaching hours, including 240 hours of pedagogical practice). However, it can be said that the structure of the standard as developed creates real opportunities for these graduates to be well prepared for their future work.  
Considering the scope of substantive content in relation to the area of ethnic and multicultural experiences we are analyzing, it should be emphasized that the standard in the field of basic pedagogical knowledge provides for, among other things, the following issues:
Issues of education as a meeting in dialogue, education for responsible freedom and a multicultural society, types of interpersonal relationships and the processes governing these relationships, main educational environments, as well as the basics of intercultural dialogue (Journal of Laws 2024, item 453).
It also assumes the need to prepare teachers of various specialties to link the content they teach with other areas of knowledge and culture, which creates space for choosing topics and opens up the possibility of using both ethnic (folk) culture content and multicultural issues. This is important from the point of view of the expected learning outcomes, as it is anticipated that in terms of skills, graduates (i.e., future teachers) will be able to "identify the need to adapt working methods to a class that is diverse in terms of cognitive, cultural, social, or material status" (Journal of Laws 2024, item 453), so they must have knowledge that is helpful in recognizing, interpreting, and practically applying  various aspects of the culture of the student's environment of origin.
Issues of intercultural education are specified in the standards for the preparation of teachers of grades I-III. Teachers are expected to be able to "work effectively in culturally diverse environments and with children with migration experience, including children for whom Polish is a second language, using intercultural and language teaching skills" (Journal of Laws 2024, item 453). At the attitudinal level, they are expected to be "ready to support appropriate attitudes of children or students towards other cultures" (Journal of Laws 2024, item 453).
In accordance with the standard, a special educator in the field of functional diagnosis (assessment), promoted in the recognition of individual needs, will be able to apply it to students "with adaptation difficulties related to migration experience, adaptation difficulties related to cultural and religious differences" (Journal of Laws 2024, item 453). In particular, they will be able to:
identify the need to adapt working methods to a class that is diverse in terms of cognitive, cultural, social, or material status [and] work with children with special educational needs, including children with adaptation difficulties related to their migration experience, coming from culturally diverse backgrounds or with limited knowledge of the Polish language (Journal of Laws 2024, item 453).
In terms of teachers' actual attitudes towards inclusive education, the results of the research suggest that there is still a need for many measures aimed at changing mindsets, but also – and perhaps above all – at analyzing the conditions for the acceptance of joint learning in a significantly diverse group of students. The available research results from different countries showed different attitudes among teachers. Just a few years ago, skepticism or even reluctance or hostility towards the prospect of accepting students with disabilities into their classrooms (with whom inclusive education was mainly associated) was often identified. This reluctance was also perpetuated in media discourse, often in statements made by teachers or parents on social media. However, Iwona Chrzanowska (2019a, 2019b), who has been researching various aspects of the functioning of the Polish education system for years, believes that the image built on earlier research should be updated. This is important from the point of view of preventing negative stereotypes, but also from the point of view of the possibility of effective change management. 
Contemporary analyses of this issue suggest that some teachers indicate acceptance of the idea of inclusive education (Black-Hawkins, Florian, Rouse 2010; Szumski 2010). However, there are still opposing voices expressing concern about the prospect of educating all students within the framework of mainstream education, or even opposition to joint learning, e.g., with students with intellectual disabilities (Gajdzica 2011). There is also a clear conditioning of accepting attitudes. Teachers indicate what conditions should, or even must, be met in order for inclusive measures to be successful (Chrzanowska, 2019b). It is worth listening to these voices in order to provide effective support to schools and teachers.
Based on a systematic review using the PRISMA method of articles from 2007–2021, available in the Scopus, Web of Science (WoS), Ebsco, and Google Scholar scientific databases, the research team of Rofiah, Kossewska, and Herviani (2023) selected 15 scientific articles on teachers' attitudes towards inclusive education, which were classified according to differentiating factors: three categories based on the occurrence of the differentiating factor: self-efficacy, demographic factors, and pedagogical practices towards problems in the classroom. The research was quantitative in nature and was conducted in 15 different countries in Europe, Asia, and Africa (there were no Polish or Kazakh studies among them). The results showed that teachers' attitudes towards inclusion are related to their sense of self-efficacy and concerns about the appropriate practices they use in the classroom. The gender of teachers is not a clear predictor of attitudes, but their positive attitude, length of service, and marital status significantly reinforce attitudes toward school inclusion.
It has been established that teachers' positive attitudes have a direct impact on the successful implementation of inclusive education. An important personal resource that regulates teachers' attitudes is their sense of self-efficacy. Demographic variables also play a role, but the direction of the relationship is not clearly established and may be moderated by the mediated influence of other variables. The complexity and ambiguity of the determinants of attitudes towards educational inclusion suggest the need for further exploration.
Thus, despite significant changes in teacher training and the expansion of its scope to include inclusive education in certain specializations (e.g., preschool and early school education—which is particularly welcome, given the role of this period of education in shaping the foundations of school skills and life attitudes), there is not much room in the Polish teacher training standard for the effective preparation of all teachers (especially subject teachers, i.e., subject didacticians) in the field of inclusive education. Teachers in this field receive more "additional training" than education in their basic fields of study. This takes place in the form of numerous methodological conferences and seminars, improvement courses, training pedagogical councils, and other training courses, conducted mainly by the central methodological institution, the Center for Education Development (current training offer of the ORE: https://e-kursy.ore.edu.pl/ ), but also by regional and local teacher training institutions. The postgraduate study system also plays an important role (some particularly relevant to the implementation of inclusive education are funded by the Ministry of National Education – see  Machałek, 2022), as does the form of self-improvement known as cooperation and self-education networks, which is developing in Poland. 
Resources supporting teachers, collected on the Integrated Educational Platform of the Ministry of National Education (ZPE, https://zpe.gov.pl/), also play an important role here. The platform contains both materials useful in supporting students with their diverse educational needs (e.g., materials and scenarios useful in the field of multiculturalism and migration) and in the implementation of specific subjects. The school subject closest in content to ethnopedagogical education in the current core curriculum (Regulation of the Minister of Education of June 28, 2024, amending the regulation on the core curriculum..., Journal of Laws 2024, item 996) is social studies. The implementation of its objectives and educational content 
is intended to shape students' civic and pro-community attitudes. The content has been structured according to the concept of environmental circles – from primary social groups through local and regional communities, national and state communities, to the international community (Core Curriculum..., p. 16; Journal of Laws 2024, item 996).
It is assumed that the subject will help students understand the basic principles of social life, including the conditions for the functioning of social groups, local and regional communities, as well as ethnic and state communities, and will broaden the content and awareness of their own local, regional, ethnic, civic, national, and European identity. 
Ethnicity in the core curriculum of Polish schools appears in the context of ethnic community, culture, history, language, identity, and heritage. Patriotism in the context of attitudes (in addition to patriotic attitudes, civic and community attitudes are also mentioned) and values. Since the issue of values is an important aspect of the research project carried out in Kazakhstan, discussed in the next chapter, it is worth emphasizing that the objectives of general education in Polish primary schools include: 
introducing students to the world of values, including sacrifice, cooperation, solidarity, altruism, patriotism, and respect for tradition, caring for the natural environment, including the climate, on a local and global scale, pointing out role models and building social relationships that promote the safe development of students (family, friends). (Core curriculum..., p. 2; Journal of Laws 2024, item 996).
The very concept of "patriotism" is highlighted in the content of the subject of History, in association with such concepts as homeland, nation, state, national symbols, and patriotism. 
Historical memory and critical thinking, civic awareness, and an attitude of respect and responsibility for one's own country are shaped. Values such as goodness, beauty, truth, responsibility, courage, solidarity, justice, tolerance, and freedom are conveyed. (Core curriculum..., p. 2; Journal of Laws 2024, item 996).
The core curriculum also refers several times to the concept of economic patriotism (geography curriculum content). 
However, an important assumption of the Core Curriculum is a comprehensive, holistic approach to content that could be described as ethnopedagogical (literally, there is no such term there). In the description of the program assumptions for the subject of Geography, we can read:
Such a holistic and relational approach promotes the comprehensive development of the student. It helps them to create a comprehensive picture of the world and their homeland, to combine reflection on the beauty and harmony of the natural world with the rationality of scientific knowledge, to develop the ability to understand the functioning of the geographical environment and to evaluate human activity within it, and to form a positive image of Poland and bonds with both their small and large homeland. (Core curriculum..., p. 17; Journal of Laws 2024, item 996).
However, this way of thinking does not apply only to this subject. In the overall picture of the world, the intermingling of patriotic, national, and ethnic content acquired in various subjects is simply an element of education, a natural concern for every teacher. Every subject shapes respect for the native language , and there is space in each to present the achievements of outstanding Poles, build national pride, familiarize students with the national heritage, compare it with the heritage of other nations , strengthen ties with the place of residence and the homeland, and shape positive emotional and spiritual ties with all things Polish. 
The Core Curriculum also aims to break down stereotypes and shape students' attitudes of respect, understanding, acceptance, and appreciation of other cultures while maintaining a sense of the value of their own nation's cultural heritage and identity.  In this context, the learning outcome that students 
justify that different socio-cultural identities (regional, national/ethnic, state/civic, European) can be reconciled; recognize manifestations of xenophobia, including racism, chauvinism, and anti-Semitism, and justify the need to oppose these phenomena (Core curriculum..., p. 17; Journal of Laws 2024, item 996).
These program assumptions show the convergence of the goals of education for life in society with the assumptions of inclusion, the consistency of the values contained in ethnopedagogy and multicultural education with inclusive education as the shaping of competences for life in a diverse society. This requires not only a harmonious combination of content from these areas of scientific knowledge, but also filling the content of future educators' education with consistent content, in line with the expectations of the Core Curriculum and the standards for teacher training.
The diversity of students' needs and abilities is nothing new; it has always been, is, and will continue to be present in schools. Inclusive education devotes a lot of attention to this issue, seeking ways to support teachers in responding to it in the best possible way. One solution could be to change teacher training standards and introduce content into study programs concerning knowledge and skills in functional diagnosis, recognizing and responding to special educational needs, including those resulting from, for example, disabilities or talents, effective support for each student, and universal design. The greatest needs in this area concern subject teachers in primary and secondary schools (Chrzanowska, in: Dąbrowska, 2022, p. 10).
While content related to disability and learning difficulties already serves this purpose, there is still a lack of sufficient multicultural content in the programs. Ethnopedagogy is practically absent from academic curricula in relation to the issue of inclusion. The subject itself is taught at Polish universities – most often in ethnology, sometimes in pedagogy, but in isolation from teacher training standards. Ethnopedagogy classes are offered by the University of Białystok, addressed, for example, to doctoral students (this is undoubtedly linked to the person of the rector of this university, the already quoted Jerzy Nikitorowicz, a leading Polish researcher in intercultural education, creator and main theorist of Polish ethnopedagogy as a scientific discipline). 
In the context of the discussed connection between ethnopedagogy and inclusive education, the presence of ethnopedagogy in the pedagogy program at the Maria Grzegorzewska Academy of Special Education in Warsaw is a positive development. It is the only university in Poland, and probably in Europe, which distinguishes the subdiscipline of "special education" in its name and mission. It is therefore an important sign, both for special educators and educators implementing inclusive education in practice, that it is worth using this subject to shape the inclusive competences of students preparing to work in conditions of diversity recognition. As this approach is still not very popular, Appendix 1 contains excerpts from the ethnopedagogy syllabi at the above-mentioned universities.
