2.2. Research on the development of students' professional values based on ethnopedagogical education - an introduction to the basics of the Kazakhstani research project
2.2.1. Achievements of Kazakhstani ethnopedagogical education and its significance for the design of educational programs
The 21st century is the century of educated people, educated humanity, educated children, and educated specialists. Education and training play a very important role in Kazakhstan's national development strategy, based on the institutionalization of the widespread belief that, in today's world, education is the main instrument for people to achieve their goals, fulfill themselves, and find their place in life. Educated citizens, in turn, are the foundation of an educated and self-developing knowledge-based society. Regardless of the strategic directions of development taken by the country's economy, or which fields of science and life will be the main factors of this development, education is the common factor that allows these fields to develop. This raises the status of the teaching profession and the importance of good, modern education, which is why Kazakh researchers, seeking inspiration and good models, begin the discussion on education in Kazakhstan with questions about the scientific meaning of this concept, where not only the issues of the definition of education are important, but also the questions arising from the philosophy of knowledge about the essence of knowledge and education (ontological aspect), the sources and formation of knowledge (epistemological and logical aspect), its evaluation and duties (axiological, teleological, and ethical aspect), and finally, the methods of knowledge transfer (creating opportunities for discovery) and the effectiveness of education (methodological aspect). These issues are also the subject of discussion in Polish and, more broadly, European pedagogy. Below, we present an excerpt based on the analyses of Karylgash Kazhimova (2015; 2016; 2017a,b,c; 2018a,b; 2024; also Kazhimova et al. 2018), which will allow us to reconstruct an outline of the views of Kazakh pedagogues on these often controversial issues. It forms the theoretical basis for her planned research on ethnopedagogical education in the development of professional values in the education of students at the Ural University. In order to understand them, it is necessary to define not only the concept of ethnopedagogy itself, but also such key concepts as knowledge, education, values, and professional values. In this chapter, we do not discuss their understanding in Poland and Kazakhstan, leaving room for the views that shaped the research project. However, we will refer to them in the last chapter, where we discuss not only the results of the research, but also the possibilities of their use in Poland. This also requires theoretical references that shape the Polish point of view. We give the floor primarily to scientists from Kazakhstan, trying to interfere as little as possible with their point of view. 
According to the assumptions of the ontology of knowledge, human knowledge as an individual is a personal resource, a benefit gained through formal and informal education, which manifests itself and can be observed in human behavior. Knowledge is formed in the psyche of the subject, using the potential of cognitive functions, but also developing them self-sufficiently in the course of learning (acquiring knowledge). This can be treated as an autotelic value of educational activity (learning undertaken intentionally for development), but also as an added value (personal development as an additional effect of educational activity focused on various types of problem solving, instrumental cognition of reality). This applies not only to the improvement of cognitive processes and the constant expansion of knowledge about the world, but also to the improvement of a person's personal culture, the development of their relationships with other people, the acquisition of individual experience and competences (improving the ability to cope in various, not only typical situations), as well as obtaining formal credentials that raise one's social status (qualifications, diplomas, certificates, licenses). Education depends on the environment in which human development takes place. Knowledge is also embedded in the internal structure of human culture (Gershunskiy, 1998, p. 154; cf. also 1986 and 1996).
In the concept of education in the continuing education system of the Republic of Kazakhstan (2009) – similar to the idea of lifelong learning widespread in Europe – "Education is an essential condition for the development of each individual and for social progress. The result of learning is knowledge" (Regulation of the Minister of Education and Science of the Republic of Kazakhstan on the approval of the concept of education in the continuing education system of the Republic of Kazakhstan of November 16, 2009, No. 521).
In Zhantan's Dictionary of Sociological Terms, "knowledge (Latin: scientia, English: knowledge) is a collection of concepts, data, and judgments of people in a certain system" (Zharykbayev and Sangilbayev, 2006, p. 26); however, it can also mean "awareness, cognition, the objective world, the subject, thinking, logic, truth, reason, science, etc., considered in close connection with complex and profound concepts" [theoretical – author's note] (Biekenov and Sadyrova, 2007, p. 19). In the iconic lexicographical work, M. Webster's encyclopedic dictionary, knowledge is considered as: 1) understanding acquired through practice (for example, knowledge of a craft); 2) awareness of something; the space (scope) of awareness; 3) the act of understanding: a clear understanding of the truth; 4) understandable and memorable information. Consequently, knowledge allows us to accumulate experience, values, and information, to integrate and evaluate them (https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/knowledge, accessed: 7.08.2025). Knowledge therefore has a subjective aspect (individual knowledge) and an objective aspect (the knowledge of specific communities, including supra-territorial communities of representatives of various sciences or scientific schools, communities of specialists, e.g., from a specific area of practical activity, or even various types of online communities). Objective knowledge (or objectified knowledge, as it may be discursive in nature) is also recorded in scientific or specialist publications, subject to theoretical and research verification (falsification), review, discussion, paradigmatic agreements, and transformations. The issue of access to sources of knowledge and the critical assessment of its reliability, which is not at all easy, remains important. These are competences developed, among other things, in the course of education, i.e., the transformation of acquired knowledge into information. When knowledge becomes meaningful, it turns into information, and when information is systematized and organized, it becomes the true, deep knowledge of a person—an educated person. Education is the wealth of skills possessed by educated specialists, it is a sufficiently high level of true, operational, complete, and deep knowledge, which means consistency of information, embedded in a specific culture and accumulated individual experience, it is a high level of cognitive development, the need for systematic learning, expanding and verifying one's knowledge, it is the need for self-education and encouraging oneself to be creative (Kazhimova, 2024). This description may seem somewhat idealistic, model-like, setting high standards for a person aspiring to the category of educated people. Referring this to the realities of today, one may sometimes have doubts as to whether all educated people (in the sense of those who have completed their studies and hold academic degrees) are actually educated (in the sense of achieving such high standards as described in the previous passage), this description serves as a model of aspiration, which is a source of continuous self-improvement. And that is what acquiring (not obtaining) an education is all about. Discussing these issues, the authors of the book recalled a memory of one of them when a professor of didactics (at a Polish university) casually gave an ad hoc definition of education in one of his lectures, describing to students that "education is what we have when we have forgotten everything we learned in school." Perhaps this "definition" contradicts the assumptions about the accumulation of knowledge, but paradoxically, it very thoughtfully shows that education is more than just knowledge itself and is expressed primarily in how it changes a person.

The introduction of ethnopedagogical education in higher education institutions also stems from the belief that this knowledge, as well as the values it brings, are desirable attributes of every educated person.

There is a noticeable close relationship between the concepts of "ethnopedagogical education," "public education," "ethnoeducation," "ethnocultural education," and "ethnodidactics" (Table 1). Following Kazhimova (2024, Table 2) in reviewing the concepts of these key terms in Kazakh literature, it can be said that:
 "ethnopedagogical education" means:
"first and foremost, knowledge which, as an image of something objective, colors the characteristics of the inner world" (Kozhakhmetova, 2013);
"knowledge that has cognitive and educational significance in the pedagogical culture of an ethnic group; reconstructed, transmitted knowledge about the ethnic upbringing of Kazakhs. It has, first, an objective feature, i.e., "the property of knowledge to connect something, to know something, and second, "the final conclusion - as a result of knowledge and experience" (Dzhanzakova, 2007);

"public education" means:
"any concept related to the phenomenon of ethnicity. However, this knowledge can be divided into ethnographic, ethnopedagogical, ethnolinguistic, etc., depending on the point of view from which it is studied" (Kozhakhmetova, Taubayeva, and Dzhanzakova, 2005);
while "ethnocultural education":
"aims to preserve ethnocultural similarities through the native language and culture in the educational process and the assimilation of world cultural values" (Nauryzbay, 1995, 1997);
"is a historically established socio-cultural phenomenon that adopts the pedagogy of different ethnic groups, interacts in the educational space on the basis of fundamental national values, and reflects the uniqueness of each nation's educational traditions" (Abildina, 2014).
From the point of view of activities that become both a means and an end in themselves (the essence of so-called autotelic activities is that they are valuable in themselves) in the field of ethnopedagogical education, the following seem to be very important: shaping valuable attitudes towards the environment; shaping a sense of deep involvement in the historical and heroic events of one's nation's past; developing the ability to perceive ethno-cultural values; developing an interest in acquiring specialist knowledge, skills, and competences in the field of ethnopedagogy; involvement in independent amateur creativity or the craft production of folk art (poetic, musical, decorative, and applied); developing a desire for creative self-expression using national inspiration; developing the native language. The latter task seems particularly important in the linguistic situation of the inhabitants of Kazakhstan, which has been consistently introducing the native Kazakh language in place of the dominant and, until recently, official Russian language since regaining sovereignty . Ethnopedagogical education also pays particular attention to issues such as mastering the traditions, folk customs, and culture of one's nation; shaping a culture of patriotism, but also interethnic relations among students based on respect for different times and nations as a fundamental and universal value. A general pedagogical conclusion affecting ethnopedagogical education programs assumes that ethnopedagogical knowledge also covers such a specific area of issues as the pedagogical culture of an ethnic group (Nikitina, Zheleznyakova, and Petukhov, 20020. This is very interesting for educators, as pedagogical culture is a set of views, knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors that often take the form of certain traditions of those involved in the process of educating the younger generation. Since education is a task for entire communities, the pedagogical culture of a given ethnic group or entire nation also shapes certain common views on educational and upbringing issues. Of course, this does not mean that the individuals who make up these groups or this nation do not differ in their individual views, but there are a number of basic educational beliefs and practices characteristic of these groups that translate into the way they think about education and how it is implemented (e.g., parents' educational choices, their educational priorities, the methods of upbringing they use, the behavior they expect from their children, the educational goals they set for them, their support for their education, their attitude towards school and teachers, their respect for education, etc.). A high level of pedagogical culture promotes optimal development and effective education, and certainly also constitutes a value of a given ethnic group that translates into its social capital.
The types of ethnopedagogical knowledge from the point of view of pedagogical theory were described by Sh. I. Dzhanzakova (2007), who distinguished: ethnic pedagogy – covering theoretical knowledge, folk pedagogy – covering spiritual and practical knowledge (existential values shared by the community, understanding oneself in relation to the community and the world outside it, one's own duties, including those towards the community, understanding the meaning of life – everything that underlies the aforementioned pedagogical culture of a given ethnic group), and folk education – covering practical knowledge about ways of transferring knowledge and transmitting related values (including the organization of folk schools or other forms of education in the community).
The goals of ethnopedagogical education can be tailored to the needs and specificities of a given community, but there are also certain goals that seem universal (they may later be specified according to the conditions of a particular community and enriched with specific content and values). The main goals of ethnopedagogical education include: 
shaping a value-based orientation towards the environment; 
developing the ability to emotionally feel the historical achievements of one's people or nation in the past; developing national pride;
developing sensitivity and the ability to perceive ethno-cultural values; 
developing the ability to assimilate specific ethnopedagogical knowledge, skills, and competences; 
getting to know, learning, understanding, and falling in love with one's own tradition and culture; 
creating conditions to meet the cultural requirements and needs of students of different nationalities and ethnic cultures; 
shaping patriotism and a culture of interethnic relations among students, based on tolerance and mutual respect (education for intercultural coexistence; intercultural education).
One of the contemporary Kazakh researchers who dealt with the issue of ethnopedagogical knowledge was Zhakip K. Asanov. He included a substantive formula for ethnopedagogical education in his research work on the didactic foundations of shaping the system of ethnopedagogical knowledge and skills of students (Asanov, 2003). According to Asanov, "ethnopedagogical education is a set of concepts, rules, and laws that combine ethnological and historical material and keywords related to the experience and upbringing of children in the family, as well as ethnopedagogical knowledge that influences moral characteristics" (Asanov, 2003, p. 57). This approach was the basis for the selection of content in the research designed by Kazhimova (2024).
Education is a multifaceted and complex process of imparting knowledge to others and, in constructivist terms, creating opportunities for them to discover it for themselves. This is particularly important in the area of identity formation and shaping, which is how ethopedagogy should be treated. Education as a vehicle for spiritual values is of great cultural and historical significance, but also of personal importance in intergenerational transmission. Ethnopedagogy provides a sense of rootedness and community, which is the basis for social identification and the formation of civic identity. Hence its great importance for society, humanity as a whole, for the individual and their families (clan values). That is why such education becomes a core value – both consciously and intuitively. It is simultaneously a goal, a tool, and a norm of human activity. The educational value of ethnopedagogy is also based on the ability to choose and evaluate one's own and others' actions and deeds from the point of view of their significance for community building. 
When designing research on the conditions for knowledge transfer, one must also ask how to measure it. How can the achieved results be confirmed? In line with current global trends in education, including the Bologna Process, it can be assumed that the indicator of knowledge is the competences acquired. Competence is the ability to apply the acquired knowledge, skills, and abilities to solve a specific problem. Each competence is assessed through the solving of theoretical and/or practical problems. Therefore, the research concept had to be based on assumptions about what knowledge and what competences are expected of a modern educated specialist in Kazakhstan – although the intention was to build an image of a modern educated specialist in the world. It is true that each country adopts its own development strategy, but in the era of globalization, competency profiles are becoming more similar. It can even be said that a satisfactory competency effect should allow for competition without complexes in the labor market, science, culture, etc. to every specialist from every country (global/universal educational achievements), and this individual trait, resulting from roots and ethnic identity, provides an additional effect of diversity and innovation, promoted in global human resource management policies as added value (individual and specific educational achievements). 
In terms of global/universal achievements, it can be assumed that a modern specialist must have in-depth general and specialist knowledge and be highly qualified. They must quickly master new and constantly changing technologies and continuously improve their level of professionalism. This is particularly important for Kazakhstan due to the rapid technological and economic progress that has taken place since regaining independence. A young, developing economy needs well-trained personnel. When assessing competencies, socially important qualities are given priority: activity, tolerance, communication skills, etc., which have a significant impact on increasing competitiveness, as evidenced by OECD research, but also in line with the values cherished by Kazakhs. Moral, civic, and other qualities are important in shaping personal competencies in vocational education. It would be a mistake to view education solely as a "carrier and accumulator of knowledge" – its personal value lies primarily in the acquisition of competencies within one's reach and in accordance with one's preferences and abilities.
Therefore, when dealing with such a complex subject, it is necessary to systematize the basic concepts – the concepts that make up the content of ethnopedagogical education, in accordance with the accepted didactic concept of Asanov (2003; cf. This is an important linguistic foundation for the problem of ethnopedagogical education, strengthening the role of ethnopedagogy as a science. It is interesting to compare the scope of interest of Kazakh researchers with the subject index of the basic Polish textbook Etnopedgaogika w kontekście wielokulturowości i ustawicznie kształtującej się rzeczywistości (Ethnopedagogy in the context of multiculturalism and the constantly changing reality) by Jerzy Nikitorowicz, a leading Polish researcher in this field. Of course, there are common areas (nation, nationality, traditions, patriotism, customs, ethnology, culture, cultural heritage, etc.), but what is most visible is the image of ethnopedagogy focused on folklore, ethnicization, building ethnic identity—one could say nationalization and the search for roots. As presented in Chapter 1, the image of ethnopedagogy described and created by Nikitorowicz is primarily an image of life at the intersection of cultures, pedagogy, and borderland people, multiculturalism, and various aspects of its interpenetration.
In light of these comparisons, it can be said that the key issues of Kazakh ethnopedagogy crystallize around the concept of a community of ethnic cultures: it is a rooting, ethnocentric ethnopedagogy, a pedagogy of permanence, stability, strengthening national identity, and integrating many ethnic identities. In contrast, Polish ethnopedagogy, as represented by Nikitorowicz (2018), is more characterized by the diffusion of foreign cultures, with key concepts such as cultural interpenetration, adaptation, and assimilation, transculturality, integration, inclusion, transgression, but also separatism, exclusion, and nationalism. This is ethnopedagogy of the road, of constant change, mobility, and instability, of "constantly evolving identity," or rather, "constantly evolving identities."
We will omit here, for the Polish reader, a detailed analysis of the content of the distinguished ethnopedagogical subdisciplines in Kazakhstan and the academic education programs in this field at local universities, as it is difficult to directly translate the meaning of this content into the experiences of Polish educators. Karylgash Kazhimova assumes that the national education of the Kazakh people is unique in the world, as the ethnic, historical, and geopolitical situation of this country is unique (as we tried to outline in the first chapter). The stage of development of the state in the early period after regaining independence also requires a special look at the issues of national values.
When analyzing the content of ethnopedagogical education, the author was guided by the ideas of such scholars as: S. Kalieva, K. Zharykbaeva, S. A. Uzakbaeva, K. Zh. Kozhakhmetova, K. K. Shalgynbaeva, Zh. Zh. Nauryzbay, R. K. Toleubekova, R. Duisembinova, U. Abdigapparova, Zh. Asanov, and Sh. I. Dzhanzakova. These sources led to the conclusion that ethnopedagogical education, in essence, can and should be directed towards shaping the inner world of the future teacher, their spiritual and moral character. Ethnopedagogy has special possibilities in this regard, because its content harmoniously combines national values with universal values. It is a valuable source on the basis of which educational opportunities can be created for reflection on the ethnic identity inherent in a nation, for building awareness and deeper understanding of it against the background of the identities of other ethnic groups and nations, as well as for combining national values with professional values. This stage of reflection is necessary in the training of teachers if they are to become mentors to their students later on. 
The selection of ethnopedagogical education content in the designed study was based on  the theoretical and methodological foundations of ethnopedagogy, the concept of ethnocultural education, but also on the main ideas and philosophy of Kazakhstan, knowledge about the foundations of the formation of national, natural, and cultural identity, and the principle of the primacy of the native language (Kazhimova, 2018). Ethnopedagogical education in the training of university specialists in Kazakhstan is also carried out in accordance with the current development strategy of the country, which was also taken into account in the project.
It has been agreed that the types of ethnopedagogical knowledge to be taken into account in the planned educational content are: 
theoretical knowledge in the field of ethnopedagogy;
spiritual practical education – resulting from the principles of folk pedagogy;
practical education – education in the national spirit. These issues are described in detail in the works of Kozhakhmetova (1999, 2013, et al.), Orazbekova (2001, et al.), and Dzhanzakova (2007, et al.).
In the program implemented with students, well-thought-out artifacts of ethnopedagogy (priznaki etnopedagogiki), i.e., objects and products reflecting the value and characteristic symbols of folk education, also played a significant role.
As already mentioned, the national education of the Kazakh people is an educational phenomenon that has no equivalent anywhere else in the world. The concept of "national" is based on respect for the country – its land, language, religion, and deeply rooted traditions, which are often rediscovered after years of Sovietization. 's national education places particular emphasis on the importance of work and instilling national thought and spirit. Shaping national consciousness is particularly important in the context of Kazakhstan's science and economy opening up to Western civilization. In today's era of globalization, this means, for example, the transfer of advanced technologies, achievements, and experiences important for organizing economic production and shaping scientific and technical culture. However, such openness can also pose certain threats: it is necessary to take a critical approach to the stagnation or even devaluation of spiritual values observed in Western countries. Shaping strong axiological roots in the education of young Kazakhs means drawing on our own resources  of spiritual values such as virtue, humanity, brotherhood, decency, morality, and love. Deeply rooted traditional morality provides protection against threats from other cultures. Openness to the world is a necessity, but the country cannot be negatively transformed in the process of globalization taking place at the global level. This means making conscious choices about what Kazakhstan needs, while strengthening what it should preserve and even share with others, in a sense of national pride and conviction about the value of its own heritage. In order to maintain the country's resilience to the negative aspects of globalization, a nation or ethnic group must preserve its upbringing, customs, way of life, position, and thus its identity, without losing its own characteristics. The result of national education is to instill in every citizen a conscious sense of ethnic and national identity, supporting them in finding their place in life as a citizen. This issue is present both in theoretical studies in the field of ethnopedagogy and is constantly raised in the Messages of the President of Kazakhstan (Kazhimova, 2017). In this way, ethnopedagogical education is inextricably linked to national education. It is part of education development policy. 
Today's vision of education is implemented through the right attitude towards the past and present of one's nation. In this context, Gabit M. Musrepov, a Kazakh writer, playwright, and social activist, expressed a conclusion for future generations: "Those who dream of the past are not suited to the present, and those who do not know the best of the past have no prospects" (as cited in Dairabekova et al., 2025.02.24, bns).
The structure of national education programs in Kazakhstan, which was an obvious point of reference for the research project, covers such issues as: national education; national holidays (seasonal, family, religious); folk art (applied, melodic-musical, visual arts, physical education, the art of the word); folklore (artistic, ritual, wedding, children's, death-related); irrationality (myths, totemism, religions); rationality – folk practices (related to nature, education, traditional and non-traditional medicine, household and everyday life); folk wisdom: about education, childbirth, taboos and ethics, traditions and customs, blessings and desires. All this involves the need to learn about the spiritual achievements of world and national culture, to study pedagogy, social sciences, history, to cultivate the customs and traditions of the Kazakh people and other peoples of the republic, to introduce future generations to social, political, economic, and cultural life, to build self-awareness, and to develop the ability to determine one's place in life. 
The culture of interethnic communication and the development of competencies related to cooperation and tolerance in the context of globalization should also be reflected in ethnopedagogical education. National education is an integral part of the education system based on training future specialists with a high degree of identification with national identity. The aim is to develop mature personalities who identify with their country, have a well-developed national consciousness, are capable of contributing to the development of national assets, and combine national and universal values. The educational task is to justify that the core of national education in changing cultural and social conditions remains the native language. This means shaping the national intellectual attitudes of young people in a spirit of respect for the Kazakh language and Kazakh history, culture and mentality, traditions and religion; preparing them for professional activity and high morale as a patriotic attitude towards work. This should ensure the development of the economy, industry, and innovation of the modern Kazakh nation; increase the competitiveness—in a spiritual sense—of education and culture in encounters with other civilizations; and shape awareness of civilizational relations between society and man, and man and nature, in a national spirit.
Ethnocultural education is directly related to the problems of ethnopedagogical education. Today, an ethnoculturally developed personality is a member of an ethnic group, adapted to a multicultural environment. They have high creative abilities, are ready to live in competitive conditions, and have well-developed national characteristics. 
As a result of extensive research since Kazakhstan gained independence in 1991, the methodological and theoretical foundations of ethnocultural education and the science studying this area, Kazakh ethnopedagogy, have been formed. In the independent country, the concept of "Cultural and Ethnic Education in the Republic of Kazakhstan," approved by a decree of President N.A. Nazarbayev, was of great importance in solving the methodological, theoretical, and practical problems of the ethnocultural education of students. This document, significant for science and theory, arose from a vital need. Since gaining independence, the Republic of Kazakhstan has been focused on recognizing human rights and freedoms regardless of nationality, maintaining equality between nations and interethnic stability, promoting Kazakh patriotism, and realizing the ethnocultural interests of its citizens. Positive changes have also taken place in the field of education: new types of educational institutions have emerged, a new generation of textbooks has been developed, national educational programs have begun to be implemented, and national values have begun to return to the content of education.
All this reinforces the argument for the need to analyze the concept of ethnopedagogical education at the university and its active implementation in the pedagogical process. It was assumed that the research would contribute to raising the level of knowledge in the field of ethnopedagogical education among students, which would contribute to the ethnopedagogical education of the entire nation as a whole. The research was guided by the educational ideal of a university graduate educated in modern conditions as a person of high moral and intellectual values: a person with a good heart, a patriot with the personality of a mature sage, with special theoretical and practical training in ethnopsychological and ethnopedagogical competences.

The issue of professional values in the education of teachers in Kazakhstan
The axiological paradigm of higher education in the professional training of students links issues of values with issues of human work.
In scientific literature, human work performed in a specific time-space zone and legal framework is discussed as "professional activity." The main feature of professional activity is professionalism, as a key praxeological distinguishing feature of performing work, as any activity based on professional skills/competences or required formal qualifications. The theoretical basis for professional activity is the philosophical assumption that activity is a means of human communication with the world. In the course of activity, humans, by mastering nature and the environment and creatively changing them, shape themselves as business and creative entities, and the natural environment they have acquired is the object of their activity. This issue is widely represented in both Russian- and English-language literature, as well as in Polish and Kazakh professional literature (J. Legowicz, J. Pieter, T.W. Nowacki, K.M. Czarnecki). The image of these issues in Kazakhstan was influenced primarily by the works of B. G. Ananyev, L. P. Buev, M. S. Kagan, A. N. Leontiev, S. L. Rubinstein and his colleagues, as well as A. M. Bulynin, E. F. Zeer, and I. F. Isaev.  The importance of professional activity in human life was analyzed by E.A. Klimov, A.K. Markova, Yu.P. Povarenkov, N.S. Pryazhnikov, A.M. Stolyarenko, and V.A. Slastenin.  Others (e.g., E. A. Klimova) have addressed the importance of professional values in the activities of individuals and various professional groups (Klimov, 1994).
The axiological paradigm of vocational education also applies to academic education, especially in pedagogical fields. Value is a fundamental concept in axiology. It is a multidisciplinary category that is dealt with not only by axiology, but also by such fields of science as philosophy, sociology, social psychology, pedagogy, and others. 
Axiology (axio - value, logos - teaching) is a science that studies the nature of value, its place in real being, the organization of the world of values and its image in the structure of personality, the relationship between value and nature, society, culture, personality, and values. Axiology is a theory of values that defines and studies the characteristics and properties of things, phenomena, and processes that are capable of satisfying people's needs, desires, and interests. Axiology defines the essence and meaning of values in human existence, the direction and motives of an individual's actions (Zagyparov, 2011).
Axiology as a doctrine developed in the mid-19th-20th centuries as an independent philosophical study, which had been developing for a long time within the framework of philosophy. Recently, axiology as a science of values has entered scientific circulation (Lapie, 1902, as cited in Nagymzhanova, 2018, pp. 164-167). Immanuel Kant, Rudolf G. Lotze, Wilhelm Windelband, Heinriche Rickert, Nicilai Hartmann, Martin Scheler, and others contributed to the development of axiology. The first philosophical analysis of the concept of value was carried out by Rudolf G. Lotze and Gerald Cohen. 
Axiology has also become a permanent fixture in pedagogical sciences and currently plays a very important role in them. Today, there is no doubt that pedagogical knowledge should be based on knowledge about values: 
(...) cutting off human existence from its axiological source means accepting the hypothesis of life on a trial basis and the ability and sufficiency of humans to self-actualize and self-determine themselves and moral norms. Leaving humans to their own devices means leaving them in solitude, which inevitably leads to the experience of nothingness. (Michałowski, 1993, p. 14). 
Education in values is a necessary condition for supporting a pupil in the process of self-realization, because a person who does not have or recognize any values, or who is confused by them for various reasons, has no point of reference in life, no moral compass. They remain lost and helpless. Education should be based on values. 
There are several axiological theories in the history of Western philosophy, such as naturalistic psychologism (Meinong, Perry, Dewey), transcendentalism (Windelband, Rickert), personalistic ontologism (Scheler, Hartmann), cultural-historical relativism (Nietzsche, Dilthey), and sociologism (Weber, Parsons, Talcott). The creators of contemporary axiological concepts were Max Weber and Emil Durkheim, who contributed to defining the meaning of values in the life of society and the individual: Weber (1990) systematized social value as a logical property of every social action; Durkheim (2008) emphasized the importance of the influence of values on everyday human life. Immanuel Kant was the first to use the concept of value in a narrow sense. For Kant, value is a requirement directed at human personality, his independent will. Although from the very beginning the concept of "axiology" has been explained in various aspects, it is still easy to see that there is no clear statement that would be accepted by all scientists. According to philosopher V.P. Tugarikova (1988), values come from knowledge about being, are generated by specific facts that can be known, important aspects of society and nature in the process of action and socio-historical experience of humanity. While philosopher V.A. Vasilenko and other researchers consider values to be "meaningful" in the context of their usefulness in satisfying material and spiritual needs, researchers such as I.S. Narsky and W. Hatcher, consider values to be a kind of "ideal": values are not an approach, a goal, a means to achieve something more important than themselves; they are not an attribute of another entity, but an autotelic entity - an end in themselves. Value is a self-evaluating phenomenon: it remains a value in itself. This point of view is widespread in ethics. In philosophy and sociology , it is said that this concept refers to objects, phenomena, their properties, and thoughts that make up social ideals (Nysanbaev, 1994).
This view of value is that it is an ideal (the highest goal to strive for), i.e., a useful thing that allows a person to satisfy a need; the pursuit of value is a model of effective and purposeful—autotelic—activity. 
In philosophy, the concept of value is interpreted as the basis of human existence: it is its goal – the ideal towards which life strives, and it is its meaning – the content of lived life, and it is also the essence of a specific object, phenomenon, or process for both the individual and the social group or even the whole of society. From a philosophical point of view, values are all those entities, objects, and phenomena that have a useful meaning for humans—not in a utilitarian sense, but in an ideal sense; that is, those that effectively contribute to the fundamental development of human society and the improvement of the human personality. Value serves to reflect and explain the social characteristics of objects in the surrounding world, phenomena in social life and nature – their positive or negative significance for humans and society from the point of view of the goal pursued and the meaning of action. The value system is closely related to socio-historical education, a specific society or social group. Values arise from people's needs, goals, and interests and are part of social experience. Needs activate certain values in human life, activating a person's attitude towards their environment, and interests contribute to the satisfaction of needs, directing our knowledge to objects in the material world, and also form the basis of value relationships. M.S. Kagan (1966) considers the attitude towards value to be a stage of authenticating human needs, related to data on the value and usefulness of the properties of things and phenomena in the environment.
Philosopher T. K. Gabitov (2014), speaking about "values – characteristics," particularly appreciates the fact that these characteristics are established in childhood – "with mother's milk." - as the basis of morality through the native language, as a result of mastering one's own history, culture, customs, and traditions, which brings us closer to the meaning of ethnopedagogy in the process of upbringing as the transmission of values. In turn, A. Z. Alipbek considers value to be a set of valuable things (personal and social interests) that emerge in the process of human life from one's personal interests and needs, placing them above others, thus creating a certain hierarchy of potential or actual choices. Sociologist B. Yerasov believes that the emergence of values causes actions that satisfy human needs to be directed towards a specific goal (Kazhimova, 2024). It is values that transform activities into actions or more structured and long-term activities. This also brings us closer to the starting point of this chapter, namely the concept of "professional activity."
Thus, if we follow the above reasoning, value is the meaning, the distinguishing feature of the meaningfulness and usefulness of something; the human, social, and cultural designation of certain phenomena in being; an assessment of life, work, creativity, thinking; a set of human characteristics, even those externally inherent to an object or phenomenon, action, or ideal, as their subjective or objectified (shared with others) interpretations. Certainly, value is a complex and multifaceted phenomenon.
In science, values are classified according to various criteria and therefore grouped differently. G. Rickert (1914) divides values into six thematic areas: values related to science, religion, art, morality, mature life, and mature "omnipotent love." According to Rickert, the source of the hierarchy of values is the "subject of evaluation" itself.
Values, as already indicated, are divided into objective and subjective. Objective and subjective values are two sides of the relationship between man and the world: the former is its object, and the latter its subject. Objective value is the object of evaluation, and subjective value is its measure and method. The value of an object includes the natural need for things, the symbolic price-pricelessness of a product. It can mean social good, shaped by centuries of cultural heritage, the meaning and practical benefit of scientific truth theory, the criterion of good and evil in human activity, as well as the aesthetic properties of natural and social objects.
Humans evaluate the world around them using values. Their attitude towards real life can only be based on conscious attitudes. Conscious value involves cognitive reflection and evaluation in a broader social context. It refers to ways of setting and achieving goals and constructing social norms. Conscious value examines how valuable a given thing is to us, what significance it has for us. Value determines how important a given object, item, or action is to a person. In this way, values give a specific price (not reduced solely to the monetary dimension, although this is also one of the measures of value) to work and creativity; they constitute the meaning of human life. The customs and norms formed on this basis, reflecting values, are the most important for society, subordinating and regulating human actions. Values orient people towards everyday life in a social environment. Values ensure public order. Value is a component of culture, an essential part of it. In this way, through culture, values regulate people's behavior and determine the order of their real activities. 
Cultural values are divided into material and spiritual. The content of values is related to the cultural achievements of society. It is the sphere of human spiritual activity, indicating the formation of human consciousness, a measure of human spiritual wealth.
In the concept of education in the lifelong learning system of the Republic of Kazakhstan (2009), a value is a socially significant, communally agreed "integral material or social object for an individual, which most people evaluate as goodness, justice, patriotism, which they approve of and share. [Value] serves as a standard, an ideal for all people." Educational values include: the individual, the family, the homeland (native land), work, health (healthy lifestyle), education, cultural heritage, language, and friendship (Republic of Kazakhstan, 2009, p. 7). The Concept of State Youth Policy until 2020 states that the most important thing for young Kazakhs is to develop the following values:
1. Honesty and reliability, honor and nobility;
2. Simplicity, hard work, and helping others.
3. Respect for work.
4. Fidelity to traditions, respect for elders, care for younger people.
5. Friendship, mutual assistance, and unity.
6. Achieving success without fear of difficulties.
7. Love for the homeland, serving its prosperity (Memlekettik zhastar..., 2020).
Values are also divided into vital (e.g., health, existence, life, virtue), social (e.g., social role, social status, social experience, socialization, family, conditions), religious (e.g., God, faith, religious practices), moral (e.g., mercy, simplicity, virtue, morality, honesty, responsibility, duty); aesthetic (e.g., beauty, harmony); political (e.g., law, legality, state, independence), material (e.g., objects, products, precious stones, money, property), natural (e.g., sun, nature, seas, rivers, lakes, mountains, flowers). 
The concept of cultural value is one of the main phenomena in philosophy, social sciences, and pedagogy. Among cultural values, philosophers, progressive thinkers, and educators have always emphasized human rights, freedom, and proper upbringing and education (Figures 6 and 7).
Depending on the time or period of existence, they are divided into specific-historical and eternal values. Depending on the subject recognizing the values, they are divided into universal, national, group, individual, or personal. W. F. Serzhantov identified material and spiritual values; W. P. Tugarikov identified material, socio-political (for example, social honesty, human rights, the role of political parties), and spiritual values. Spiritual values give direction to the purpose and method of human activity, expressed in the form of norms, tastes, and ideals. A. Maslow divided values into higher (truth, virtue, beauty, etc.) and lower (peace, sleep, security, etc.). V. Frankl distinguishes as values those things that give meaning to life: creative values (work, action), experiential values (experiencing beauty, love) and attitudinal values (responding to suffering with dignity) (Kazhimova, 2024).

Acquired values include decency, kindness, respect, compassion, openness, calmness, prudence, responsibility, etc., which a person possesses as intellectual or moral virtues. Absolute values seem eternal, timeless, unchanging, and of great importance to all of humanity. Absolute values include both natural and acquired values . In the context of Kazakhstan's modernization, national values are of great importance. Kazakh researchers agree that national values occupy a special place in the development of the nation's history. The preservation of values such as the native language, ethnic consciousness, the culture of ancestors, the nomadic lifestyle, traditions, customs, and love for the homeland have ensured the nation's existence for centuries. National values are a historically shaped national (patriotic) element that arose from universal values and is formed in the process of preserving the unity and integrity of a particular nation in the course of socio-political changes. It also serves as an ideological driving force for individuals or the state. Values in society regulate the socio-normative and political-legal situation in human behavior and the social environment, prevent the disintegration of political processes, and contribute to making citizens aware that they are an integral part of this process. Values shape, develop, and unite humanistic relations between nations.
Universal human values do not exist only in their "pure" form, on their own. National values are part of universal human values. National and universal human values reflect the value of things, phenomena, and ideas for a specific society or global community.
National values are the source of a nation's resilience. Therefore, universal values include life, nature, goodness, happiness, creativity, truth, responsibility, respect, dignity, faith, honor, morality, health, nature, necessity, beauty, work, curiosity, etc. National values include traditions, customs, language, national unity, culture, freedom, national integrity, national honor, an educated and insightful generation, family relationships, homeland, country, land, civilization, freedom, solidarity, spiritual values, social values, religion, tolerance, social order, social justice, national honor, national security, etc. As can be seen from this chain of values, national and universal values are not contradictory: they complement and enrich each other's content and mutual meanings. These values will never become obsolete because they are a force that cannot be measured by anything, and they contribute to strengthening the foundations of the country and the consciousness of the Kazakh people. The features that unite these two categories of values as a whole are: community (a determinant of a person's belonging to both the local community and humanity as a whole) and integrity (a sense of continuity and coherence of human destinies and systemic belonging, despite changes accompanying the development of society, including the transition from one form of state to another). As a result, this national value becomes the National Code, evoking a sense of national and human duty to preserve this value and pass it on from generation to generation. This is how a country becomes a country and a nation becomes a nation (Kazhimova, 2024). 
The research work of the Institute of Political Science and Sociology of the National Academy of Sciences of the Republic of Kazakhstan, entitled Universal and National Values in a Changing Society, presents the highest values for Kazakh society and for individuals living in that society. These are: peace in the family, unity, peace in the country, interethnic harmony, and decent wages dependent on success; freedom, economic independence, promotion of the country's achievements; transparency in business (Kazhimova, 2024).
In the 1990s, researchers identified several values as a result of their research: diligence (perseverance) - to work hard to bring a business to completion and overcome life's difficulties; help and care - to help others, to care for them; honesty - speaking truthfully and doing what one believes is right; justice - being a fair leader. Here, both prosperity and well-being are identified individually as a prerequisite for sustaining people's physical and mental activity (Kazhimova, 2024).
The famous sociologist, Professor S. S. Frolov, identifies people's values in the work process: success (including health and safety), wealth (various material achievements), skills (professionalism in a particular activity), education (knowledge, information potential, cultural connections), honor (status, fame, honor, prestige). The group of moral values includes virtue, honesty, and other human qualities. A value such as power is one of the universal and important values because it allows many values to be shaped (Kazhimova, 2024).
To feel like a full-fledged person, you also need to be able to see the beauty of your surroundings. It would also be useful to make a list of values that are an integral part of your life, and even the meaning of your life.
Every person has basic life values that are part of their daily existence. Sometimes they can be found in a certain period of time and are directly related to a person's sphere of life, upbringing, and environment. Even if a person has different values in childhood, over time, a certain value system may change depending on age, priorities, status, some may be supplemented, some may be changed.
Psychologists have begun a comprehensive study of a person's character, aspirations, and goals from the very beginning. Experts have compiled a list of a standard value system in psychological terms: family life (love, mutual understanding, harmony in the family, children); professional activity (work, business, status); education; spiritual life (inner world, faith, spiritual maturity); political and social activity (communication, relationships, power, career); material well-being; interests (friendship, self-development, personal maturity); beauty and health (Kazhimova, 2024).
A value system helps a person understand others. In any situation, each person's reaction will be different. For example, in a stressful situation, one person refuses to look for a solution to an important issue, while another searches and struggles until they find a solution. The diversity of such actions is directly related to the values that a person has and, consequently, to the values that guide them.
Value is embedded in social consciousness and culture as a measure of discipline and disorder, virtue and cruelty, truth and falsehood, justice and injustice. Values presented in a normative form give direction to human activity. In any case, a value only acquires subjective meaning when one encounters it. Personal values are general components consciously perceived by a person, constituting the meaning of life.
Values are important to a person, allowing them to defend themselves and protect themselves from other people's intrusions into their lives. Personal values belong to each person. While some values belong to only one person, some values can also connect different people, grouping them around certain categories of values. For example: freedom of creativity, innovative ideas, respect for intellectual property – these are values that distinguish creative people. Faith, God, morality, honesty, charity – these connect followers of certain religions (although they may be defined differently). Social and economic justice, equality, freedom – these are the main ideas of democrats. Tradition, nation, religion, family, and state – these are the values shared by conservatives. Values connect people and define the common ethos of their activities. However, they are universal in meaning: there are values that (almost) all people share, regardless of the above-mentioned divisions, but also other divisions. These include, for example, peace, freedom, the success of loved ones, respect, and love. Shared values help people understand each other and build relationships of cooperation, help, and support. The lack of values or the adherence to opposing values leads people to divide into opponents, adversaries, and even rivals or enemies (Kazhimova, 2024).

To explain the essence of the concept of a teacher's "professional values," it is useful to compare them with the concept of a teacher's professional competencies. A teacher's competencies are understood as their theoretical and practical preparation for carrying out pedagogical activities. Professional competences result from the individual abilities of a teacher, allowing them to make independent and effective decisions in solving pedagogical problems. This requires knowledge of pedagogical theory and the development of skills and abilities to apply it in practice. This is a professional and personal characteristic of a teacher, reflecting the level of knowledge, skills, abilities, and experience that allows them to fully carry out their pedagogical activities. However, competencies are more than just knowledge and skills, as the concept also includes a certain attitude of openness: a readiness to act (Figure 10). This is clearly illustrated by the example of professional competencies, in which it is expressed as a readiness to undertake and solve professional tasks.

In modern management, employee competencies are becoming increasingly important, and the competency model contrasts with the model of duties assigned to a position. Especially in complex, specialized professions, such as teaching, the competency-based model expresses the expectation that the employee will deal with emerging problems in a flexible manner, rather than automatically performing the tasks on the list of duties assigned to the position (especially since not all situational tasks can always be predicted in every job):
Flexibility is becoming a key factor in today's business environment, and awareness of competencies and skills within an organization is becoming a priority. According to Deloitte, 71% of employees already perform tasks outside their core responsibilities. What's more, 65% of employees report that the competencies and skills needed to do their jobs have changed in the last two years. This phenomenon is also confirmed by the latest PWC report, according to which as many as 44% of key job skills will change in the next five years. In light of this data, limiting the role of an employee to their basic duties or making personnel decisions based solely on their position is becoming increasingly impractical. Viewing competencies and skills as organizational resources allows for better management and timely response to changes, e.g., through flexible modification of development paths within the organization (Tyczyj, brw).
Professional values seem to play a major role in the competency model. They are the main signposts that allow you to choose, master, and perform your professional activities: they allow you to be more competent in situations that require choices and flexibility. Moreover, professional values are a tool that ensures a personally and socially meaningful outcome in any professional activity: value-based work stands out for its significance and importance.
Historically, the emergence of professional values as an internal guide is directly explained by the emergence of the teaching profession. But professional values are not eternal values, they are subject to change. In their development, professional values are continued according to their relevance - their adequacy to professional needs. They can be transformed when changing needs require it; new values can emerge. A lack of understanding and internalization of professional values by future specialists, and even a lack of exposure to them in teacher training (e.g., in academic programs), imposes limitations on life, social, and professional experience and is evidence of unpreparedness for productive pedagogical activity. Shaped professional values form the basis of a humanistic attitude in the formation of a teacher's personality and determine the proper nature of the relationships built between the subjects of the educational process. 
In a broad sense, professional values are essential for satisfying the personal and social needs associated with the performance of pedagogical activities. The material side of professional values is made up of specific forms of social values that reflect teleological orientations and social norms. Professional values, which define the purpose and tasks of professional activity, semantically complement its content, being in this area a vector of personal development and the main direction of choice and mastery of professional activity (Kazhimova, 2014). E. N. Shiyanov (1991, p. 79) systematized this as follows: "pedagogical value is the means that allow the teacher to satisfy material, spiritual, and social needs , goals oriented towards social and professional activity." According to the author, these are: values related to the self-affirmation of the individual in society, in the social environment, based on the needs of the individual and compliance with the duties of the teaching profession; values related to satisfying needs in relationships; values of self-improvement; values of self-expression; and utilitarian-pragmatic values (Shiyanov, 1991).

Values related to the personal and motivational sphere of the teacher: the prospect of professional maturity; continuation of family traditions; compatibility of the profession with preferences and interests; the desire to be the center of attention.

Rokeach (1969) groups values into two classes: terminal - belief in the desire to achieve the ultimate goal of independent existence; instrumental - belief that in a given situation one of the actions or personality traits dominates. This classification corresponds to the traditional value as a goal and value as an instrument.
Analyzing this value system, D. A. Leontiev grouped it in his own way. Interesting work, productive life, creativity, active life activity (among terminal values) were assigned to professional value; responsibility, business efficiency, strong will, diligence were assigned to instrumental value (Isaev, 2004).
Analyzing this system of values, D. A. Leontiev grouped it in his own way. Interesting work, productive life, creativity, and activity (among terminal values) were assigned to professional values, while responsibility, efficiency, strong will, and diligence were assigned to instrumental values. In turn, I. F. Isaev (2004) systematized the professional values of teachers related to the system of professional and pedagogical activity, based on the concept of ultimate and instrumental values, but in a slightly different way. The researcher classified values as socio-pedagogical, professional-group, and individual-personal:
Socio-pedagogical values are values realized on a social scale, concentrated in social consciousness in the form of morality, religion, and philosophy.
Professional-group values are a set of views, concepts, and norms that guide and organize pedagogical activity; this union of values ensures integrity, stability, and variability.
Personal and pedagogical values are goals, motives, ideals, guidelines, etc., forming a system of shaping a cumulative orientation towards values, reflecting the teacher's personal worldview (Isaev, 2004).
This system includes: values related to the self-affirmation of the individual in the social and professional environment (the importance of the teacher's work in society, the status of pedagogical activity, the perception and understanding of the profession by loved ones, etc.):
values that satisfy the need for communication and expand the circle of communication (communication with children, team members, reference groups, exchange of spiritual values);
values aimed at developing independent creativity (the opportunity to develop professional and creative skills, involvement in global culture, continuous self-improvement, pursuing favorite activities, etc.);
values that enable self-fulfillment (creative nature of teaching, interest in the teaching profession in a romantic vision, opportunity to support children in need);
values that allow for the satisfaction of pragmatic needs (duration of paid leave, promotion, etc.) (Isaev, 2004).
Among these values, we can distinguish between target values (in themselves) and instrumental values, classified according to the content of the subject. The latter serve as a means to achieve other, higher, more significant goals or professional values.  The latter are achieved for their own sake, as their gratifying value consists of the creative nature, status, and social significance of the teacher's work, responsibility to the state, the opportunity for self-affirmation, and love for students. Values of this type are the foundation for the development of both the teacher and the student. Goal values play a dominant axiological role within a given system of pedagogical values. After all, it is goals that give fundamental meaning to all pedagogical activity. The goal of pedagogical activity is determined on the basis of specific motives resulting from needs. This allows us to establish the place of values in the hierarchy of needs, which consists of self-development, self-realization, self-improvement, and others. 
Focusing on personal development and student development, as well as professionalism, are intertwined: the former is contained within the latter, because when looking for ways to achieve the goal of pedagogical activity, teachers choose a professional strategy based on developing themselves and others. The state's educational policy and the level of development of pedagogical sciences, which in axiological and semantic terms are the most important factors in pedagogical activity, influence the so-called instrumental values. Instrumental values consist of subsystems that are closely related to each other: pedagogical activity focused on solving professional, educational, personal, and developmental tasks (teaching and education technologies); communication activities in solving personal and professional orientation problems (communication technologies); activities reflecting the teacher as a subject. Professional value in the work of a teacher consists of value-attitudes, value-properties, and value-knowledge. Value relationships allow the teacher to purposefully and appropriately organize the pedagogical process and relationships between subjects. 
The result of pedagogical activity can be assessed differently depending on (the definition of) the teacher's success, and therefore on the degree to which their professional and personal needs are met. In terms of values, it is also important for teachers to treat themselves as individuals and professionals. Teachers have a real "self," a retrospective "self," an ideal "self," a reflective "self," and a professional "self." The dynamics of these images are determined by the level of the teacher's personal and professional development. In the hierarchy of pedagogical values, personal characteristics occupy the highest ranks. After all, they manifest the personal and professional character of the teacher. Personal values include personal characteristics, status role determinants, and professional activities, which are numerous and interrelated. These characteristics are directly related to the teacher's predictive, communicative, creative, empathetic, intellectual, reflective, and interactive abilities. Values-attitudes and values-properties cannot be used to conduct pedagogical activities without values-knowledge. Values-knowledge/values-education include not only psychological, pedagogical, and subject knowledge, but also the level of awareness and the ability to choose and evaluate based on a conceptual-personal model of pedagogical activity (Kazhimova, 2024).
Value-education and the business system, placed and organized in a specific order based on pedagogical theories of development, socialization of the individual, patterns and principles of upbringing, can determine the scope of expectations and even be the basis for expectations of a teacher's professional competence. It is worth noting that this is not a restrictive framework (not every teacher has to be the same, formed according to a "prescriptive model"), but a field for professional growth. The competency model described above allows for reconciling the expectations of the system, which sets certain common goals, values, tasks, and expected competencies, with space for human individuality and diversity, as teachers bring their personality and uniqueness to their professional relationships with students. It is possible to effectively fulfill one's role while maintaining basic professional values, in a slightly different way than other teachers. What is more, it can be said that teachers "work with their personality" because by bringing this uniqueness and individuality, they give their students a better chance of growing up as unique, free, creative individuals who fulfill their potential in accordance with the common good, which is guarded by commonly recognized values. Therefore, the issue of teachers' professional competences is so closely linked to the issue of values, which should lead to what is common, through this and with respect for what is individual. This last sentence is perfectly filled with ethnic and national, patriotic experiences, which leads us to conclude our professional considerations with a methodological bracket from the field of ethnopedagogy. The combination of professional psychological and pedagogical knowledge with internalized issues of duty (teleological) and axiological issues creates conditions for the development of creativity, enables work with open professional information (national and foreign methodological resources open to everyone), as well as unlimited access to information about the world (including misinformation and ideological distortions that are inevitable in the era of globalization). Thus prepared and equipped with professional values, teachers can face the gifts but also the threats of globalization, solve not always predictable pedagogical problems at the level of contemporary theory and technology, using productive techniques of creative pedagogical thinking (Kazhimova, 2024). A teacher who is to be a guide for their students cannot feel lost in the modern world themselves. In this context, it is necessary to emphasize once again, following I. F. Isaev (2004), how much pedagogical value groups constitute the core, the substantive basis of professional and pedagogical culture, which, however, cannot be built in an axiological vacuum, but in a world of real, personal, and character-building experiences. In accordance with the research problem and the theoretical analyses carried out, the following groups of values were distinguished in the development of students' professional values based on ethnopedagogical education:
Group 1 values: GOALS - revealing the meaning and essence of professional and pedagogical activity;
Group 2 values: MEANS - revealing the importance of the ways and means of carrying out professional and pedagogical activities;
Group 3 values: COMMUNICATION - revealing the importance and essence of communication as the main mechanism (main medium) for carrying out comprehensive pedagogical activities;
Group 4 values: KNOWLEDGE - revealing the importance and essence of psychological and pedagogical knowledge in the process of carrying out pedagogical activities;
Group 5 values: QUALITY - revealing the essence and importance of a teacher's personal qualities.
The groups of pedagogical values distinguished in this way complement each other and create a syncretic (holistic) axiological model. 
The developed structural and substantive model consists of the following blocks: 1) values-goals, 2) normative content, 3) content-process, 4) technological content, and 5) evaluation criteria.
In the value-target block of the model, we emphasize the ethnocultural conditions and external environmental factors that influence the development of students' professional values based on ethnopedagogical education. Currently, these are primarily: globalization, modernization of social awareness, and social challenges in the field of educating competitive specialists. The target orientation of the model is focused on raising the level of professional knowledge and entrepreneurship among students, shaping their needs and interest in the image of the profession; on developing professional independence and professional improvement. The goal is the most important element of the model, ensuring the effective organization of the pedagogical process.
The value-goal block serves as the basis for the need to achieve the goal. Regulatory documents (legal and programmatic frameworks) concerning the organization of vocational education define the basic principles, directions of organization of this education, and the country's educational policy. These documents constitute the regulatory block of the model. Ideally , the vocational education profile of each student should correspond to the requirements of society.
In accordance with the task, a content and procedural block is defined. We offer the following stages of the process of shaping students' professional values based on ethnopedagogical education: internalization - the transformation of external activity into internal activity. This concept was first introduced by French psychologists J. Pierrot, J. Pione, A. Wallon, and L. S. Vygotsky in Soviet scientific circles. Internalization is a process that belongs exclusively to humans. The means of internalization is the word, and the means of transition from situational to situational is the act of speech. Through the process of internalization, a person can master the accumulated experience of humanity, the experience of ancestors, even of people they do not know, regardless of distance; everything happens through the word. The correct use of words influences the correct perception of the concept of an object, phenomenon, or process. According to the researcher, all functions of the human psyche are shaped on the basis of work or activity as an external, social form of communication with people. According to L.S. Vygotsky, internalization is the transformation of external action into conscious internal action of a person.
Thus, in our example, the stage of internalization is understanding, understanding the external need for a profession, tactile perception of a task, reflection, immersion in the depths of consciousness.
Identification (uniqueness) is the process of integration (identification) of the subject itself with other people or with a group based on the creation of an emotional bond, as well as the acceptance of individual norms and values as if they were its own. Identification is a mechanism by which the subject puts itself in another person's place. Identification is associated with a sense of belonging, through which a person identifies with the group to which, in his opinion, he himself belongs. In our example, the future specialist's compatibility with the same profession, harmony with the profession. Internalization is the conscious perception of the environment, the active application of learned norms and values, the presentation of important moments as the result of one's own actions.
