Methodological assumptions of the research conducted
The research problem posed in the project carried out at the M. Utemisov West Kazakhstan University in Uralsk was an attempt to explain the place of ethnopedagogical knowledge as a source of substantive content and professional values in the education of future specialists – educators. The research task was to build a model of professional preparation.
Between 2015 and 2018, experimental work was conducted at L.N. Gumilov Eurasian National University in Astana and M. Utemisov West Kazakhstan State University. A total of 107 students majoring in Social Pedagogy and Self-Awareness took part in the experiment. The experimental group consisted of 53 students from M. Utemisov West Kazakhstan State University , while the control group consisted of 54 students from L.N. Gumilov Eurasian National University in Astana. 
The experiment consisted of three stages: identification, formation, and observation.
At the stage of defining the scope of experimental work, the following research tasks were carried out:
The main directions of development of the national education system, the content of national education and ethnopedagogical education, as well as the national values contained therein, which are reflected in the basic legal acts of the Republic of Kazakhstan, were analyzed; this was considered to be the basic determinants of the development of this subject in strategic documents setting out the prospects for social and economic change in the country.
The current state of teaching the subdiscipline (academic subject) of ethnopedagogy at universities in Kazakhstan was analyzed.
Using methods of diagnosing professional values (K. Zamfir's method, modified by A. Rean, "Diagnosing the actual structure of individual value orientations" and "Professional value"), the level of professional values of students developed on the basis of ethnopedagogical education was determined, and S.S. Bubnova's method was used to determine the hierarchy of values recognized by them.
The content of the Ethnopedagogy course was analyzed from a didactic perspective using Bloom's taxonomy (an analysis of the Ethnopedagogy course program according to objectives and tasks based on Bloom's taxonomy is included in Appendix 3 - Table 9).
Empirical pedagogical research methods were used to determine changes in the level of students' professional values related to ethnopedagogical education as part of comprehensive research implemented in a pedagogical experiment. The following were used: observation, interviews, questionnaires, test questionnaires, and statistical methods to determine the initial and final levels and reflect the differences in the experimental and control groups in terms of professional values and the hierarchy of values of students. The original methodology of S. S. Bubnova ("Diagnosing the actual structure of individual value orientations" and "Professional value") was applied.
According to Zamfir's methodology, motivation for professional activity is influenced by a combination of internal and external factors. Internal factors include personal values, beliefs, and desires, while external factors include environmental conditions, social influences, and external rewards (Salifu and Agbenyega, 2013). A. Rean's modification of this methodology emphasizes the role of individual agency and the ability to proactively shape motivators, specifically as follows:
A key element of Zamfir's methodology is the concept of setting clear and achievable goals as a basis for shaping and maintaining motivation and focusing on the main, designated line of development in professional activity: A. Rean's modification emphasizes the importance of linking these goals to personal values and aspirations perceived in the long term. By consciously placing professional activity in a broader teleological and axiological context, people find it easier to maintain motivation and goal orientation even in the face of challenges and failures.
The second important aspect of Zamfir's methodology is the motivational role of feedback: positive reinforcement (recognition of achievements) in sustaining motivation vs. negative reinforcement as a demotivating factor. A. Rean's modification emphasizes the need for constructive feedback as conducive to learning and development, not just results orientation. A high level of motivation and commitment can be maintained by creating a culture of continuous improvement and development. 
Zamfir's methodology also takes into account the influence of social and environmental factors on motivation. Motivation and engagement are fostered by a supportive and positive work environment, while a toxic or unfavorable one can weaken them. A. Rean's modification emphasizes the importance of creating a network of colleagues and mentors who provide guidance, support, and inspiration. The author also emphasizes the significant impact of building strong professional relationships on motivation and overall job satisfaction.
Zamfir's methodology examines the role of internal and external rewards in motivating professional activity: external rewards (e.g., raises, promotions) can provide short-term motivation; internal rewards (a sense of fulfillment and personal development) are more effective in the long term. A. Rean's modification emphasizes the need to use internal motivators that appeal to autonomy, mastery, and the purpose of professional activity. A sense of meaning and satisfaction from work helps maintain a high level of motivation and mental resilience (Mendzhment, 2024.11.13).
According to this concept, motivation is not a static state, but a dynamic process requiring constant attention and improvement, self-reflection, and introspection in understanding one's own motivational factors, which indicates simultaneous work on values. Regular (self-)assessment and self-reflection on one's own values, goals, and sources of self-fulfillment allow one to build one's own system of internal motivation and, as a result, to improve oneself and one's professional activity (Salifu and Agbenyega, 2013). Rean's modification in particular emphasizes the need to link professional activities with personal values and internal motivations, which is an important guideline for training courses that develop teachers' professional values, for which ethnopedagogical content can be a good axiological basis and even constitute valuable, desirable material. By setting valuable goals for oneself, preferably aligned with some higher goal (such as strengthening the country's prosperity and working for the national good), seeking constructive feedback, developing positive relationships, and using internal rewards, people can increase their motivation and achieve greater success in their professional activities, while contributing to the realization of patriotic goals.
The professional motivation of the students surveyed was assessed on a scale of 1 to 5, using K. Zamfir's method as modified by A. Rean (Appendix X). The highest score was 5 and the lowest was 1. Students rated "desire for promotion" as the highest motivation and "desire to avoid punishment and negative situations" as the lowest. S.S. Bubnova's method was used to assess the specific structure of individual value orientations. As part of the method, students were presented with 66 values (described in the theoretical part of the introduction to the study). According to the instructions, students were asked to answer "yes" or "no." A total of 66 values were grouped into 11 factors—categorical values that can also shape actual motivation to work. These include: 
Having fun; relaxation;
High material well-being;
Seeking and enjoying beauty;
Helping people and showing them compassion;
Love;
Learning new things about the world, nature, and people;
High social status and managing people;
Recognition and respect for people and influencing others;
Social activism to bring about positive change in society;
Communication;
Health.
Detailed analyses of all 66 values are available in Kazhimova's research report (2024). However, in this study, we will present more general results and conclusions, giving Polish readers a broader overview of the situation , although we also refer to some specific observations in our research conclusions.

In this section, we omit Kazhimova's analyses of the specific ethnopedagogical content currently present and suggested for inclusion in academic education in Kazakhstan. Kazhimova (2024) argues in her monograph that the nature of the subject of ethnopedagogy and its importance in the education of specialists also requires a reflective didactic analysis of the conditions for improving the quality of education.  The source of the development of students' professional values are or may be ethnopedagogical subjects studied at universities as compulsory or optional components, but the way in which they are implemented is also important.  In accordance with the research question posed, it should be assumed that it is not only the subject itself, but also the quality of education at the university that will influence the final educational outcomes. This is important because in the structure of academic achievements, the main emphasis is usually placed on knowledge and skills, while social competences are treated somewhat less rigorously and are not verified as thoroughly as the two previous categories of outcomes. These experiences are comparable to those of Polish academics. 
In the case of ethnopedagogical education, it is a matter of both knowledge and skills (especially in the case of pedagogy students, who will themselves teach similar subjects to their students in the future) and attitudes and the values underlying them, as documented by the entire argument presented so far. Shaping attitudes as an educational priority requires slightly different methodological tools and different psychological conditions for the formation of these attitudes. 
N. Ippolitova and N. Sterkhova (2012) treat psychological and pedagogical conditions as a set of related educational and material-spatial possibilities of the environment focused on the development of the individual, and through their quality allowing them to productively implement the learning process. Based on this conclusion, we define the psychological conditions for the development of students' professional values based on ethnopedagogical education. The following should be taken into account here:
The age and psychological characteristics of students. The effectiveness of any activity in class largely depends on the relevance of the content to the age and characteristics of the learners. Since we are working with future specialists, it is advisable to give them problem-based tasks, which are largely aimed at developing professional qualifications and therefore gradually become more complex. Presenting students with tasks of maximum complexity directly reduces their interest in finding a solution.
The need to create a creative and relaxed atmosphere during classes. Ethnopedagogical content is so rich and diverse that it allows for a whole range of inspiring activities.
Active interaction between the teacher and students. The teacher remains in the role of advisor, guide, and assistant.
Taking into account the level of professional and intellectual development of individual students and the group. This will help the teacher choose effective methods, means, and forms of training.
In the context of the goals of ethnopedagogical education, the psycho-pedagogical conditions for the development of students' professional values can and should take into account:
the formation of personally meaningful motivations for students to develop professional values;
the joint use of traditional and innovative teaching aids; this allows students to experience the differences between the two approaches, which they can use in their future work. 
the use of research methods in lessons and in students' educational and cognitive activities in cooperation with others, which allows them to encounter another person as a different, always unique individual with their own personal history (including ethnic history), but also to develop professional independence and autonomy and create space for their own history.
the use of hermeneutic orientation in the learning process. This means the ability to read and write with understanding, hermeneutic work with information (collecting facts necessary to solve a known problem, analyzing them, forecasting, constructing patterns, reaching a justified conclusion, etc.). The use of this concentration develops students' professional creative potential and their ability to make decisions when dealing with professional situations in pedagogical activities.
As a result, psychological and pedagogical conditions strengthen the emotional and personal component in shaping a positive attitude towards the development of professional values based on ethnopedagogical education, stimulate cognitive interests, develop motivation to master a professionally relevant axiological orientation, and ensure its implementation in pedagogical practice.
The didactic conditions are aimed at mastering the values of the teaching profession in the process of theoretical preparation of students for lectures, practical classes, and independent creative work. The teaching status is determined by the use of various forms of work, methods, and techniques in the educational process. Today, little ethnopedagogical knowledge can be conveyed using the traditional methods, techniques, and technologies that we use in the learning process. Therefore, another task facing scientific research is to incorporate new techniques, technologies, and sources of knowledge (including direct experience of contact with different cultures and contact mediated by the media). The close connection between fieldwork (close to the ethnographic method) in the subject of Ethnopedagogy and pedagogical practice yields effective results. The materials developed by the student can be collected in a portfolio, analyzed in class, and then used in their teaching practice. It is a valuable experience to learn about innovative solutions in educational and cultural institutions in the field of national education and upbringing, to consult with teachers, to participate in other events, 
The development of students' professional values based on ethnopedagogical education depends largely on the professional competence of teachers. Today, universities need experienced teachers who are able to guide activities aimed at developing students' professional values, who have their own well-formed and internalized professional values, who are fully proficient in their profession, and who work creatively, supplementing their knowledge with new information. They are inquisitive, with a well-developed personal and professional identity, and also possess spiritual, artistic, and creative abilities, thanks to which they are more credible in immersing themselves in cultural activities (e.g., through singing, dancing, storytelling, painting, and creative crafts).
Thus, the further development of ethnopedagogy largely depends on scientific, but also methodological ideas and innovations brought into educational practice. Therefore, specialists, theorists, and practitioners should work together to explore the potential of this area of activity and strengthen ethnopedagogy in the education process, both for pupils and students, especially students of pedagogy.

Research results and conclusions
Karylgash Kazhimova's three-year pedagogical experiment yielded many interesting observations, which she describes in detail in her monograph and other publications (Kazhimova 2017, 2018, 2024). The statements and works of students collected during this period deserve separate discussion, but there is no room for them here due to the need to open new threads. In this section, we will only present some of the most general results, i.e., the effects of changes in the level of values that are key from the point of view of professional specialization, including changes in the hierarchy of values. We will only summarize the remaining results, and for complete tables and statistical calculations, we refer to Kazhimova's full report (2024). In it, the author traced changes in 66 specific values (here we present only 11 categorical values), examined the significance of differences and correlations.
A methodological dilemma in longitudinal social research is always the inference of factors influencing change, while other factors are also at play: the maturation of participants, the process of studying and delving into a chosen specialization, and teaching practice. It is impossible to control all of them, but based on the canon of difference, it is possible to draw conclusions with some caution about the changes that have taken place in the experimental and control groups (those who took and did not take classes in ethnopedagogical education during their studies). 
As the first series of results, we present an assessment of the professional motivation of both groups studied (between 157 and 16 students answered each question – not all of them provided all answers). Chart 1 illustrates the distribution of results concerning the importance of the material aspects of this motivation. Not just roots: ethnopedagogy and multicultural projects and the promotion of Kazakhstan on the international stage
Ethnopedagogy encompasses both internally oriented educational activities and goals (rooting, identification with an ethnic group, shaping national identity) and externally oriented ones (encountering another culture/other cultures, multicultural projects). Internal projects in Kazakhstan seem to be an obvious task for pedagogy strengthening political change, and so far, the reading may give the impression that this is the only direction of ethnopedagogical activities. However, this is not the case, and for a complete picture of Kazakh ethnopedagogy, we will also present activities at the intersection of cultures. 
Kazakhstan's multicultural activities and projects include both tangible and intangible initiatives aimed at preserving and promoting the country's diversity, both within its territory and abroad, as well as in virtual space – on the Internet and social media. They serve to promote the country internationally. The most well-known initiatives of this type include:
the inclusion of Kazakhstani sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List 
promoting cultural diversity through various festivals and exhibitions,
state programs aimed at supporting languages and the development of creative industries.
The UNESCO World Heritage List includes many Kazakhstani material and cultural sites that reflect various aspects of the country's complex history and its extraordinary nature. The list of places worth visiting in this country is long, and the most famous architectural sites include, for example:
The Mausoleum of Khoja Akhmet Yasawi, a prominent 12th-century Sufi master, built between 1389 and 1405 on the orders of Timur, the ruler of Central Asia. The mausoleum is considered an outstanding achievement of Timurid architecture. It is located in southern Kazakhstan, in the northeastern part of Turkestan (the city of Yasi). 3.1. Ethnicity - between self-knowledge and knowledge of the Foreign/Other - pedagogical conclusions 

Experiences related to ethnopedagogical education can vary in nature. After reviewing the results of Karylgash Kazhimova's research, it turned out that the content of ethnopedagogical education used in a project implemented in Kazakhstan differs from Polish expectations and experiences, which are currently mainly related to the problems of migration and multiculturalism in the face of foreignness and even cultural hostility (fears and active resistance of some communities to the influx of immigrants, mainly from Africa, war fatigue in Ukraine and the associated presence of large numbers of Ukrainians, difficulties in adapting for Poles returning from abroad). 

Figure 15. Main directions of development and challenges of ethnopedagogy in Kazakhstan and Poland in the context of educational inclusion (source: own study).
The comparative analysis even allowed us to capture these perceived differences in the form of a diagram based on the relationship between two opposing vectors: the internal orientation of ethnopedagogy in Kazakhstan and the external orientation in Poland (Fig. 15). This insufficiency may lead to a rather superficial conclusion about the low usefulness of Kazakh research results for inclusive education, especially in Poland. However, a deeper analysis allows us to uphold the thesis about the need to simultaneously develop internal ethnopedagogical competences (cultural self-awareness) and knowledge of the Other/Stranger. In the case of ethnic differences between many different groups making up the same nation, this will mainly be the concept of the Other (confirmation of separateness), while in the case of an encounter with an external Other (a migrant, an expatriate, or even a representative of a national minority), the concept of Foreignness may be activated. Although in multicultural pedagogy, the Other and the Foreign are sometimes semantic equivalents, they are not equivalent. In Poland, the exploration of the situation of encountering and coexisting with the Foreign therefore takes on particular significance.
In Polish research in 2003 and 2004, interesting analyses and studies by Elżbieta Chromiec were published on this topic in a book entitled Dziecko wobec obcości kulturowej (2004). The author places her research in the context of children's encounters and accumulation of personal experiences in meeting a person identified as a stranger (a meeting between students and a foreigner initiated by a teacher). Based on her observations and the students' statements, Chromiec gathered a wealth of material that became the basis for her theory (partly) grounded in the form of a model of the evolution of attitudes towards the Stranger. It is worth recalling this interesting concept, as it seems to have been somewhat forgotten today, and in our opinion it has great potential for multicultural and transcultural education, as well as for ethnopedagogy and special education (Podgórska-Jachnik, 2007a, 2009a), including inclusive education. Its advantage is that it captures the dynamics of a multiphase process in the complexity of emotional and cognitive components, as well as complementary images: the Other, constructed in relation to knowledge about oneself, and the image of oneself, constructed in relation to the knowledge acquired about the Other in the course of getting to know them. It is therefore a dialectical process that seems to combine into an axiological and epistemological whole what was referred to earlier in this book as the external and internal aspects of ethnopedagogy. 
So how does one's attitude toward the Other develop? This is illustrated in Figure 16.
Figure 16. The formation of attitudes towards the Other/Foreign according to Elżbieta Chromiec's theoretical concept. (source: own study, based on Chromiec, 2004; Podgórska-Jachnik, 2007a, 2009a).
The successive stages of the formation of attitudes towards the Other are shown in the form of a cascade of arrows representing possible choices, by analogy with water flowing from a drawn dome, turning into a cascade when it encounters turning points. Theoretically, it can reach any place at the bottom, but in practice, the direction taken at earlier turning points determines further differences. The initial impulse may be internal or external, related to previous or current experience. The very identification of the Other (realizing foreignness, otherness, difference) can, as a result of the interaction of these experiences, elicit a reaction of interest or surprise. At the same time, the former (surprise) has a certain negative connotation (the discomfort of being unprepared for the encounter), while the latter (curiosity) has a positive connotation (it motivates us to learn). There is also the option of a neutral observation of the existence of differences. Ambivalence means that the initial surprise can turn into anxiety, and curiosity into curiosity. A neutral observation of differences allows us to examine (analyze) these differences. 
The initial impulse, reinforced and preliminarily directed through the filter of these three feelings, moves to the level of emotions, which can only be positive or negative, with varying intensity: there are no neutral emotions. This is an important moment of initial polarization, which, as can be seen in Figure 16, cannot always be redirected to the other pole in the course of educational activities. While this is possible in the case of less intense emotions (acceptance – a positive emotion; or negation – a negative emotion), extreme emotions (sympathy or antipathy) will lead to equally or even more polarized attitudes. Attitudes constitute the deepest, third level of attitude towards the Other, the most entrenched, but also the most diverse in terms of quality (as many as five different attitudes). Less intense emotions, combining a tendency to maintain contact with a simultaneous need to keep a safe distance, form the basis of a centrally located attitude of tolerance. This is related to a more general desire for coherence, which in this case can be explained by the need for comprehensibility and predictability of the world, and thus for testing certain hypotheses about the Other. In the absence of both knowledge and self-knowledge (a set enabling effective comparisons), stronger vectors of approach and distance come into play. This could be called the positive and negative poles, but this is too much of a simplification and, at the same time, a certain trap in relations with the Other. Attitudes directed towards the external poles, with a tendency to maintain contact, take the form of solidarity or fascination, and with a tendency to avoid contact, take the form of chauvinism and xenophobia. Solidarity, as a moderate pursuit of the Other, is defined as "a sense of community and shared responsibility resulting from a convergence of views and aspirations." (Słownik Języka Polskiego, https://sjp.pwn.pl/sjp/solidarnosc;2575796.html , [accessed: 12.07.2025]). The meaning of this word also includes a sense of shared responsibility, cooperation, and support for someone. 
Chauvinism in everyday usage has a decidedly pejorative meaning (calling someone a chauvinist is treated as an epithet). In Elżbieta Chromiec's classification, it can be a moderately distancing attitude, certainly marking a boundary and separating "us" from "them." In dictionary terms, it can be "an attitude characterized by intolerance and the granting of a privileged position to one's own gender, race, or group," but it can also be "extreme nationalism expressed in an uncritical attitude toward one's own nation and in contempt and hatred toward other nations ." (Słownik Języka Polskiego, https://sjp.pwn.pl/slowniki/szowinizm.html , [accessed: 12.07.2025]). However, what is common at the cognitive level with the attitude of solidarity is the need to learn about both Foreignness and Familiarity – without this, there can be no effective comparisons, which are then assigned emotional value. This can already be a threat to relationships, as it brings us closer to extreme attitudes on the Chromiec continuum: chauvinism, in which negation is reinforced by antipathy, leads to xenophobia. The Great Dictionary of the Polish Language (2018) defines this attitude as "aversion or hostility towards people of other nationalities and cultures and towards everything associated with such people" ( https://wsjp.pl/haslo/podglad/82806/xenophobia , [accessed: 2.06.2025]), which reveals many emotions, but also cognitive narrowing (sometimes even an aversion to learning in order to avoid unpleasant cognitive dissonance), probably resulting from the assimilation of negative stereotypes. 
It is necessary to build cognitive and emotional resources in this area in parallel. The PWN Online Dictionary of the Polish Language (1997-2025) defines the social meaning of the word tolerance (derived from the Latin tolerantia – patience, perseverance) as "respect for someone's views, beliefs, and preferences that differ from one's own." ( https://sjp.pwn.pl/sjp/tolerancja;2529924.html , accessed: 12.06.2025]. The definition emphasizes the difference – the otherness, the strangeness of these views, beliefs, and preferences.

The pace of the classes was lively, and the presentation and communication were informal – it did not resemble a lecture or structured compulsory classes. The expected effect of arousing curiosity and openness to comparisons was certainly achieved. It was only against this introductory background that the results of Karylgash Kazhimova's (2024) research were presented, initiating a discussion focused on three questions:
What do you know about Kazakhstan and the Kazakhs?  To what extent are your ideas about Kazakhstan reflected in the presented materials?
What reflections do the presented results of research on the shaping of professional values of Kazakh students based on ethnopedagogical education evoke?
How do you see the possibilities of using the knowledge gained for the purposes of inclusive education ?
Below are the most important statements and conclusions obtained from the participants of the classes. 
The classes aroused great interest among students, as they considered the lecturer's internship in Kazakhstan to be "an unusual academic experience in an unusual geographical direction" (student 1, University of Łódź), and the very idea of an academic exchange with the university in Uralsk to be inspiring and valuable. Several people expressed the opinion that while it would never have occurred to them before to go on a student exchange to Kazakhstan, for example (they mainly considered European countries – the United Kingdom, Germany, Spain, Portugal, Austria, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, and the United States), they would now be willing to consider such a destination. Austria, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, and the USA), they would now be willing to consider such a destination. It is worth adding, however, that in the groups surveyed, there was little real interest in any longer stays abroad (Erasmus+ scholarships cover at least one semester of study for students). 
After the workshops, some people expressed their regret that they had never really thought about this way of gaining student experience, that "now they are unlikely to do so" (student 1, UKW), especially since many of them are already combining their studies with paid work in their second degree. They felt that universities did not encourage this type of activity enough from the very beginning of their studies. An additional limitation is the anticipated language barrier. The presence of guests from abroad on scholarship programs is for them "an interesting attraction that opens up other worlds" (student 2, University of Łódź), as well as "a model of courage, because it is a journey into the unknown and into completely different cultural conditions" (student 3, UKW). An additional reinforcement of the idea of going on an internship from Poland to Kazakhstan and vice versa was the fear caused by the war in Ukraine, which also geographically separates our countries, and "in uncertain times, being stuck somewhere far from home is a big risk" (student 1, University of Łódź).
When it came to knowledge about Kazakhstan and Kazakhs, the students admitted that "they imagined it completely differently, or did not imagine it at all" (student 1, University of Łódź). This means, most often, a lack of direct interest and asking questions about how people live there: "All in all, Asia is so distant that I don't think anyone would even think they could end up there. No one has ever asked me to think about it" (student 1, University of Łódź). Other students say:
I admit that my ideas are a bit like this map: somewhere beyond the Urals, it's just one big blur, an image of vast, empty spaces. I didn't even think about whether there were any cities there. It's so difficult to talk about it because it's as if I were some kind of limited person who isn't interested in anything, and that's not the case. I can say that my imagination doesn't work there anymore and I see this empty map (student 2, University of Łódź).
If I were to consider that for some reason I was going to Kazakhstan, I would rather think about what dangers might await me there, what threats I might face, whether I should get vaccinated against any diseases, what the hygiene situation is like there – I think those are the first things that come to mind (student 2, UKW).
For those who had some idea about Kazakhstan, history and the displacement of Poles played a major role:
For me, Kazakhstan was a country of exile, and when it comes to exile, I don't think anyone is sent there to live in luxury. So I associate it with difficult living conditions, a harsh climate, and winter. I was surprised that there aren't that many Poles in Kazakhstan now, and that there are so many different nationalities (student 2, University of Łódź).
I read a book about these exiles, how hard it was for them, how they searched for something in the steppe for fuel. I associated it with a train that took several days to travel. So it was empty, cold, far from home. When I saw the steppe full of tulips in this recording, it didn't fit at all. I don't think we really know what the steppe is. And it's beautiful, really. I'd like to see it someday (student 3, UKW).
Kazakhstan was a place of exile, some nuclear explosions. I associate it with the repatriation of some Polish families from Kazakhstan. I thought there were a lot of Poles there and that they needed help to return. I was a little surprised that it is such a beautiful country. All in all, I guess it can't be as bad there as it was during those exiles. I'm not really sure anymore (student 3, University of Łódź).
 
The students were surprised by both the size and level of development of the country in the materials presented: 
I think I imagined a different level of civilization, so I'm surprised that the houses, cities, universities, and restaurants are so normal. Actually, they're just like ours (student 6, UKW). 
What can I say, I'm a little ashamed that I imagined they still live in yurts or something similar. I guess I expected some poverty, or maybe not poverty, but something that must be different and comparable to Europe or Poland at least half a century ago. I was surprised by the smiling people in these photos (student 4, University of Łódź).
I knew it was a country with rich resources, they have many deposits, oil, but this Sovietization certainly limited them. Now they have a huge opportunity. Some of these indicators are impressive. It is a giant as a country – ninth in the world in terms of size. And it has potential (student 3, University of Łódź).
I actually admire them, because to get the country back on its feet so quickly after Sovietization, well, thank you. We also liberated ourselves, although we were not a Soviet republic, but communism was their doing, after all (student, 2, University of Łódź). 
The presentation of folk and contemporary culture aroused many positive emotions. Until then, the participants had no knowledge of folk costumes (one student mentioned something about a Kazakh hat, but could not describe what it looked like) and did not know any examples of Kazakh cuisine. They had heard something about kumis as a healthy milk drink. They were surprised by the great fondness for meat and feasting. They accepted many things with curiosity. Here are a few examples of their opinions:
I was surprised by turquoise as their national color. I can't say why, but it would never have occurred to me that this could be a national color. I don't know why, it's hard to say, but it surprised me. I really like their ornaments. Actually, I've seen them somewhere before, but I didn't know they were Kazakh patterns (student 5, University of Łódź).
They look so good in it! When they dance, they're like real Cossacks. Not bad! There's a lot of pride and strength in it – it's hard to even describe. I really like it (student 6, University of Łódź).
This Dimash is amazing! I hadn't heard of him, but he's so talented, such a voice. And he has fan clubs all over the world, and I didn't even know about it? Those hundred instrumentalists at the concert make an incredible impression, and that singing. He also looks great in that costume, he's handsome – if it's a folk costume, then I take my hat off to him (student 5, UKW)..
But what? Was that falcon or eagle you're holding alive? I've heard about those falcons in Dubai. In Kazakhstan too? Do they keep these birds like that? (student 6, University of Łódź).
The comparisons arose spontaneously, without additional guidance or suggestions. They concern various aspects – they are not imbued with a sense of superiority or inferiority. It is as if they were a model example of a "centripetal movement" – a movement towards openness in Chromiec's model:
Well, both we and they have this eagle in their coat of arms as a symbol. But I wouldn't even say it's an eagle, it looks completely different (student 7, University of Łódź).
We also had some Soviet times, although not as certain as they did. But in our country, too, parents or grandparents used to know Russian well. Now it's more like English (student 6, UKW).
When it comes to religion, we also have some Slavic roots; we had some kind of Światowid even before the baptism of Poland; totems, herbalism, it's like our Tengri. I think everyone finds it interesting to know where their faith comes from (student 4, University of Łódź).
Words expressing acceptance sound similar. It is still a fragile acceptance, due to the incidental, one-off nature of the classes, but the following statements contain words of acceptance (praise) and words of comparison. 
How cute are these kids? Children all over the world are probably the same! (student 8, University of Łódź)
Actually, they only differ a little in appearance, but they are basically the same students as us. They study and dress similarly. The girls are pretty. I wonder how they see us. (student 4, University of Łódź).
Did they make these speech therapy aids? It's a cool idea, because they're like Velcro. I don't know if I would put so much work into it, they're quite the workers, everything had to be laminated, oh dear. Although we also make similar aids ourselves. Maybe not exactly the same, but you can get inspired (student 7, UKW).
These costumes are beautiful! I think they're prettier than our folk costumes, because ours are kind of thick and clumsy, our aprons. And these girls look like princesses in these dresses and hats. The feathers are a little funny, but everything together is very pretty. And these men's vests – very interesting (student, 9, University of Łódź).
The students paid attention to the universities and the conditions of study, although this did not arouse any particular interest, as no significant differences were really noticed in the material:
Well, normal schools, classes. The website has a slightly different aesthetic – you can immediately see that it's a slightly different world. Some classrooms may be a little lower – are they tall? There are a lot of students in the group, maybe it's a lecture, but overall I don't see anything different here from Polish universities. Projectors, laboratories, conference rooms – normal stuff. (student, UKW).
However, the most important part of our conversation was about the research project. Polish students formulated the following opinions about the results of the study:
Yes, I think I agree that it's important for teachers. I think I could choose similarly, it's hard to say because everything seems important. It's different when you have to choose (student 2, UKW).
I don't know if it's a question of a different country or more of age, that we are similar, I mean we are the same age, we are students. I am not surprised that the possibility of promotion is more important than money right now (student 1, University of Łódź).
When we talk about values, our values, I have the impression that we already come to college with them. There are subjects – ethics, theory of education, for example – but they talk about shaping values in children, in students, because we already have them. Such a subject can be useful because it's as if we were starting over, from ourselves, from our family, from our roots. But it all depends on how they teach it, because unfortunately, everything can be ruined. (student 8, University of Łódź).
However, the most controversy was caused by the hierarchy of values (remember that we did not examine it in this project for fear of artifacts resulting from the interpretation of possible differences). Comments indicating a lack of understanding of the choices made by students from Kazakhstan probably most strongly emphasize the differences in values (especially the low status of love). Here are some comments from Polish students:
I don't know why they are so afraid of this criticism. After all, young people have the right to make mistakes. Maybe it's not always pleasant, but everyone learns from their mistakes. There is no need to be afraid of criticism. (student 3, University of Łódź).
Did anything surprise me? Yes, that love is so low on their list. I am convinced that everyone here would say that love is the most important thing. Well, maybe sometimes something else might be second or third. But I don't understand that. Do they get married for love? (student 5, University of Łódź).
I also thought about love, that it's probably the only difference. Because we also differ from each other in other things. But in our country, maybe only a few people would choose love. (student 4, University of Łódź).
It's impossible for me to believe that only one in three people choose the values that we consider to be 100% the most important: love, health, and respect for other people. The other things may differ, but I just don't understand it, because for us it will always be in first place. I'd bet my life on it (student 2, University of Łódź).
I find it a bit strange that having fun is ranked so high, while other really important things are somewhere behind. I can understand this in teenagers, but students are adults. Money is last on their list, and fun is first. I guess there could be an explanation for this, because it's like, how should I put it – well, frivolous, frivolous, I guess. (student 7, University of Łódź)
I am surprised by this need for high status and ruling over people. It is much higher for them than health, love, and money, i.e., prosperity. Besides, I don't understand how you can choose ruling over others over the respect of others? Why do I need high status if there is no prosperity, no respect, and no love? (student 6, UKW)
We would like to quote one slightly longer statement in its entirety, as it very accurately diagnoses certain problems of coexistence in the differences that divide Poles and pose a real threat to cooperation and even national unity:
When you started talking about this nation, about patriotism, it sounded a bit artificial to me at first, that you could even devote an entire course to it at university. We had that in school, some lessons about patriotism, about the homeland. But there's no such thing at university, and I don't think we know how to use such words. We don't know how to talk about it. These are topics for children or for some inspired party members, some political parties. We don't talk about patriotism because it has become a political issue in Poland. We don't talk about political issues because everyone will immediately start arguing. That's the truth. When you started talking, I also thought that maybe we would get into politics, into political topics. And immediately it gets slippery. But as I listen, as I look at these materials, I don't know. I think it's a shame that we don't have such subjects. Well, we don't really have them. On the other hand, I don't know if we need a separate subject, another one. Do we need a separate subject from patriotism? I'm also a little afraid of that. I don't want anyone to shape me in their own way. (student 5, UKW).
Our students responded in different ways to the question: How do you see the possibilities of using the knowledge you have gained for the purposes of inclusive education? There were those who did not really see the connection, as the project did not really show the work of an inclusive teacher. At least not directly. Responses such as the following appeared. 
I don't know, I don't really see it. Well, maybe if there were some disabled children in this minority, then you would have to overcome two barriers. And now I'm thinking, by what means, and which one is easier to overcome (student 1, University of Łódź).
I know that different minorities face greater barriers. For example, there is a lot of talk about American schools in so-called colored neighborhoods. It's not the same here, and you didn't really show us how children from these ethnic minorities learn. That would be interesting. I think that such topics, about these children in their schools, should be added to this ethnopedagogy. For example, in their language lessons (student, 6 UKW).
Oh, it gave me a lot. I finally understood why people keep saying that every child may need support. But these examples are not as convincing as what we saw here (student 3, University of Łódź).
There were also very specific observations in the context of the role of a future or current teacher (as mentioned, some Polish students worked in schools or kindergartens). Interestingly, the students pointed out in their statements other groups of students who need support (they talked about children from Ukraine, communication barriers in autism, children of emigrants and expats (educated people coming or going  to work in specialist positions, for whom the terms emigrant or immigrant are not used). I will quote a few characteristic statements:
As speech therapists, we know a little about bilingualism, but obviously not about everyone. It's like an extra lesson in additional diversity in what we already know (student 3, UKW).
I'm just thinking about what else teachers in schools should learn and how to support these minority children. Does anyone use such ethnopedagogy with Roma children in Poland? I doubt it. Does anyone talk to them about their Roma roots? I was reminded of the film about Papusza, but does anyone show it to pedagogy students? And I think that's also ethnopedagogy (student 2, University of Łódź).
I think about children from the countryside, or rather young people from the countryside, when they commute to schools in the city. Are they proud to be closer to folk culture, to folklore? There's nothing to be ashamed of, but sometimes they are ashamed. They hide the fact that they are from the countryside. Or maybe they don't hide it, but we just don't know anything about each other. My mom comes from near Warsaw and she had this accent, like "pończochi" (stockings). She couldn't pronounce it any other way, and I was ashamed. Maybe it's not a full-fledged ethnic group, but it's still a dialect. No one taught me that I could or should be proud of it. Maybe some child is suffering? How many people speak dialect for fun? I sense a topic for inclusion here (student 9, University of Łódź).
Now I see these differences everywhere. Some people have a problem with it. Others don't. The point is to understand ourselves better and so that no one feels like they don't belong, like they're a stranger. If someone doesn't have a problem, that's fine, but if you do, they will learn to understand you, to see you better. Inclusive education is about understanding each other better. And ethnopedagogical education is basically for that too (student 7, UKW).
It reminds me of an assertiveness mantra: you're okay, I'm okay. I'm okay, you're okay. Inclusive education is about being able to say: you are okay. Ethnopedagogical education is about being able to say: I am okay. And I will say that the latter is not easier at all (student 5, UKW).
Many of these answers were very surprising to us. They surprised us with their accuracy, hitting the nail on the head. We will certainly remember the "OK definitions" of both areas of education for a long time. They are exceptionally accurate. It was these few reflections that convinced us of the correctness of the direction we had taken in our search. National, ethnic, and religious differences are an experience available to everyone. In our opinion, it is perfectly suited for discussing diversity, exclusion, and inclusion.

Conclusion

The content of this book is a kind of ethnopedagogical document of the exchange of views and mutual inspiration of an international Polish-Kazakh team, in the course of inter-university cooperation within the framework of academic exchange programs. As announced, it was not our ambition to create a textbook on ethnopedagogy or inclusive education – these two pedagogical subdisciplines, or rather research areas within pedagogical subdisciplines and at their interdisciplinary intersection with other subdisciplines, have already been covered in more complete and comprehensive studies. For example, ethnopedagogy as a separate science of development is discussed in Kazakhstan in the works of  Gennady N. Volkov (2000, 2002), who is frequently cited here,  and many other Kazakh ethnopedagogues (from Zharykbaev, Tuleubekova, Ashaevich,  Kizimova, Sadirmekova, and others to the more contemporary Slambekova and Buribekova). In Poland, it is primarily Jerzy Nikitorowicz, the "first Polish ethnopedagogical pen," and his entire series of monographs, which constitute a synthesis of the author's entire series of studies on multicultural and intercultural education (Nikitorowicz 2005, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2014, and 2018).  But it also includes (indirectly, without using the term ethnopedagogy) other researchers of multiculturalism, such as Dyczewski (1996), Korporowicz (1997), Gnitecki (2002), Chromiec (2004), Grzybowski (2007), Cudowska (2011) and others. We do not even attempt to compete with these studies. But we share our intercultural experience.
We have certainly learned a lot about ourselves as researchers from different countries. We have certainly experienced transversality and mutual influence on our pedagogical view of the world. Each of us has experienced fascination with the partner country: the Polish researcher with Kazakhstan, the Kazakh researcher with Poland. We have known each other for several years now. Each of us has spent several months in the partner country. This is both a short and a long time. It is too short to make general judgments; it is long enough to have enough experience to try to make sense of it. We have experienced "different ethnopedagogies" or "different faces" of the same ethnopedagogy. We are leaving this project more sensitive and more open to all differences. We leave with gratitude for the times in which, as academic researchers, we can easily obtain funding for scientific trips to distant countries. Distant, but now very close. We are grateful to the Bolashak International Programs Center, to the Ministry of National Education of Kazakhstan for creating such opportunities for us, and to the authorities of our universities for allowing us to organize such trips. This is our most valuable trans experience, which will continue to pay dividends in our future scientific endeavors for a long time to come.
The implementation of the project provided us with many mutual inspirations – and in this formulation, we emphasize the word "mutual" above all. At the beginning of our joint work, we probably imagined its course, and perhaps also the final result, a little differently. For us as authors, it was probably the most specific "research in action" – with a marked starting point and reason, with a set direction and goal, but a path full of additional question marks and turning points, a path of hermeneutic surprises and hermeneutic "aha!" discoveries, a path full of discursive discoveries in our work on this book – and not only on this book. This is not and was never intended to be research using comparative methodology, although comparison accompanied us throughout. 
Our work is not over – we are just getting started. During the course of our work, new ideas emerged on how to plan and implement this type of inter-university, international, and intercultural projects. These are valuable experiences that may one day result in the continuation of joint research. In search of the best summary, we will use a quote from the research that we did not include in the previous subsection – we left it for the end. We agree with our Polish student, who best expressed what we ourselves feel after the completion of this project 
After the introductory classes and research, I expected more Kazakh folklore and more of what I associate with inclusive education. What these classes and knowledge about this research have given me is that I will never again think of inclusive education as the education of children from a list of those selected for support (disability, etc.). This research does not explicitly mention inclusive education, but it makes you think inclusively, and you immediately associate it with all the diversities that exist and may exist in the classroom. They work somewhere in a different layer of thinking about inclusion. (student 5, University of Łódź).

What is an acmeogram and how is it used to support professional development?
ACME/AKME – comes from the Greek word akmē, meaning "peak," "highest point." Metaphorically, in supporting human development on the path of life, including supporting professional development, it can mean "the peak of excellence," the culmination of power, agency, and competence; the point at which someone becomes the best, reaches the highest level of their abilities.
AKMEOLOGY – is the science of adult development throughout life, in pursuit of the state/states of acme (Boganov and Zazykin, 2000; Kuzmina, 2001). It is a source of knowledge about human professional development, based on a holistic approach and the idea of subjective synergy between three basic spheres of human activity: cognition, action (work), and interpersonal communication (Ronginska, 2015). It is recognized as a modern science with educational applications, integrating psychological and pedagogical knowledge to optimize human development paths (Pautova and Zharinova, 2021). 
Acmeology studies a world in which individuals with varying degrees of professionalism, from outstanding to average, function, attempting to determine at what point the professional and life culminations of individuals with different levels of professional preparation intersect. (Kuzmina and Derkach, 1994, as cited in: Ronginska, 2015, p. 27).
The creator of this science was Nikolai A. Rybnikov, a psychologist at Moscow University (1920, 1923, as cited in: Ronginska, 2015). The science is developing primarily in Russia and Russian-speaking countries, but despite being nearly 100 years old, it only gained popularity in the early 1990s, after the collapse of the Soviet Union. Its development was linked to the search for a new framework for understanding a world detached from previous ideological entanglements. Currently, acmeology is a popular subject in academic education in Kazakhstan as well. As part of this subject, pedagogy students learn the principles and techniques of managing their own professional development in the process of becoming professionals and striving for developmental culmination. An acmeologist supports adults in the implementation of their professional development plans . Acmeological work can be compared to a form of career counseling or coaching, focused primarily on the development of creativity in the performance of professional tasks:
In the acmeological approach, future teachers will be the central element of the pedagogical creativity system, with a creative component reflecting the ability to engage in effective creative activity. Creating creativity is one of the main goals of shaping the pedagogical creativity of future teachers based on the acmeological approach. As we know, innovative thinking is one of the most important qualities of a future teacher. The creative component includes creative thinking, creative teaching, educational and research activities, the ability to innovate, rational solving of pedagogical tasks, the ability to independently design activities and create intellectual situations that allow them to solve professional and creative tasks. (Muhmudova, 2020, p. 464).
In contemporary Russian acmeology, acmeograms are used for several purposes. Among other things, they are used for:
researching professionalism and its basic characteristics;
analyzing the relationship between professionalism and human health;
developing technologies for the prevention of professional deformation;
providing acmeological support to people on their life and career paths;
developing programs for training specialists in various professions;
forecasting the professional future (career) of employees;
strengthening awareness of one's own influence on the choice of profession; 
developing practical techniques for achieving professional mastery (Ronginska, 2015).
AKMEOGRAM – is the main method used in acmeology. It graphically reproduces an individualized system of requirements, conditions, and factors that enable the gradual development and professionalism of an individual. It represents an individual's profile, enabling the effective identification of their capabilities and prospects, strengths and weaknesses. It allows for the determination of realistic conditions for the development and improvement of creativity in one's profession and the achievement of professional success (Muhmudova, 2020). 
As a basic acmeological technique, it is used for professional research and setting the optimal path for professional development. It is:
a comprehensive description of a person's career path in a specific profession, which includes indicators of professional suitability and personality traits relevant to the profession, determining the likelihood of success in the chosen profession. (...) It is based on a holistic, systemic approach to forecasting the effectiveness of a specialist's work in a given field, allowing the detection of potential opportunities and limitations of an individual on the path to acme. (Ronginska, 2015).

Appendix No. 8
Motivation for professional activity (methodology by K. Zamfir, modified by A. Rean) 
(source: Metodika izucheniya motivatsii professional'noy deyatel'nosti Zamfir (br.), А. Я. Psikhologiya, https://azps.ru/tests/tests2_zamfir.html – own translation)
This methodology can be used to diagnose motivation for professional activity, including motivation for professional and pedagogical activity. It is based on the concept of internal and external motivation.
Let us recall that internal motivation refers to the perceived value of a given person in the activity itself. However, if the motivation for professional activity is based on the desire to satisfy other needs external to the activity itself (motives of social prestige, remuneration, etc.), then it is customary to speak of external motivation. External motivations are distinguished here as external positive and external negative. External positive motivations are undoubtedly more effective and desirable from every perspective than external negative motivations.
PROCESSING
The indicators of internal motivation (IM), external positive motivation (EPM), and external negative motivation (ENM) are calculated according to the following formulas:
IM = (result from item 6 + result from item 7) / 2
EPM = (score from item 1 + score from item 2 + score from item 5) / 3
ENM = (score from item 3 + score from item 4) / 2
The intensity of each type of motivation will be measured using a number from 1 to 5 (including fractional values).
INTERPRETATION
Based on the results obtained, an individual motivational complex is determined. The motivational complex represents the type of relationship between the three types of motivation: IM, EPM, and ENM.
The following two combinations should be considered the best, optimal motivational complexes:
IM > EPM > ENM and IM = EPM > ENM
The worst motivational complex (...) can be presented as follows:
ENM > EPM > IM
Between these complexes there are other motivational complexes that are intermediate in terms of effectiveness.
When interpreting, one should take into account not only the type of motivational complex, but also the degree to which one type of motivation is more pronounced than another (...)
According to our data, job satisfaction significantly correlates with the optimality of a teacher's motivational complex (positive and significant correlation, r = +0.409). In other words, the more optimal the teacher's motivational complex is, the higher their satisfaction with their chosen profession: a high proportion of internal and external positive motivation and a low proportion of external negative motivation.
In addition, we also found a negative correlation between the optimality of the motivational complex and the level of emotional instability of the teacher's personality (significant correlation, r = -0.585).
The more optimal the motivational structure, the more the teacher's activity is motivated by the content of the teaching activity itself and the desire to achieve specific positive results, and the lower the emotional instability. Conversely, the more the teacher's activity is driven by motives of avoidance, blame, and the desire to avoid embarrassment (which begin to outweigh motives related to the value of the teaching activity itself, as well as external positive motivation), the higher the level of emotional instability.

ЭВМ-ге арналған бағдарламаның атауы: Электронды оқулық «Элементар математика»

Құрылған күні: 12.12.2025 ж.
Қолдану саласы: Білім саласы
Мақсаты: «Элементар математика» пәнінен электронды оқулықты пайдалану.
Орнатылатын бағдарламаның көлемі (самораспаковывающийся архив): 23 Мб, Компьютерге орнатқаннан кейін белгішесі бар бағдарламаның көлемі: 23,7 Мб.
Функционалдық мүмкіндігі: 
Бұл электрондық оқулық алгебра курсының мазмұнын тереңірек меңгертуге, логикалық ойлауды дамытуға және математикалық тілде өз ойын сауатты жеткізуге бағытталған. Оқу материалы теория мен практиканың үйлесімі сақтала отырып берілген: негізгі ұғымдар түсіндіріліп, артынан мысалдар мен жаттығулар ұсынылады. Әр бөлімнің басында күтілетін нәтижелер “Бөлімді оқып-білу арқылы…” форматында нақты көрсетіледі (мысалы, екі айнымалысы бар теңдеудің анықтамасын білу, шешімін табу, графигін салу, геометриялық мағынасын түсіну, y=kx+b түріндегі түзу теңдеуін қолдану).  Комбинаторика бөлімі де осы тәсілмен беріліп, қосу/көбейту ережелері, орналастыру, алмастыру, теру және Ньютон биномын қолдану дағдылары күшейтіледі.  
Оқулықта білімді бекіту үшін “Бекіту сұрақтары” енгізілген (тақырыпты түсінгенін тексеруге арналған сұрақтар).  Сонымен бірге есептер жүйелі түрде беріліп, тапсырмалар деңгейлер бойынша (A, B, C) топтастырылғаны байқалады — бұл оқушының қабілетіне қарай ілгерілеуіне ыңғайлы. Мәтінді есептерді теңдеулер жүйесі арқылы шешуде математикалық модель құру дағдыларын дамытуға ерекше назар аударылған. Теориялық бөлімдерде анықтама → түсіндіру → формула шығару → мысал шешуі → есептер логикасы сақталады (мысалы, арифметикалық прогрессияның n-мүшесінің формуласын шығару, кейін мысалын шешу және “ЕСЕПТЕР” беру). Оқулықта координаталық жазықтықта графикпен түсіндіру, геометриялық мағына беру кең қолданылған (жарты жазықтық, дөңгелек сияқты бейнелер; суреттерге сілтеме бар). Жалпы алғанда, авторлардың мақсаты — оқушының өздігінен ізденуіне, дәлелдеуге, талдауға және математиканы өмірлік жағдайларда қолдануға дағдылануына жағдай жасау, ал мұғалімге әдістемелік қолдау көрсету.

Введение
Современное общество уделяет большое внимание организации досуга, удобству покупки продуктов питания и готовых блюд. Интернет-рестораны и службы доставки становятся популярными благодаря возможности быстро и удобно заказать еду, не выходя из дома. С ростом числа клиентов, заказов и ассортимента блюд возникает необходимость систематизации процессов управления рестораном, включая ведение меню, учет заказов, работу с клиентами, оплату и доставку.
Ручное ведение этих процессов с использованием бумажных журналов или простых электронных таблиц становится неэффективным, приводит к ошибкам, дублированию данных и потере времени. В связи с этим разработка автоматизированной информационной системы является актуальной задачей. Такая система позволит повысить эффективность работы ресторана, упростить взаимодействие с клиентами и персоналом, а также обеспечить точность учета финансовых операций.
Цель работы: разработка автоматизированной информационной системы для интернет-ресторана, обеспечивающей централизованное хранение данных, удобное управление заказами, меню и доставкой, а также формирование аналитических отчётов.
Задачи:
Разработка базы данных для хранения информации о клиентах, заказах, блюдах, доставке и оплате.
Проектирование и реализация пользовательского интерфейса.
Создание приложения на C# с возможностью CRUD операций и формирования отчётов.
Объект исследования: Интернет-ресторан и процессы онлайн-заказов.
Предмет исследования: Программная реализация автоматизированной системы управления интернет-рестораном.

1 АНАЛИЗ И ФОРМИРОВАНИЕ ТРЕБОВАНИЙ К СИСТЕМЕ
1.1 Цели и назначение системы
Информационная система (ИС) «ERAFOOD» представляет собой специализированное программное решение, предназначенное для автоматизации деятельности предприятий общественного питания и служб доставки. В условиях высокой конкуренции на рынке FoodTech, ресторан сталкивается с необходимостью оперативного управления меню, заказами и лояльностью клиентов.
Основной целью разработки является создание единого информационного пространства для учета ассортимента блюд, контроля финансовых операций и оптимизации взаимодействия между персоналом и клиентами.
Система решает ряд критических задач, разделенных на функциональные блоки:
Блок «Управление меню»: регистрация новых позиций, классификация блюд по категориям (Паста, Пицца, Стейки) и мониторинг актуальных цен.
Блок «Клиентский сервис»: формирование корзины заказов, автоматический расчет стоимости и управление бонусной системой (лояльность).
Блок «Администрирование и персонал»: ведение базы данных сотрудников, управление их ролями и правами доступа.
Назначение системы заключается в минимизации ошибок при приеме заказов, обеспечении прозрачности учета выручки и предоставлении руководству актуальных данных для управления ассортиментом.

Сфера ответственности: Оформление заказов.

1.3 Анализ бизнес-процессов предметной области
Для эффективного проектирования системы был проведен детальный анализ жизненного цикла продуктов питания и готовых блюд в интернет-ресторане «ERAFOOD». Были выделены следующие ключевые бизнес-процессы:
Процесс управления ассортиментом и запасами: Данный процесс инициируется администратором на основе анализа популярности блюд или остатков ингредиентов на складе. В системе фиксируется поступление новых позиций меню или расходных материалов от поставщиков. При получении товара количество единиц в базе данных обновляется автоматически, что позволяет избежать ситуации «отсутствия блюда в наличии» при заказе клиентом.
Процесс обработки и выполнения заказа: Основной процесс, начинающийся с формирования корзины клиентом. После подтверждения заказа в системе создается запись со статусом «Принят». По мере готовности блюда повар меняет статус на «Готовится», а затем на «Передан курьеру». Цветовая индикация в панели администратора позволяет отслеживать заказы, которые задерживаются: если время ожидания превышает 45 минут, запись подсвечивается красным цветом.
Процесс лояльности и работы с клиентами: Система автоматически анализирует историю покупок. После каждого завершенного заказа клиенту начисляются бонусы (5% от суммы). Этот процесс исключает ручной подсчет скидок. Заявки на обратную связь или жалобы проходят стадии: «Новая» -> «В обработке» -> «Решена».

2.2 Проектирование базы данных
Проектирование базы данных для информационной системы интернет-ресторана «ERAFOOD» выполнялось с целью создания надежной структуры хранения данных, которая исключает избыточность (дублирование) и обеспечивает высокую скорость обработки запросов при ведении учета блюд, формировании заказов, фиксации оплат и управлении персоналом.
Логическая модель базы данных
Логическая модель АИС «Интернет-ресторан» была разработана в специализированном CASE-средстве проектирования ERwin Data Modeler. Модель приведена к третьей нормальной форме (3НФ). Это гарантирует, что каждый неключевой атрибут таблицы зависит только от первичного ключа, что предотвращает аномалии при вставке, обновлении или удалении данных о меню, клиентах, сотрудниках и транзакциях.
Перечень сущностей, атрибутов и связей
На основе разработанной EER-диаграммы, структура базы данных включает следующие ключевые сущности:
Роли (Roles): справочник уровней доступа пользователей к системе (Администратор, Клиент).
Атрибуты: RoleID (PK), RoleName.
Пользователи (Users): учетные записи для авторизации в системе.
Атрибуты: UserID (PK), Login, Password, RoleID (FK).
Меню (FoodItems): перечень блюд, доступных для заказа в ресторане.
Атрибуты: FoodID (PK), Name, Description, Price, ImagePath.
Сотрудники (Staff): данные о персонале интернет-ресторана.
Атрибуты: StaffID (PK), FullName, Position.
Клиенты (Clients): информация о зарегистрированных покупателях и их бонусах.
Атрибуты: ClientID (PK), FullName, Phone, Bonuses.
Заказы (Orders): сведения о совершенных покупках.
Атрибуты: OrderID (PK), ClientID (FK), OrderDate, TotalSum, Status.
Детали заказа (OrderDetails): таблица для связи заказов с конкретными блюдами (состав заказа).
Атрибуты: DetailID (PK), OrderID (FK), FoodID (FK), Quantity.
История бонусов (BonusLog): журнал начисления и списания баллов лояльности.
Атрибуты: LogID (PK), ClientID (FK), ChangeAmount, Date.
Описание связей в системе
В спроектированной модели реализованы следующие типы связей, обеспечивающие целостность данных:
Связь «Роли — Пользователи» (1:N): одной роли (например, «Администратор») может соответствовать множество учетных записей, но каждый пользователь наделен строго одной ролью.
Связь «Клиенты — Заказы» (1:N): один клиент может совершать неограниченное количество заказов за все время использования системы.
Связь «Заказы — Детали заказа» (1:N): один заказ может включать в себя несколько позиций из меню (детализация состава заказа).
Связь «Меню — Детали заказа» (1:N): одно и то же блюдо может фигурировать в составе множества различных заказов.
Связь «Клиенты — История бонусов» (1:N): для каждого клиента ведется детальный лог всех изменений его бонусного баланса.

3.1 Архитектура программно-аппаратного комплекса
Разработанная АИС «ERAFOOD» представляет собой современное десктопное приложение, построенное по классической двухзвенной архитектуре «клиент — сервер базы данных». В рамках данной модели клиентская часть, реализованная на платформе WPF, отвечает за логику интерфейса (меню, корзина, кабинет), обработку событий и визуализацию данных. Серверная часть, базирующаяся на СУБД MS SQL Server, обеспечивает надежное хранение информации о заказах, блюдах и пользователях, соблюдение ссылочной целостности и высокую скорость выполнения поисковых запросов.
Аппаратные средства: Для обеспечения стабильного функционирования системы на рабочих местах администратора и персонала ресторана требуется оборудование со следующими характеристиками:
Процессор: x64-разрядный с тактовой частотой от 2.0 ГГц (минимум 2 ядра) для плавной отрисовки графических элементов XAML.
Оперативная память: не менее 4 Гб (рекомендуется 8 Гб для быстрой обработки заказов и объемных списков меню).
Дисковое пространство: не менее 500 Мб для исполняемых файлов клиента и 2 Гб для локального экземпляра базы данных (SQL Express).
Монитор: разрешение не менее 1280x720. Широкоформатный монитор рекомендуется для комфортной работы с панелью управления заказами без использования горизонтальной прокрутки.
Системные и прикладные программные средства:
Среда разработки: Microsoft Visual Studio 2022, выбранная за мощный инструментарий отладки и интеграцию с дизайнерскими инструментами .NET.
СУБД: MS SQL Server 2019/2022. Использование данной СУБД гарантирует поддержку транзакций при оплате заказов и защиту персональных данных клиентов.
Проектирование: Редактор Figma использовался для создания UI-кита в розово-черных тонах, что позволило перенести дизайн в код с точностью до пикселя.
Требования к программной платформе:
ОС: Windows 10/11, обеспечивающая поддержку последних обновлений безопасности и графических библиотек DirectX для рендеринга WPF.
Среда выполнения: .NET Desktop Runtime 6.0 или выше.

Декларативный язык XAML: позволил отделить дизайн от бизнес-логики. Это обеспечило гибкую настройку стилей для карточек блюд в соответствии с макетом в Figma.
